units.title: IDENTITY AND BELONGING
units.theme: Who we are, where we feel at home, labels and roots

overview.intro: This unit is about the stories we tell about ourselves — where we come from, where we feel at home and which labels we accept or reject. At C2 the challenge is not to describe identity but to talk about it with precision: choosing the exact aspect that frames an experience as settled or provisional, using past forms to soften what could sound blunt, and bending ‘stative’ verbs to describe behaviour and change.
goals: Choose perfect and continuous forms deliberately to signal permanence, temporariness, incompleteness or attitude.
Use past tenses and past continuous forms to create politeness and social distance in requests and suggestions.
Use stative verbs dynamically (be being, have, see, think, feel) and explain the change in meaning.
overview.outcome: By the end you can give a two-minute talk on what ‘home’ means to you, shading your story with aspect, make a delicate request with distancing past forms, and write a magazine article on belonging at C2 standard.

vocab.def: the feeling of being accepted as a natural member of a group or place.
vocab.use: Collocates with verbs of creating and losing: foster, cultivate, erode. It is a key phrase in sociology and education writing, so it works in essays as well as conversation.
examples: Volunteering gave her a sense of belonging that her job never had.
Rapid gentrification can erode residents’ sense of belonging almost overnight.
vocab.colloc: foster a sense of belonging · a deep / strong sense of belonging · lose your sense of belonging

vocab.def: uncomfortable because you are in a situation or place that is completely unfamiliar.
vocab.use: Usually with ‘feel’: ‘I felt like a fish out of water.’ It describes a temporary mismatch between person and setting, not a personality trait.
examples: At my first academic conference I felt like a fish out of water among all the professors.
Raised on a farm, he was a fish out of water in the city’s financial district.
vocab.colloc: feel like a fish out of water · be a bit of a fish out of water

vocab.def: having no settled home or no strong ties to a place or community.
vocab.use: Mostly negative or melancholy in tone; compare ‘footloose’, which celebrates the same freedom. The noun is ‘rootlessness’.
examples: Years of moving between postings left the diplomat’s children feeling rootless.
The novel captures the rootlessness of a generation raised online.
vocab.colloc: a rootless existence · feel rootless · a sense of rootlessness

vocab.def: to settle in a place and start to feel that you belong there.
vocab.use: Implies a decision and a period of time; often in the present perfect or with ‘finally’. The opposite image is ‘to pull up stakes’ (to leave a place for good).
examples: After a decade of contracts abroad, they finally put down roots in Valencia.
It takes years to put down roots in a village where everyone’s grandparents knew each other.
vocab.colloc: put down roots somewhere · finally put down roots · never quite put down roots

vocab.term: to stick out like a sore thumb
vocab.def: to be very obviously different from everyone or everything around you.
vocab.use: Neutral to negative; it describes visibility, not exclusion. Formal equivalents: ‘to be conspicuous’, ‘to stand out’.
examples: In my bright yellow raincoat I stuck out like a sore thumb at the funeral.
A modernist glass cube would stick out like a sore thumb in the old town.
vocab.colloc: stick out like a sore thumb · rather stick out

vocab.term: to have a foot in both camps
vocab.def: to have a connection with two different groups, cultures or sides at the same time.
vocab.use: Often used about bicultural identity or divided loyalties. It can be positive (bridge-builder) or suggest you are not fully committed to either side.
examples: As the child of a Korean mother and a Chilean father, she has always had a foot in both camps.
Mediators are effective precisely because they have a foot in both camps.
vocab.colloc: have / keep a foot in both camps · with a foot in each camp

vocab.def: a person whose interests, attitudes or feelings are very similar to your own.
vocab.use: Warm and slightly literary. You ‘find’ or ‘recognise’ a kindred spirit; it suggests instant understanding rather than long friendship.
examples: In the back row of the choir she finally found a kindred spirit.
Reading his letters, I recognised a kindred spirit across two centuries.
vocab.colloc: find a kindred spirit · recognise a kindred spirit · kindred spirits

vocab.def: no longer satisfied with or loyal to a group, system or idea that you once supported.
vocab.use: Common in journalism about voters, young people and employees. Stronger than ‘dissatisfied’: it implies emotional withdrawal. Noun: ‘disaffection’.
examples: The party is struggling to win back disaffected voters in former industrial towns.
Disaffected teenagers often seek belonging in subcultures rather than institutions.
vocab.colloc: disaffected youth · disaffected voters · growing disaffection with

vocab.def: to refuse to accept any connection with someone or something, especially a relative or a past belief.
vocab.use: The prefix ‘dis-’ here reverses ‘own’ (acknowledge as yours). Compare ‘disavow’ (formal, for statements and beliefs) and ‘disinherit’ (legal, for property).
examples: His family threatened to disown him if he married outside the faith.
She has since disowned the nationalist views she held as a student.
vocab.colloc: disown a child · publicly disown · disown your past

vocab.def: modest; not wanting to draw attention to yourself or your abilities.
vocab.use: Always positive. Note that ‘assuming’ on its own is not used as an adjective in this sense — the word exists only in its negative form, like ‘unkempt’ and ‘uncouth’.
examples: Behind the unassuming shopfront is one of the best bakeries in the city.
For a Nobel laureate, she was remarkably unassuming.
vocab.colloc: an unassuming manner · quiet and unassuming · unassuming exterior

vocab.def: the quality of being an individual person with your own identity.
vocab.use: Academic and philosophical register. ‘-hood’ forms abstract nouns of state or condition (childhood, nationhood, personhood); use ‘identity’ in everyday speech.
examples: Adolescence is when a fragile sense of selfhood begins to take shape.
The essay explores how migration reshapes selfhood and memory.
vocab.colloc: a sense of selfhood · selfhood and identity · nationhood · personhood

vocab.def: the quality of being, or being seen as, different and foreign from the group you are measured against.
vocab.use: Common in cultural criticism. The focus is often on perception: people are ‘marked’ by otherness. Related verb: ‘to other someone’ (to treat them as fundamentally different).
examples: The film explores the otherness a refugee child feels in a new classroom.
Exaggerated accents in comedy can reinforce a sense of otherness.
vocab.colloc: a sense of otherness · cultural otherness · mark someone’s otherness

grammar.name: Aspect and nuance: perfect and continuous forms
grammar.short: Perfect looks back from a reference point; continuous frames an action as ongoing, temporary or charged.
grammar.rule: Tense locates an event in time; aspect shows how the speaker chooses to view it. The perfect connects an earlier event to a later reference point — now, a moment in the past or a moment in the future. The continuous presents an action as in progress, temporary, incomplete or emotionally coloured. At C2 the choice is rarely about right and wrong: it is about what you want your listener to infer.
form: Present perfect: have/has + past participle → I’ve lived here for a decade.
Present perfect continuous: have/has + been + -ing → I’ve been living out of a suitcase.
Past perfect continuous: had + been + -ing → She’d been feeling like an outsider for years.
Future perfect: will + have + past participle → By June I’ll have spent half my life abroad.
Attitude: be + always / forever + -ing → He’s forever reminding me where I’m from.
notes: Finished or unfinished: “I’ve read her memoir” suggests the book is finished; “I’ve been reading her memoir” suggests it isn’t, or that the reading explains something about now.
Settled or provisional: “I’ve lived in Lyon” sounds permanent; “I’ve been living in Lyon” frames the stay as temporary, even after several years.
Attitude: always / constantly / forever + continuous shows the speaker’s feeling, usually irritation and sometimes affection — “She’s forever correcting my accent.”
Result or activity: count results with the simple form (“I’ve written three chapters”) and describe the activity with the continuous (“I’ve been writing all morning”).
The past perfect is optional when the order of events is obvious, but essential when you tell events out of order or need a ‘before the past’ viewpoint.
examples: I’ve been feeling more at home here since I started volunteering.
By the time she applied for citizenship, she had been living in Canada for eleven years.
He’s always telling people he’s from nowhere, which isn’t strictly true.
grammar.watch: Don’t use the continuous to count completed events: say “I’ve visited the village four times”, not “I’ve been visiting the village four times”.
grammar.deep: Aspect is the grammar of point of view. The same facts can be packaged as a closed result (“I’ve moved house six times”), as an open activity with present consequences (“I’ve been moving around so much that I don’t know where to register to vote”) or as a habit that annoys the speaker (“My parents are always moving”). The perfect is fundamentally relational: it needs a reference point and says that something earlier matters at that point, which is why it combines naturally with ‘since’, ‘by the time’ and ‘already’. The continuous is fundamentally about boundaries: it removes the start and end from view, so the action feels unfinished, temporary or vivid. When the two combine, as in the perfect continuous, you get an activity seen from inside and connected to a later moment — the classic source of ‘evidence’ uses such as “You’ve been crying.” Proficient speakers exploit these contrasts constantly: a migrant who says “I’ve been living here twenty years” may be signalling that she still does not consider the arrangement final. The grammar quietly carries the emotional message.

chart.title: What each aspect adds
rows: I come from a mining town.
I’m staying with my aunt for now.
I’ve been trying to fit in.
activity up to a past point
I’d been feeling homesick, so I called.
In May I’ll have been living here ten years.

more: I’ve been meaning to visit my grandmother’s village for years, but something always gets in the way.
We had only just put down roots when the company transferred us again.
By the end of this year, I’ll have spent more time in Berlin than in my home town.
She’s been describing herself as ‘European first’ lately, which surprised her parents.
They’d been arguing about where to settle long before the baby arrived.
I’ve always felt like a bit of a fish out of water at family weddings.

fix.wrong: I’ve been living here since five years.
fix.right: I’ve been living here for five years.
fix.why: ‘For’ introduces a period; ‘since’ introduces a starting point (since 2020).

fix.wrong: I’ve been writing three articles about migration this month.
fix.right: I’ve written three articles about migration this month.
fix.why: A counted result normally takes the simple perfect; the continuous describes the activity, not the number.

fix.wrong: When I arrived, she already left.
fix.right: When I arrived, she had already left.
fix.why: ‘Already’ marks an event before another past event, so the past perfect is needed.

drill.name: Shade the same fact
drill.prompt: Say each fact about your own life in three ways — closed (perfect simple), open or provisional (perfect continuous) and irritated (always + continuous) — and explain what changes.
items: live in this city
try to learn my grandparents’ language
move house
explain where my surname comes from
think about going back

dialogue.line: How long have you lived in Edinburgh now?
I’ve been living here eight years — I still say ‘living’, you’ll notice.
As if you’re about to leave?
As if I’ve been waiting for permission to stay. Everyone back home keeps asking when I’m coming back.
And by the time you finally decide, you’ll have spent half your life here.

contrast.title: Same verb, different message
rows: finished result vs activity (and paint on my hands)
He’s always asking about my origins.
a past event vs visible evidence of an activity
I’ll have been working for ten hours by six.
completion vs duration at a future point
neutral vs more tentative and polite

grammar.sound: In fluent speech the perfect auxiliaries almost disappear: “I’ve been living” is /aɪv bɪn ˈlɪvɪŋ/, with ‘been’ reduced to /bɪn/. Stress falls on the main verb, so listen for the -ing ending rather than the auxiliaries.

grammar.name: Past tenses for distancing and politeness
grammar.short: Past forms that refer to the present or future, to make a request or suggestion less direct.
grammar.rule: English often uses a past form not to locate an action in the past but to create distance — between the speaker and the request, or between the speaker and the listener. ‘I was wondering if you could…’ refers to now, yet the past (and the continuous) make it sound tentative and easy to refuse. The further from ‘present simple’ a form is, the more polite and cautious it sounds.
form: Past simple: I wondered / Did you want…? → Did you want to sit by the window?
Past continuous: I was wondering / hoping / thinking + if / whether → I was wondering whether you’d be free on Friday.
Past perfect: I had hoped / intended / meant + to-infinitive → I had hoped to talk to you in person.
Just + past: I just wanted / thought + to-infinitive or clause → I just wanted to check you’re all right with this.
Modal distancing: would / could / might + base verb → Would you mind if I asked about your family?
notes: Degrees of tentativeness: “I wonder if…” → “I wondered if…” → “I was wondering if…” → “I was just wondering whether you might…” — each step adds distance.
Unfulfilled hope: the past perfect often implies the plan failed — “I had hoped to stay longer” means I didn’t.
The time reference is present or future: “Were you thinking of coming tonight?” asks about tonight, not the past.
Over-distancing sounds sarcastic or cold between close friends: “I was wondering whether you might pass the salt” can sound ironic at a family dinner.
In formal emails, distancing past forms pair well with conditionals: “I was wondering whether it would be possible to…”.
examples: I was wondering whether you’d be willing to tell me a little about your family history.
We were hoping you might join us for Lunar New Year at my parents’ place.
I had intended to ask you before booking, but it slipped my mind.
grammar.watch: After distancing past forms, keep the sequence: say “I was wondering if you could help”, not “I was wondering if you can help” in formal requests — ‘can’ sounds abrupt after the softened opening.
grammar.deep: The past tense in English carries a basic meaning of remoteness, and time is only one kind of remoteness. A past form can also signal distance from reality (the unreal past of ‘if I were you’ and ‘I wish I knew’) and distance from the listener, which is the politeness use. When we say “I wanted to ask you something”, we refer to a present wish but present it as if it belonged to a moment already gone, so the listener is not confronted with a raw demand. The continuous adds a second layer of softening, because it presents the wish as unfinished and provisional: “I was hoping…” sounds like a thought still being formed, which leaves room for refusal. The past perfect goes further and frequently implies that the hope has already been abandoned, which makes it ideal for regret and diplomatic complaint: “I had expected a reply by now.” At C2, the skill lies in calibration. Too little distance sounds brusque; too much, between equals or intimates, sounds cold or ironic. Proficient speakers move up and down this scale according to status, imposition and relationship.

chart.title: The politeness scale
rows: Can you tell me about your parents?
I wondered if you could tell me…
I was wondering whether you might tell me…
I had hoped you would tell me…
I was just wondering whether it would be possible to…

more: Did you want me to translate your grandmother’s letters, or would you rather do it yourself?
I was thinking we could visit the old neighbourhood while we’re in Naples.
I just thought I’d mention that the forms need to be in by Friday.
We had been hoping to hold the reunion in the village hall, but it has been sold.
I wondered whether you had ever considered writing your story down.
I was going to ask you whether you’d mind being interviewed for the project.

fix.wrong: I am wondering if you would helping me.
fix.right: I was wondering if you would help me.
fix.why: The distancing form is past continuous ‘was wondering’; after ‘would’ use the base verb.

fix.wrong: I had hoped to see you, and I saw you.
fix.right: I was hoping to see you, and here you are!
fix.why: ‘Had hoped’ implies the hope was not fulfilled; use ‘was hoping’ when it came true.

fix.wrong: I wanted to know where do you come from.
fix.right: I wanted to know where you come from.
fix.why: An embedded question keeps statement word order: no auxiliary inversion.

drill.name: Turn up the distance
drill.prompt: Make each blunt request three times, moving up the politeness scale. Then decide which version you would use with a close friend, a new colleague and an elderly stranger.
items: Tell me where your family is from.
Lend me your flat for the weekend.
Speak more slowly.
Change the date of the meeting.
Introduce me to your neighbours.

dialogue.line: Sorry to bother you — I was wondering if you had a minute.
Of course. What did you need?
I’m researching family names in the region, and I was hoping you might tell me where yours comes from.
Ah. I had always meant to look into that myself, but I never got round to it.
Then perhaps we could look into it together?

contrast.title: Real past or distancing past?
rows: I wondered about it all night.
I wondered if you could help.
I was looking for my keys when you called.
I had hoped to finish by now.
I had hoped to finish, but the power went off.

grammar.sound: Politeness is half intonation. “I was wondering…” usually starts high and falls gently, with a slight pause before the request; a flat or rising-falling contour on ‘wondering’ can make the phrase sound impatient or sarcastic.

grammar.name: Stative verbs used dynamically
grammar.short: ‘State’ verbs (be, have, think, see, feel) in the continuous to describe behaviour, process or a different meaning.
grammar.rule: Stative verbs describe states, feelings, possession and perception, so they normally resist the continuous. But many of them have a second, dynamic meaning, and some can be ‘stretched’ into the continuous to show that a state is temporary, developing or deliberately performed. ‘You are selfish’ describes character; ‘You’re being selfish’ describes behaviour now.
form: Behaviour now: be + being + adjective → You’re being unusually quiet tonight.
Change of meaning: be + -ing (have, see, think, weigh, taste, appear) → We’re seeing a counsellor about it.
Gradual change: be + -ing + more and more / increasingly → I’m understanding her culture more and more.
Tentative or emotional: be + -ing (hope, want, feel, wonder) → I’m wanting to spend more time with my roots these days.
Recent repeated experience: have / has + been + -ing (hear, feel) → I’ve been hearing a lot about your family.
notes: Meaning change: “I think she’s Basque” (opinion) vs “I’m thinking of moving to Bilbao” (considering); “I have two passports” (possession) vs “I’m having a crisis” (experience).
Be being: only with adjectives describing controllable behaviour — kind, rude, silly, difficult, stubborn. Never “He is being tall” or “She is being Spanish” (except as a joke about performance).
Perception: “This soup tastes of cumin” (quality) vs “I’m tasting the soup” (deliberate action); “I see your point” vs “I’m seeing the doctor at four”.
Gradual development: “I’m liking this city more every day” is widely used in speech for growing appreciation, but keep “I like this city” in formal writing.
‘Feel’ for physical or emotional condition works in both forms with little difference: “I feel / I’m feeling out of place here.”
examples: You’re being very diplomatic about your home town — what do you really think of it?
We’re thinking of applying for dual nationality.
I’m understanding more and more of my grandmother’s dialect each time I visit.
grammar.watch: Don’t use ‘being’ with fixed qualities: say “He is tall and very shy”, not “He is being tall”; but “He’s being shy” is fine if he is usually outgoing.
grammar.deep: The traditional list of ‘verbs not used in the continuous’ is a useful simplification that breaks down at higher levels. What matters is not the verb but the meaning in context. A verb is used statively when it describes something that simply holds — a property, a belief, a relationship, involuntary perception. It is used dynamically when it describes something that happens, can start and stop, and is often under the subject’s control. ‘Have’ means possession in “I have Irish ancestry” but activity in “We’re having a family reunion.” ‘Be’ is the most striking case: ‘be being’ converts a trait into a performance, which is why it so often carries judgement — “You’re being ridiculous.” A second family of dynamic uses expresses change in progress: “I’m forgetting my Portuguese”, “She’s resembling her mother more as she gets older.” Here the continuous shows a state still forming. Finally, the continuous with ‘want’, ‘hope’ and ‘wonder’ is a softener rather than an aspect choice, linking this point to the distancing grammar earlier in the unit. Proficient users choose the continuous to make a precise claim about how temporary, active or emotionally loaded a state is.

chart.title: Stative meaning vs dynamic meaning
rows: They’re weighing the pros and cons. (assessing)

more: I think of myself as Catalan, but lately I’m thinking more about what my Andalusian side means.
Stop it — you’re being deliberately provocative.
We’re having second thoughts about moving back.
The committee is still weighing whether to grant her residency.
I’ve been hearing wonderful things about your community choir.
He’s resembling his father more and more as he gets older.

fix.wrong: I’m knowing her since we were children.
fix.right: I’ve known her since we were children.
fix.why: ‘Know’ has no dynamic meaning here; with ‘since’ use the present perfect simple.

fix.wrong: She is being Irish.
fix.right: She is Irish.
fix.why: Nationality is a fixed state, not controllable behaviour, so ‘be being’ is not possible.

fix.wrong: I’m not agreeing with labels like that.
fix.right: I don’t agree with labels like that.
fix.why: ‘Agree’ expresses an opinion (a state) and stays in the simple form.

drill.name: Trait or performance?
drill.prompt: For each adjective, say one sentence about someone’s character (is) and one about their behaviour at a specific moment (is being). Add the context that explains the difference.
items: stubborn
polite
secretive
patriotic
unreasonable

dialogue.line: Why do you keep saying you’re ‘not really from anywhere’?
I’m not being evasive, honestly. I have three passports and no home town.
But you’re thinking of settling here?
We’re weighing it up. I’m liking the place more each month, which is new for me.

contrast.title: Simple or continuous with state verbs
rows: He’s being shy — he’s normally the life of the party.
I’m thinking about changing my surname.
She’s smelling the herbs to identify them.

grammar.sound: In ‘be being’, the two forms are easy to swallow: “You’re being” sounds like /jɔː ˈbiːɪŋ/, with stress on ‘being’ and on the adjective. Stressing ‘being’ strongly adds criticism: “You’re BEING difficult.”

speaking.text: Speak for two minutes on the question ‘Can a person truly belong to more than one place?’ Your prompt card suggests three ideas: language, family memory and official documents. You don’t have to use all three. Your partner then responds and asks one follow-up question.

Look at five possible images for a museum poster on migration: a suitcase, a passport stamp, a kitchen full of spices, a school photo, a front door. Discuss what each says about identity, then agree on which one would best represent belonging and which would be least effective. Use distancing forms to suggest and disagree (‘I was wondering whether…’, ‘I’d been thinking…’).

Do labels such as ‘expat’, ‘immigrant’, ‘local’ and ‘third-culture kid’ help or harm us? Discuss who uses each label, how it makes people feel and whether some people are labelled while others are not.

You are researching a local-history project. Approach an elderly neighbour (your partner) and persuade them to share memories of the neighbourhood, using a gradual politeness ladder. Your partner starts reluctant and gradually warms up.

tips: Choose aspect for the message, not just for time: ‘I’ve been living here’ quietly tells the listener you don’t yet consider the arrangement permanent.
Climb the politeness ladder gradually: ‘I wonder…’, ‘I was wondering…’, ‘I was just wondering whether it might be possible…’ — and come back down with close friends.
Use ‘be being’ only for behaviour people can control: ‘you’re being stubborn’, never ‘you’re being tall’ or ‘being Italian’.
In CPE Speaking Part 3, organise your two-minute long turn with a clear opening view, two developed points and a short conclusion; don’t just list the prompts.

quiz.q: I ___ whether you might be willing to talk about your family’s journey for our podcast.
quiz.explain: ‘I was wondering whether…’ is a distancing past continuous: it refers to now but makes the request more tentative and polite.

test.q: By next spring, she ___ in Oslo for a decade, though she still calls it temporary.
test.explain: Future perfect continuous: duration up to a future point, with the continuous reinforcing the ‘temporary’ framing.

test.q: ‘You ___ very evasive about your home town tonight,’ she said with a smile.
test.explain: ‘Be being + adjective’ describes behaviour at a particular moment rather than a permanent trait.

test.q: I ___ to visit the village before my grandfather died, but the trip kept being postponed.
test.explain: The past perfect ‘had hoped’ signals an unfulfilled plan.

test.q: Which sentence implies the speaker has NOT finished the book?
test.explain: The present perfect continuous presents the activity as ongoing and incomplete.

test.q: We ___ applying for dual citizenship, but we haven’t decided yet.
test.explain: ‘Think of / about + -ing’ in the continuous means ‘consider’, a dynamic meaning.

test.q: My brother ___ me that I’ve ‘lost my accent’. It drives me mad.
test.explain: ‘Forever / always + continuous’ expresses the speaker’s irritation at a repeated action.

test.q: After two years of moving between hostels, he longed to ___ somewhere.
test.explain: ‘To put down roots’ means to settle and start to belong somewhere.

test.q: At the gala, in my hiking boots, I stuck out like a ___.
test.explain: The fixed idiom is ‘to stick out like a sore thumb’.

test.q: Choose the word that completes the sentence: Adolescence is when a fragile sense of ___ begins to form.
test.explain: ‘-hood’ forms abstract nouns of state or condition: selfhood, childhood, nationhood.

test.q: ‘Behind its ___ façade, the museum holds an astonishing collection.’
test.explain: ‘Unassuming’ (modest, not showy) exists only in this negative form.

test.q: Polls suggest that ___ voters in the region feel no party represents them.
test.explain: ‘Disaffected’ = no longer loyal or satisfied; ‘unaffected’ means not influenced.

test.q: Which request is the MOST tentative?
options: I wonder if you could sign this.
I was just wondering whether you might be able to sign this.
test.explain: Past continuous + ‘just’ + ‘whether’ + ‘might be able to’ stacks several distancing devices.

dynamics.name: Aspect detectives
dynamics.how: Each pair receives six short statements by fictional migrants (e.g. ‘I’ve been living here twenty years’). They must say what each speaker implies through aspect alone — permanent, provisional, irritated, unfinished — then rewrite two statements to send the opposite message.
dynamics.payoff: Students discover that aspect carries attitude, not just time.

dynamics.name: The politeness ladder
dynamics.how: Groups get cards with requests of increasing imposition (borrow a pen → borrow a car → stay for a month). They build a five-step ladder of distancing forms on the board and assign each request a ‘rung’, justifying the choice by relationship and imposition.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the scale of distance visible and links grammar to social judgement.

dynamics.name: Being or is?
dynamics.how: The teacher acts out short scenes (sulking, being generous, being stubborn). Students describe the behaviour with ‘be being’, then contrast it with the person’s ‘real’ character in the simple form.
dynamics.payoff: A memorable, physical anchor for the trait vs performance contrast.

writing.title: Where is home?
writing.brief: An international magazine is running a series called ‘Where is home?’. Write an article in which you explore what makes a place feel like home, whether it is possible to belong to more than one place, and what is lost and gained when people move. Make your article engaging for a well-educated readership.
writing.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista internacional sobre qué hace que un lugar se sienta como un hogar y si se puede pertenecer a más de un sitio.
criteria: An engaging title and opening that draws the reader in, with a consistent, personal yet polished voice.
Deliberate aspect choices: at least two perfect continuous forms and one future perfect used to frame experience as provisional, ongoing or a milestone.
One stative verb used dynamically (being, having, thinking, seeing) and one distancing past form, used naturally.
Four items from the unit vocabulary (e.g. put down roots, a sense of belonging, rootless, a foot in both camps), with ideas developed rather than listed.
writing.model:
Home Is a Verb

For most of my adult life I have been answering one question badly. ‘Where are you from?’ sounds innocent enough, yet I have never found a reply that fits on a single breath. I was born in Montevideo, grew up in Toronto and have been living in Lisbon for the past nine years — and I still say ‘living’, as if the lease might be cancelled at any moment.

We tend to imagine home as a noun: a house, a city, a flag. My experience suggests it behaves more like a verb, something we do rather than something we have. A place starts to feel like home not when we arrive but when we start participating in it — when the woman at the bakery stops asking what I want and simply reaches for the rye loaf.

Can we belong to more than one place? People with a foot in both camps are often told they must choose, as though loyalty were a finite resource. I would argue the opposite. Every move I have made has added a layer rather than erased one. What is lost, admittedly, is the effortless belonging of childhood — the feeling of never having to explain yourself. I had hoped, when I first moved, that it would eventually return. It hasn’t, quite. Instead, I have been learning a different skill: the art of putting down roots on purpose.

Rootless people are sometimes accused of being restless or superficial, but I suspect many are simply being cautious, testing the ground before committing to it. By next spring I will have spent more years in Lisbon than anywhere else. Perhaps then I will drop the continuous and say, without hesitation, that I live here.

Until then, home remains something I am still doing — and, I am beginning to think, something none of us ever quite finishes.

homework.task: Write a 150-word paragraph about a move or change in your life three times: first neutrally, then framing the experience as temporary and unfinished (continuous and perfect continuous forms), then as complete and settled (simple and perfect forms). Underline every verb phrase and add a one-line note explaining how the reader’s impression changes. Finally, write a short, highly polite email asking a relative to share a family story, using at least three distancing past forms.

units.title: THE POWER OF WORDS

overview.intro: This unit is about how words move people — in speeches, headlines, advertisements and the endless scroll of social media. At C2 you need not only to understand persuasion but to use its tools yourself: shifting the focus of a sentence with clefts, fronting the information you want to stand out, and inverting after negative adverbials for rhetorical force. You will also learn to report what others say with precision, choosing between ‘insinuate’, ‘concede’ and ‘allege’ rather than settling for ‘say’.
goals: Use it-clefts and wh-clefts to control focus, correct a misunderstanding and build emphasis.
Front and invert elements of a sentence for contrast, cohesion and dramatic effect in formal writing and speeches.
Invert after negative and restrictive adverbials (never, not only, no sooner, only when, little) accurately and in the right register.
overview.outcome: By the end you can analyse the rhetoric of a short speech, deliver a persuasive one-minute statement using at least three emphatic structures, and write a CPE Part 1 essay that summarises and evaluates two texts on persuasion.

vocab.def: to suggest, indirectly and usually unpleasantly, that something bad is true.
vocab.use: A reporting verb that judges the speaker: you insinuate THAT… The suggestion is hidden, not stated. Compare ‘imply’ (neutral) and ‘allege’ (stated openly but unproven).
examples: Are you insinuating that I made the figures up?
The article insinuated that the senator had been bribed, without offering a shred of evidence.
vocab.colloc: insinuate that · darkly insinuate · an insinuation (noun) · a veiled insinuation

vocab.def: to admit, often reluctantly, that something is true or that you have lost.
vocab.use: Signals reluctance and is perfect for balanced argument: ‘While it must be conceded that…, …’. Also used for elections and matches: concede defeat.
examples: The minister conceded that the campaign had been misleading.
Critics concede the speech was brilliantly crafted, even if they reject its message.
vocab.colloc: concede that · grudgingly concede · concede a point · concede defeat

vocab.def: to state that someone has done something wrong, without having proved it.
vocab.use: Journalistic and legal. Often passive or adverbial to protect the writer: ‘It is alleged that…’, ‘the alleged fraud’, ‘He allegedly…’.
examples: The documentary alleges that the company knew about the risks for years.
She is alleged to have leaked the memo to a rival newspaper.
vocab.colloc: allege that · it is alleged that · the alleged victim · allegedly

vocab.def: to prove with evidence or argument that a statement or theory is wrong.
vocab.use: Strictly, ‘refute’ means to disprove, not merely to deny; many careful writers object to it as a synonym of ‘deny’. ‘Rebut’ means to argue against a claim, successful or not.
examples: The study convincingly refutes the claim that vaccines cause autism.
She denied the allegations but made no attempt to refute them.
vocab.colloc: refute a claim / an argument · conclusively refute · rebut an accusation

vocab.def: (of words or questions) containing hidden assumptions or strong emotional associations meant to influence people.
vocab.use: A loaded question presupposes something the listener may not accept (‘Why do you support censorship?’). Loaded language uses emotive words like ‘invasion’ or ‘handout’.
examples: ‘Have you stopped misleading voters?’ is a classic loaded question.
The report was criticised for its loaded language about migrants.
vocab.colloc: a loaded question · loaded language · a politically loaded term

vocab.def: a deliberately favourable interpretation of facts, especially by politicians or their advisers.
vocab.use: Disapproving. ‘Spin doctors’ put a positive spin on bad news. The verb is often used with ‘as’: they spun the defeat as a moral victory.
examples: No amount of spin could disguise the scale of the defeat.
The press office spun the job losses as ‘a streamlining of operations’.
vocab.colloc: put a positive spin on · a spin doctor · media spin · spin something as

vocab.def: to speak frankly and directly, even if it offends people.
vocab.use: Almost always negative in form: ‘She didn’t mince her words.’ Often used approvingly about honesty, or as a warning before criticism: ‘I won’t mince words.’
examples: The judge did not mince her words: the evidence had been ‘wilfully distorted’.
I won’t mince words — this campaign has been a disaster.
vocab.colloc: not mince words · not mince your words · without mincing words

vocab.def: to repeat what someone said in a way that changes its meaning.
vocab.use: A common accusation in interviews and debates: ‘You’re twisting my words.’ Related: ‘to take something out of context’.
examples: The interviewer twisted her words to make her sound heartless.
That’s not what I said — stop twisting my words.
vocab.colloc: twist someone’s words · take something out of context · quote selectively

vocab.def: not sincere, especially pretending to know less than you do or to be more innocent than you are.
vocab.use: A sophisticated, controlled way of accusing someone of dishonesty. Not the opposite of ‘ingenious’: compare ‘ingenuous’ (naively honest).
examples: It is disingenuous to claim the advert was ‘just a joke’.
His surprise at the backlash seemed somewhat disingenuous.
vocab.colloc: deeply disingenuous · it would be disingenuous to · a disingenuous claim

vocab.def: to say you support something without doing anything to help it.
vocab.use: Critical; very common in essays about politics and institutions. The object is an idea or value: lip service to equality, to free speech.
examples: Many platforms pay lip service to fact-checking while profiting from outrage.
The government paid lip service to transparency but published nothing.
vocab.colloc: pay lip service to an idea · mere lip service · more than lip service

vocab.def: a short, memorable phrase taken from a longer speech, designed for repetition in the media.
vocab.use: Often implies oversimplification: ‘politics reduced to sound bites’. Also spelled ‘soundbite’.
examples: The speech was crafted around three sound bites for the evening news.
Complex policy cannot be reduced to a sound bite.
vocab.colloc: a catchy sound bite · politics by sound bite · deliver a sound bite

vocab.def: to produce an emotional response because people recognise something true in what is said.
vocab.use: Positive and widely used in reviews and journalism. ‘Strike a false note’ is the opposite: to sound insincere.
examples: Her story about her father’s factory struck a chord with voters across the region.
The campaign’s message clearly struck a chord with young people.
vocab.colloc: strike a chord with someone · strike a false note · a responsive chord

grammar.name: Cleft sentences (it-clefts and wh-clefts)
grammar.short: Split one sentence into two clauses to put a spotlight on one element.
grammar.rule: A cleft sentence divides a single message into two parts so that one element is placed in focus. It-clefts (It was the tone that…) highlight new or contrasting information, often to correct someone. Wh-clefts (What persuaded them was…) delay the key information to the end, building expectation and treating the rest as shared knowledge.
form: It-cleft: It + be + focus + that / who + clause → It was the slogan that won the election.
Wh-cleft: What + clause + be + focus → What persuades people is repetition.
Reversed wh-cleft: focus + be + what + clause → Repetition is what persuades people.
Verb focus: What + subject + do + be + (to) + base verb → What the editor did was (to) cut the quote.
All-cleft: All + subject + verb + be + focus → All he did was repeat the question.
Noun heads: The reason / The thing / The place + clause + be + focus → The reason it worked is that it was short.
notes: Correcting: it-clefts are ideal for contrast — “It wasn’t the content that offended people; it was the tone.”
Time with it-clefts: “It was only when the transcript appeared that the truth emerged.” / “It wasn’t until 2016 that the term went mainstream.”
Verb as focus: a wh-cleft needs ‘do’ in the first part — “What she did was rewrite the speech”, and ‘to’ before the verb is optional.
Agreement: after a what-clause the verb is normally singular — “What we need is facts” — though a plural complement often attracts ‘are’ in speech: “What we need are facts.”
Who or that: in it-clefts with a person in focus, both are possible — “It was the intern who / that leaked it.” Use ‘that’ for things and for adverbials of time and place.
examples: It was the photograph, not the headline, that went viral.
What worries me is how quickly the rumour spread.
All the spokesperson did was repeat the official line.
grammar.watch: Don’t repeat the subject inside the clause: write “It was the minister who said it”, not “It was the minister who he said it”.
grammar.deep: Clefts are a tool of information management. English likes to begin a sentence with what the listener already knows and end with what is new and important — the principle of end-focus. A cleft lets you override the default order of a sentence so that the element you care about lands in the most prominent position. The it-cleft places the focus straight after ‘It + be’, where it receives the main stress, and presents the rest of the sentence as given: “It was the editor who changed the headline” assumes we know the headline was changed and identifies who did it. That makes it the natural form for correction and contrast. The wh-cleft works the other way round: it presents a gap first (“What the campaign understood was…”) and fills it at the end, creating a small moment of suspense that orators and essayists exploit. Clefts also improve cohesion, because the first part can pick up an idea from the previous sentence. In spoken English, wh-clefts are extremely common as discourse openers (“What I’m saying is…”, “What happened was…”), so they belong to both formal and informal registers.

chart.title: Cleft types and their effect
rows: It was the intern who leaked it.
It + be + not until / only when + … + that…
It wasn’t until later that we knew.
All I asked for was a source.
The reason / thing / place + clause + be…
The reason it spread is that it was funny.

more: It was her pause before the final line, rather than the line itself, that people remembered.
What the campaign understood, and its rivals didn’t, was the power of a simple story.
It’s not what you say that matters so much as how often you say it.
The thing that troubles me about the video is that nobody checked the source.
What fact-checkers do is slow the conversation down.
It was in this very hall that the famous speech was first delivered.

fix.wrong: It was the headline what misled readers.
fix.right: It was the headline that misled readers.
fix.why: It-clefts use ‘that’ (or ‘who’ for people), never ‘what’.

fix.wrong: What she did was she rewrote the speech.
fix.right: What she did was (to) rewrite the speech.
fix.why: After ‘What … did was’, use the base form or to-infinitive, not a new clause.

fix.wrong: It was in 2016 when the phrase became popular.
fix.right: It was in 2016 that the phrase became popular.
fix.why: The it-cleft is completed by ‘that’, even when the focus is a time expression.

drill.name: Spotlight shift
drill.prompt: Take each neutral sentence and produce three clefts: an it-cleft focusing on the subject, an it-cleft focusing on the time or reason, and a wh-cleft. Say each aloud with the stress on the focused element.
items: A teenager started the rumour on a gaming forum last March.
The repeated slogan convinced undecided voters.
The newspaper corrected the error three days later.
Emotional stories persuade people more than statistics.
The spokesperson avoided the question.

dialogue.line: So the speech lost them the election?
No — it wasn’t the speech that lost it. It was the clip someone cut from it.
The eight-second one?
Exactly. What people saw was a man laughing at a question about poverty.
And what he was actually laughing at…
…was a joke his opponent had made. All the context had been cut away.

contrast.title: Neutral, it-cleft or wh-cleft?
rows: It was the tone that offended people.
What offended people was the tone.
The tone is what offended people.
All that offended people was the tone.
only the tone; the rest was fine
It wasn’t the content that offended people.

grammar.sound: The focused element takes the nuclear stress: “It was the TONE that offended people.” In wh-clefts there is often a small pause before the focus: “What offended people … was the TONE.”

grammar.name: Fronting and inversion for emphasis
grammar.short: Move an element to the front — sometimes with verb–subject inversion — for contrast, cohesion or drama.
grammar.rule: In English the normal order is subject–verb–object, so moving another element to the start of the sentence makes it stand out. Fronting can link back to the previous sentence or set up a contrast. With adverbials of place and with fronted complements such as ‘gone’, ‘such’ or ‘so + adjective’, the verb and subject often change places too — a full inversion that is formal, literary and highly rhetorical.
form: Object fronting: object + subject + verb → That kind of rhetoric I simply cannot accept.
Place inversion: adverbial of place / direction + verb + subject → On the podium stood a nervous young senator.
Complement inversion: adjective / participle + be + subject → Gone are the days when facts settled arguments.
So + adjective: So + adjective + be + subject + that-clause → So persuasive was her speech that the vote changed.
Such: Such + be + noun phrase + that-clause → Such was the outrage that the advert was withdrawn.
Concessive fronting: adjective / adverb + as / though + subject + verb → Eloquent as he is, he rarely says anything new.
notes: Full inversion after place adverbials happens with noun subjects and intransitive verbs of position or movement (stand, lie, sit, come, go): “Here comes the speaker” — but with a pronoun, no inversion: “Here she comes.”
Cohesion: fronting often picks up something already mentioned — “Most of the speech was forgettable. The ending, however, I will never forget.”
Comparatives and ‘equally’: “More troubling still is the silence of the regulator.” / “Equally important is the question of who funds the site.”
Concessive ‘as’: the adjective goes first — “Clever as the slogan was, it misled people.” This means ‘although the slogan was clever’.
Style: one or two fronted structures give an essay or speech punch; too many make it sound theatrical.
examples: Gone are the days when a newspaper correction reached the same readers as the original story.
So effective was the slogan that rival parties began to copy it.
Persuasive as the argument sounds, it rests on a single disputed statistic.
grammar.watch: Don’t invert with pronoun subjects after place adverbials: write “Into the room she walked”, not “Into the room walked she”.
grammar.deep: Fronting exploits the two most prominent positions in a clause: the beginning, which sets the topic, and the end, which carries the new and important information. When you move an object or complement to the front, you either connect it to what came before (“This argument I find unconvincing”) or set up a contrast (“Facts they ignore; feelings they amplify”). Full inversion goes one step further. After a fronted adverbial of place, a heavy noun subject is pushed to the end of the sentence, where it receives maximum emphasis — a classic technique in narrative and oratory: “At the back of the hall sat the very journalists he had insulted.” The ‘so … that’ and ‘such … that’ patterns invert to foreground degree and consequence, while ‘Gone are the days’ and ‘Equally significant is…’ are fixed rhetorical frames worth learning as chunks. Concessive fronting with ‘as’ or ‘though’ (“Tempting though it is to blame the algorithm, …”) is a hallmark of sophisticated argument, because it concedes a point and pivots in a single, elegant clause. All these structures are marked: they are noticed. Proficient writers ration them so that each one lands.

chart.title: Fronting patterns at C2
rows: On the stage stood the candidate.
Gone are the days of trusted anchors.
So bold was the lie that nobody questioned it.
Such was the demand that the site crashed.
Clever as it is, it misleads.

more: This much we know: the video was edited before it was shared.
Equally worrying is the speed with which the correction was buried.
Such was the public appetite for the story that few stopped to verify it.
Tempting though it is to blame the algorithms, the appetite for outrage is ours.
Out of the archive came a recording that contradicted everything.
Brilliant speaker that she is, she knows exactly when to fall silent.

fix.wrong: So persuasive the speech was that people cried.
fix.right: So persuasive was the speech that people cried.
fix.why: After fronted ‘so + adjective’, the verb comes before the subject.

fix.wrong: Although clever as the slogan was, it misled people.
fix.right: Clever as the slogan was, it misled people.
fix.why: The ‘adjective + as’ pattern already expresses concession; don’t add ‘although’.

fix.wrong: Here comes he.
fix.right: Here he comes.
fix.why: Full inversion after place adverbials does not happen with pronoun subjects.

drill.name: Rewrite for the podium
drill.prompt: Turn each plain sentence into a fronted or inverted version suitable for a speech, then read both aloud and decide which suits a conversation and which suits a rally.
items: The days of trusted news anchors are gone.
The response was so angry that the company apologised.
Although the argument is persuasive, it is flawed.
The real victims sat at the back of the courtroom.
The silence of the regulators is equally troubling.

dialogue.line: How did the debate go?
Strange as it sounds, the moderator stole the show.
Not the candidates?
Their scripts we’d heard before. Her questions, though, nobody expected.
And the audience?
So stunned were they by the last question that the hall went completely silent.

contrast.title: Neutral vs fronted
rows: The days of print are gone.
Gone are the days of print.
The speech was so good that…
So good was the speech that…
The cost is even more worrying.
More worrying still is the cost.

grammar.sound: Fronted elements usually form their own tone unit, followed by a short pause: “That claim | I simply cannot accept.” The fronted word carries strong stress and often a fall-rise to signal contrast.

grammar.name: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials
grammar.short: Never have I…, Not only did she…, No sooner had…, Only when… did…
grammar.rule: When a negative or restrictive adverbial (never, rarely, not only, no sooner, only when, little, at no time) is placed at the start of a clause for emphasis, the subject and the auxiliary verb change places, as in a question. If there is no auxiliary, ‘do / does / did’ is added. This inversion is formal and typical of speeches, essays and dramatic narrative.
form: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + verb → Never have I heard such a cynical speech.
Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb, but + subject + also → Not only did she lie, but she also blamed the press.
No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than → No sooner had he spoken than the backlash began.
Hardly / Scarcely / Barely + had + subject + past participle + when → Hardly had the polls closed when the claims of fraud began.
Only + time / condition clause + auxiliary + subject + verb → Only when the transcript appeared did the truth emerge.
Little / At no time / Under no circumstances + auxiliary + subject + verb → Little did they realise the clip was fake.
notes: Only after / only when / not until: the inversion happens in the MAIN clause, not in the time clause — “Not until the recording surfaced did anyone believe her.”
No sooner … than, but hardly / scarcely / barely … when: don’t mix them — “No sooner had he finished than…”, “Hardly had he finished when…”.
Little = ‘not at all’, with verbs of knowing and realising: “Little did the editors suspect…”.
Not every adverbial with ‘no’ is negative in meaning: “In no time, the post had a million views” (= very quickly) — no inversion. Compare “At no time did the editor check it.”
‘Only’ + object or subject doesn’t invert: “Only the editor knew” (subject). But “Only then / Only by checking / Only in this way” all invert.
examples: Rarely has a single tweet caused so much damage.
Only by reading the full report can you see how misleading the headline was.
Under no circumstances should a journalist reveal a confidential source.
grammar.watch: Invert in the main clause only: write “Only when I read it did I understand”, not “Only when did I read it I understood”.
grammar.deep: Negative inversion is a fossil of an older English word order that survives because it is so useful rhetorically. Placing a negative or limiting word at the very start of the sentence gives it maximum prominence, and the question-like inversion that follows signals to the reader that something marked is happening. The rule is mechanical once you see it: the adverbial is ‘negative’ in scope (it negates or restricts the whole clause), so the auxiliary moves before the subject, with do-support where needed. The adverbials fall into families. Frequency (never, rarely, seldom, hardly ever), time sequence (no sooner … than, hardly / scarcely … when, not until), restriction (only + adverbial, little), emphasis of extent (not only, not once, nowhere, in no way, on no account) and prohibition (under no circumstances, on no account). The hardest cases involve ‘only’ and ‘not until’ with a subordinate clause, because the inversion skips the time clause and lands in the main clause. At C2 the challenge is register as much as form: inversion is natural in a speech, a formal essay or a suspenseful story, but sounds pompous in a casual message, where ‘I’ve never heard anything like it’ does the job perfectly.

chart.title: Negative and restrictive adverbials
rows: Seldom do we see such honesty.
no sooner … than, hardly / scarcely / barely … when
Scarcely had it aired when the complaints began.
not until, only when, only after, only then
Only then did the editor apologise.
only by / in this way / if, little
Only by checking sources can we stop it.
not only, not once, nowhere, in no way
Nowhere is the bias clearer than here.
under no circumstances, on no account, at no time
On no account should you share it.

more: Not once did the presenter acknowledge the error.
No sooner had the clip been posted than it was being shared by thousands.
Little did the senator know that the microphone was still on.
Nowhere is the gap between rhetoric and reality wider than in campaign promises.
Not until the archive was opened did historians realise the speech had been ghostwritten.
In no way does this excuse the spreading of falsehoods.

fix.wrong: Never I have seen such blatant spin.
fix.right: Never have I seen such blatant spin.
fix.why: After a fronted negative adverbial, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

fix.wrong: No sooner had she spoken when the crowd booed.
fix.right: No sooner had she spoken than the crowd booed.
fix.why: ‘No sooner’ pairs with ‘than’; ‘hardly / scarcely’ pair with ‘when’.

fix.wrong: Not until the video appeared people believed her.
fix.right: Not until the video appeared did people believe her.
fix.why: The inversion goes in the main clause, with do-support when there is no auxiliary.

drill.name: From chat to podium
drill.prompt: Say each everyday sentence in a formal, emphatic version starting with the adverbial in brackets. Then say which version you would use in a speech and which in a message to a friend.
items: I’ve never been so misrepresented. (Never)
We only understood it after reading the report. (Only after)
They didn’t realise the account was fake. (Little)
The post went up and the trolls arrived immediately. (No sooner)
You mustn’t share unverified content. (Under no circumstances)

dialogue.line: Did you watch the minister’s statement?
I did. Not only did she refuse to apologise, but she also accused the journalist of bias.
Bold move.
No sooner had she finished than the original recording was trending.
Little did she know someone had kept a copy.
Rarely have I seen a career turn so fast.

contrast.title: Inversion or not?
rows: Only then did the editor know.
In no time the post went viral.
At no time did the editor check it.

grammar.sound: Stress the adverbial and the main verb, and let the auxiliary stay weak: “NEVer have I HEARD such…” → /ˈnevə həv aɪ ˈhɜːd/. A slight pause after ‘Not only…’ prepares the listener for ‘but also’.

speaking.text: Speak for two minutes: ‘Is it ever acceptable for a politician to simplify the truth?’ Prompt ideas: winning trust, sound bites, the public’s attention span. Use at least one cleft and one negative inversion to signal your key points.

You are advising a charity on a campaign to stop the spread of health misinformation. Discuss five possible approaches (a celebrity video, school workshops, a fact-checking app, a slogan on public transport, a partnership with influencers), then agree on the two most effective. Use clefts to clarify what you mean: ‘What I’m suggesting is…’, ‘It’s the tone that matters.’

‘Words are never neutral.’ Discuss with examples: news headlines, labels used for groups of people, advertising language. Practise reporting others precisely: did a source claim, allege, insinuate or concede?

Deliver a 60-second persuasive speech on a cause you care about. You must include one ‘Not only…but also’, one ‘So + adjective + was…’, one it-cleft and one fronted concession (‘Tempting though it is…’). The class votes on the most persuasive speech and identifies the devices.

tips: Use an it-cleft to correct someone without repeating the whole sentence: ‘It wasn’t the content I objected to — it was the timing.’
With ‘only when / not until / only after’, invert in the main clause: ‘Only when the facts emerged did they apologise.’
Report with precision: choose ‘concede’ for a reluctant admission, ‘allege’ for an unproven accusation and ‘insinuate’ for a hidden, unpleasant suggestion.
In a CPE Part 1 essay, summarise BOTH key points of EACH text in your own words, evaluate them, and add your own view; never copy whole phrases from the input.

quiz.q: No sooner ___ the video than it was being shared across every platform.
quiz.explain: After fronted ‘No sooner’, invert the past perfect auxiliary and subject: ‘had she posted … than’.

test.q: ___ the editor who changed the headline, not the reporter.
test.explain: It-cleft: ‘It + be + focus + who/that…’ to identify and contrast.

test.q: What the campaign did ___ the debate entirely.
test.explain: In a wh-cleft with ‘do’, the focus is a (to-)infinitive: ‘was (to) avoid’.

test.q: Not until the full recording surfaced ___ the truth.
test.explain: With ‘Not until + clause’, invert in the main clause with do-support.

test.q: Hardly had the minister finished speaking ___ the protests began.
test.explain: ‘Hardly … when’; ‘No sooner … than’.

test.q: ___ the outrage that the advert was withdrawn within hours.
test.explain: ‘Such + be + noun phrase + that’ expresses degree and consequence.

test.q: Persuasive ___ her argument is, it relies on a single study.
test.explain: Concessive fronting: ‘adjective + as + subject + verb’ = although her argument is persuasive.

test.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Only then did the editor know the source.
Only then the editor knew the source.
Only the editor did know the source.
Only did the editor know then the source.
test.explain: ‘Only + time adverbial’ at the front triggers inversion; ‘only’ + subject does not.

test.q: ‘Are you ___ that I invented the quote?’ she asked coldly.
test.explain: ‘Insinuate’ = suggest indirectly that something bad is true.

test.q: After the recount, the challenger finally ___ defeat.
test.explain: You ‘concede defeat’ — admit, reluctantly, that you have lost.

test.q: The company claims to value privacy, but it merely pays ___ to it.
test.explain: ‘To pay lip service to’ = to support something in words but not in action.

test.q: It would be ___ to pretend we didn’t know about the risks; the memo proves we did.
test.explain: ‘Disingenuous’ = insincere, pretending to know less than you do.

test.q: The study conclusively ___ the claim, using data from ten countries.
test.explain: ‘Refute’ = prove wrong with evidence, not merely deny.

dynamics.name: Speech surgery
dynamics.how: Each group receives a flat, 100-word draft speech. They must rewrite it for maximum impact, adding exactly one it-cleft, one wh-cleft, one fronted concession and two negative inversions. Groups perform their speeches; the class identifies each device and judges which one was most effective.
dynamics.payoff: Students feel how emphatic structures change persuasive force, and learn not to overuse them.

dynamics.name: Reporting verb auction
dynamics.how: The teacher reads out short quotes (‘Well, perhaps we did make a mistake…’). Teams ‘bid’ the most precise reporting verb (concede, insinuate, allege, deny, refute) and must report the quote correctly with the right pattern. Points for precision and grammar.
dynamics.payoff: Moves students beyond ‘say’ and ‘tell’ to evaluative reporting.

dynamics.name: Correct the record
dynamics.how: Student A reads false statements about a famous speech or news story; Student B must correct each one with an it-cleft (‘No, it wasn’t Churchill who said that; it was…’). Then they swap roles with new cards.
dynamics.payoff: Practises the natural conversational function of it-clefts: contrastive correction.

writing.title: Rhetoric: a democratic skill or a danger?
writing.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Teach persuasion, not suspicion: Rhetoric has an undeservedly poor reputation. In ancient Athens, learning to persuade was considered a civic duty, since every citizen might have to argue a case before the assembly. Today, schools spend years on grammar but barely an hour on how arguments are built. Yet a student who has written a persuasive speech is far quicker to recognise the tricks used in one. Rather than warning young people about manipulation, we should give them the tools of persuasion themselves.

Text 2 — When emotion outruns evidence: Persuasion once had to pass through editors and broadcasters who, for all their faults, filtered out the most outrageous claims. Online, the most emotive message travels furthest, and algorithms reward anger over accuracy. In this environment, teaching rhetoric to individuals is like teaching swimming during a flood. Responsibility should lie with the platforms that amplify content, which must be required to slow the spread of claims that have not been verified.

criteria: Both key points from each text are summarised accurately in your own words, without lifting phrases from the input.
Each text is evaluated (strengths, weaknesses, assumptions) and your own view is clearly developed and justified.
At least one cleft sentence, one fronted or inverted structure and one negative inversion, used to signal key points rather than as decoration.
Formal, cohesive essay register with precise reporting verbs (contend, concede, maintain, overlook) and clear paragraphing.
writing.model:
Both texts address the question of how societies should respond to persuasive language, but they locate the solution in very different places.

The first writer contends that rhetoric is unfairly regarded with suspicion. Drawing on the example of ancient Athens, where persuasion was seen as part of every citizen’s responsibilities, the author maintains that schools neglect the skill. What the writer proposes is an education in which pupils practise persuasion themselves, on the grounds that those who construct arguments become better at detecting manipulation. This is a persuasive point: few things expose a technique as effectively as having used it. However, the argument assumes that the individual is the main line of defence, an assumption the second text directly challenges.

The second writer argues that the conditions for persuasion have changed fundamentally. Whereas traditional gatekeepers once filtered extreme claims, online platforms now reward emotional content regardless of its accuracy. Consequently, the author concludes, responsibility should shift to the companies that amplify messages, which ought to be obliged to restrict the circulation of unverified material. The image of teaching swimming during a flood is striking, although the writer perhaps concedes too little to individual judgement.

In my view, the two positions are complementary rather than contradictory. Only by combining regulation of platforms with a genuine education in rhetoric can a society hope to protect public debate. Regulation without education produces citizens who rely on others to decide what is true; education without regulation leaves them struggling against a system designed to exploit their emotions. It is this balance, rather than either solution alone, that offers the most realistic way forward.

units.title: MIND AND PERCEPTION

overview.intro: This unit is about the mind’s quiet tricks — the memories we rewrite, the biases we cannot see and the snap judgements we mistake for reason. Talking about the mind means talking about uncertainty, so at C2 you need a precise toolkit of modal verbs: to speculate about the present, past and future with exactly the right degree of confidence, to judge past decisions with hindsight, and to use ‘will’ and ‘would’ for assumptions and characteristic behaviour as native speakers do.
goals: Speculate and deduce about the present, past and future with finely graded certainty (must, can’t, may well, is bound to, might have been doing).
Distinguish ‘needn’t have’ from ‘didn’t need to’, and use should / might / could have to criticise, regret and reproach.
Use ‘will’ and ‘would’ for assumptions (‘That’ll be Sam’) and for typical or annoying behaviour (‘She will keep checking her phone’).
overview.outcome: By the end you can analyse a puzzling situation by weighing possible explanations, discuss a decision you regret with nuance, and write a CPE review of an exhibition about perception.

vocab.def: to notice, recognise or understand something that is not obvious.
vocab.use: Suggests effort and subtlety; it collocates with abstract objects (a pattern, a difference, a motive). The adjective ‘discerning’ means having good judgement: a discerning reader.
examples: It took years of data before researchers could discern any pattern in the dreams.
Infants can discern differences in pitch long before they understand words.
vocab.colloc: discern a pattern / a trend · barely discernible · a discerning eye

vocab.term: to glimpse / to catch a glimpse of
vocab.def: to see something or someone only for a moment and not completely.
vocab.use: Also figurative: a glimpse into someone’s mind, a glimpse of the future. Compare ‘glance’, which is a quick look you choose to take; a glimpse often happens by chance.
examples: I only caught a glimpse of the driver, so I can’t describe him with confidence.
The diary offers a rare glimpse into the mind of a grieving scientist.
vocab.colloc: catch / get a glimpse of · a fleeting glimpse · a glimpse into

vocab.def: to notice something with the senses, or to understand or regard something in a particular way.
vocab.use: Common in the passive with ‘as’ to describe reputation or interpretation: ‘She is perceived as cold.’ Noun: perception; adjective: perceptive (quick to notice).
examples: We tend to perceive confident speakers as more competent than they are.
Colour is perceived differently depending on the light around it.
vocab.colloc: be perceived as · widely perceived · perceive a threat · public perception

vocab.def: the tendency to notice, believe and remember information that supports what you already think.
vocab.use: A key term in psychology and journalism. You fall prey to, succumb to or guard against it.
examples: Confirmation bias explains why both sides of a debate read the same report as a victory.
Good scientists design experiments specifically to guard against confirmation bias.
vocab.colloc: fall prey to confirmation bias · guard against bias · a cognitive bias · unconscious bias

vocab.def: with the understanding you have of an event only after it has happened.
vocab.use: Frequently introduces a ‘should have’ sentence. ‘Hindsight bias’ is the illusion that we ‘knew it all along’. Idiom: ‘Hindsight is a wonderful thing’ (= it’s easy to judge afterwards).
examples: With the benefit of hindsight, the warning signs should have been obvious.
Hindsight bias makes past decisions look far more foolish than they were.
vocab.colloc: with hindsight · in hindsight · hindsight bias · hindsight is twenty-twenty

vocab.def: an area in which a person fails to understand or notice something, often about themselves.
vocab.use: Literally, the part of the eye that cannot detect light; figuratively, a gap in awareness or judgement. Often used with ‘when it comes to’.
examples: He’s brilliant at reading other people but has a blind spot when it comes to his own children.
Every institution has blind spots that outsiders notice immediately.
vocab.colloc: have a blind spot about / when it comes to · a cultural blind spot · a moral blind spot

vocab.def: to help someone remember something.
vocab.use: The subject is usually the trigger: a photo, a smell, a question. Neutral register.
examples: Perhaps this old photograph will jog your memory.
The detective read the timeline aloud to jog the witness’s memory.
vocab.colloc: jog someone’s memory · help jog the memory · a memory-jogger

vocab.def: to think very hard in order to remember something or solve a problem.
vocab.use: Informal to neutral; usually in the continuous or with ‘trying to’. Also spelled ‘wrack’, though ‘rack’ is standard.
examples: I’ve been racking my brains, but I can’t remember where we parked.
She racked her brains for a polite way to refuse.
vocab.colloc: rack your brains for · rack your brains trying to

vocab.term: to lose your train of thought
vocab.def: to forget what you were thinking or saying, usually because of an interruption.
vocab.use: Useful as a recovery phrase in speaking exams: ‘Sorry, I’ve lost my train of thought.’ ‘Train of thought’ itself means a connected sequence of ideas.
examples: The phone rang and I completely lost my train of thought.
Interrupting a speaker can derail their entire train of thought.
vocab.colloc: lose / follow someone’s train of thought · interrupt a train of thought

vocab.def: to make someone less able to think clearly and make sensible decisions.
vocab.use: The subject is a feeling or factor: emotion, fatigue, loyalty. Note the British spelling ‘judgement’; American English prefers ‘judgment’.
examples: Don’t let your loyalty to an old friend cloud your judgement.
Exhaustion had clearly clouded the pilot’s judgement.
vocab.colloc: cloud your judgement · impair your judgement · an error of judgement

vocab.def: the belief that something is true or will happen because you want it to, not because of evidence.
vocab.use: Often in the structure ‘That’s just wishful thinking’ or ‘more wishful thinking than…’. Mildly critical.
examples: Expecting the market to recover by next month is pure wishful thinking.
The forecast owed more to wishful thinking than to data.
vocab.colloc: pure / mere wishful thinking · a case of wishful thinking

vocab.def: a strong belief based on instinct rather than reasoning.
vocab.use: Common in conversation and journalism; ‘gut instinct’ and ‘gut reaction’ are close. In formal writing use ‘intuition’.
examples: I had a gut feeling that something was wrong before the results came in.
Experienced nurses often trust their gut feelings, with surprising accuracy.
vocab.colloc: have a gut feeling · trust your gut · gut instinct · gut reaction

grammar.name: Modals of speculation and deduction (present, past, future)
grammar.short: must, can’t, may well, might have been, is bound to — graded certainty about now, then and later.
grammar.rule: Modal verbs let us express exactly how sure we are about something we cannot verify. ‘Must’ and ‘can’t / couldn’t’ express logical deduction (almost certain); ‘may’, ‘might’ and ‘could’ express possibility; ‘should’ and ‘ought to’ express reasonable expectation. For the past, add ‘have + past participle’; for ongoing activities, use the continuous infinitive. For the future, ‘will’, ‘be bound to’, ‘be likely to’ and ‘may well’ create a finely graded scale.
form: Present: must / might / can’t + base verb → She must be exhausted after the night shift.
Present continuous: must / might / can’t + be + -ing → He can’t be sleeping — the light’s on.
Past: must / may / might / could / can’t + have + past participle → The witness must have misremembered the colour.
Past continuous: must / might + have been + -ing → She might have been daydreaming when the alarm went off.
Future: may well / is bound to / is likely to / should + base verb → The results are bound to surprise people.
Negative possibility: may not / might not + have + past participle → He might not have noticed the change.
notes: Negative certainty: the opposite of ‘must’ is ‘can’t’ or ‘couldn’t’, not ‘mustn’t’ — “He can’t have seen it; he was asleep.”
Can’t have vs might not have: “She can’t have known” (impossible) is much stronger than “She might not have known” (possible that she didn’t).
Strengthening possibility: add ‘well’ — “The memory may well be false” means it is quite probable.
Can vs could for possibility: “Memory can be unreliable” (general, theoretical) vs “This memory could be unreliable” (a specific case).
‘Should’ for expectation, not obligation: “The test results should be back by Friday” means I expect them to be.
Hedging verbs and adverbs complement modals: ‘it seems’, ‘presumably’, ‘in all likelihood’, ‘conceivably’.
examples: You must have been concentrating hard — you didn’t hear me come in.
The participants can’t have noticed the gorilla; most of them were counting passes.
Brain-scanning technology may well transform how we diagnose memory loss.
grammar.watch: For negative deduction, don’t use ‘mustn’t’: write “It can’t have been him”, not “It mustn’t have been him”.
grammar.deep: Epistemic modality — the grammar of how sure we are — is where English is at its most nuanced, and C2 users are expected to place a claim precisely on a scale from near-certainty to faint possibility. Deduction (must, can’t) is not a guess but a conclusion from evidence: “The lights are off, so they must have left.” Possibility (may, might, could) leaves alternatives open, with ‘might’ and ‘could’ often slightly more tentative than ‘may’, although the difference is small in speech. Time is handled not by the modal but by what follows it: the simple infinitive for present states, ‘be + -ing’ for activities in progress, ‘have + past participle’ for past events and ‘have been + -ing’ for past activities. Future speculation draws on a wider set of semi-modal expressions — be bound to, be sure to, be likely / unlikely to, there is every chance that — which are useful precisely because they can be modified (highly likely, almost bound to). Psychologists and journalists rely on these forms constantly, because careful claims about the mind must distinguish what the evidence shows from what it merely suggests. Over-certainty is as much a C2 error as grammatical inaccuracy.

They must have been standing below him — on the steps, perhaps.
Or they might have been influenced by the first news report.
