grammar.sound: In speech, ‘have’ after a modal is reduced to /əv/: “must have” sounds like /ˈmʌstəv/, “can’t have” like /ˈkɑːntəv/. This is why learners sometimes write ‘must of’ — always write ‘have’.

grammar.name: Needn't have vs didn't need to; should have, might have, could have
grammar.short: Judging the past: unnecessary actions, regrets, criticism and missed possibilities.
grammar.rule: ‘Needn’t have + past participle’ means that someone did something which turned out to be unnecessary. ‘Didn’t need to + infinitive’ simply says something was not necessary, and usually implies it wasn’t done. ‘Should have / ought to have’ express regret, criticism or an unmet expectation. ‘Might have’ and ‘could have’ express possibilities that did not happen — and, with stress and intonation, irritation or reproach.
form: Unnecessary but done: needn’t have + past participle → I needn’t have worried — the exam was easy.
Not necessary (usually not done): didn’t need to + base verb → I didn’t need to revise, so I went out.
Regret / criticism: should / ought to + have + past participle → We should have trusted our instincts.
Unmet expectation: should + have + past participle (+ by now) → The results should have arrived by now.
Unrealised possibility: could + have + past participle → She could have become a concert pianist.
Reproach: might / could + have + past participle → You might have warned me the test was today!
notes: Didn’t need to + stress: if you stress ‘need’ and add context, it can mean the action was done anyway — “I didn’t NEED to take a taxi, but I was tired” — while ‘needn’t have’ always means it was done.
Shouldn’t have: regret about something that was done — “I shouldn’t have trusted my memory.” “You shouldn’t have!” is also a polite reply to an unexpected gift.
Could have vs was able to: ‘could have’ = possible but did not happen; for a single past achievement use ‘was able to / managed to’ — “Despite the noise, she was able to concentrate.”
Might have: in a conditional it means ‘possibly would have’ — “If I’d slept more, I might have remembered the answer.”
Hindsight: these forms naturally follow phrases like ‘with hindsight’, ‘looking back’, ‘in retrospect’.
examples: I needn’t have brought my notes — the talk was recorded and shared afterwards.
With the benefit of hindsight, the board should have listened to the junior analyst.
You could have told me you’d already booked the tickets!
grammar.watch: Keep the forms apart: write “I needn’t have bought it” (I bought it), not “I didn’t need to have bought it”.
grammar.deep: Talking about the past is rarely neutral: we evaluate it. English provides a compact set of modal perfects for exactly this purpose. ‘Needn’t have done’ and ‘didn’t need to do’ form a famous pair. The first reports an action that took place and then judges it superfluous; the second reports an absence of necessity and, by default, suggests the action did not happen, although context can override this. ‘Should have’ and ‘ought to have’ measure the past against a standard — what was sensible, expected or right — and can be pointed at oneself (regret) or others (criticism). ‘Could have’ opens a window onto an alternative world in which something was possible but did not occur, which makes it the language of near-misses (“It could have been a disaster”) and lost potential. ‘Might have’ overlaps with it and, said with a reproachful fall-rise, becomes a complaint: “You might have asked!” Psychology research on regret and counterfactual thinking explains why these forms matter: much of how we feel about our decisions depends on the alternative worlds we imagine, and these modals are how we put them into words.

And?
I needn’t have bothered. They asked me nothing technical at all.
Well, you didn’t need to stay up that late — you knew the material.
I know, I should have trusted myself. And you might have told me they’d interviewed you last year!

I took one; it was warm.
I didn’t need to take a coat.

kind or reproachful, depending on tone
it was a mistake (or a polite thank-you)

grammar.sound: Reproach lives in the intonation: “You MIGHT have told me” with a high fall on ‘might’ sounds annoyed, while a neutral, low ‘might’ sounds like simple speculation. ‘Needn’t have’ is pronounced /ˈniːdntəv/.

grammar.name: Will and would for assumption and characteristic behaviour
grammar.short: ‘That’ll be Sam’, ‘She’ll sit for hours…’, ‘He WOULD say that’ — assumptions and typical behaviour.
grammar.rule: Beyond the future and the conditional, ‘will’ and ‘would’ have two important uses. First, assumption: ‘will’ expresses a confident guess about the present (‘That’ll be the courier’) and ‘will have done’ about the past. Second, characteristic behaviour: ‘will’ describes typical habits or tendencies in the present, and ‘would’ describes repeated actions in the past. When stressed, both express irritation at behaviour that is typical of someone.
form: Present assumption: will + base verb → That’ll be my sister — she always rings at seven.
Ongoing assumption: will + be + -ing → Don’t call now; they’ll be having dinner.
Past assumption: will + have + past participle → You’ll have heard the news by now.
Present habit / tendency: will + base verb → A tired brain will fill gaps with guesses.
Past habit: would + base verb → As a child, I would spend hours watching clouds.
Irritation (stressed): WILL / WOULD + base verb → He WILL keep interrupting. / She WOULD say that.
notes: Would for past habits, not states: “I would play chess every evening” is fine; for states use ‘used to’ — “I used to live in Porto”, never “I would live in Porto”.
Assumption about a past situation with would: “That would have been around 1995” / “The man you met would be her uncle.”
Refusal: won’t / wouldn’t express unwillingness, even for objects — “The door won’t open.” “He wouldn’t listen.”
General truths and properties: ‘will’ expresses what something characteristically does — “Memory will distort details over time.”
Stressed ‘would’ often means ‘That is typical of him/her’: “Of course she would forget — she always does.”
examples: The phone’s ringing. That’ll be the clinic with my test results.
My grandfather would sit by the window for hours, recalling names from his youth.
Under pressure, people will often choose the first option they see.
grammar.watch: Don’t use ‘would’ for past states: write “I used to believe I had a perfect memory”, not “I would believe I had a perfect memory”.
grammar.deep: These uses of ‘will’ and ‘would’ share a core meaning of predictability. An assumption with ‘will’ is a prediction applied to the present or past: when you hear the doorbell at the usual time and say “That’ll be Ana”, you are predicting that, if you check, you will find Ana. ‘Will have done’ extends the same logic backwards, which is why it is so useful for polite assumptions about shared knowledge (“As you’ll have noticed…”). The habitual use is predictability across time: “She’ll read a whole novel in one sitting” describes what she can be expected to do, and in scientific and psychological writing ‘will’ describes the characteristic behaviour of systems (“Participants will tend to overestimate…”). ‘Would’ is the past counterpart, typical of nostalgic narrative, and it needs an established past time frame, so stories often open with ‘used to’ and then continue with ‘would’. Finally, stress turns predictability into criticism: “He WILL leave the lights on” means it is maddeningly typical of him. This use is impossible to read correctly on the page without context, which is why it appears more in speech than in writing.

She would read for hours as a child.
People will believe what flatters them.

fix.right: That will be the postman.
fix.why: After ‘will’ use the bare infinitive (or ‘be + -ing’ for an ongoing activity).

drill.name: Predictable people
drill.prompt: Describe someone you know well using ‘will’ for three typical habits, ‘would’ for two habits they had in the past and one stressed ‘WILL’ for a habit that drives you mad. Then make two assumptions about what they’ll be doing right now.

a childhood friend
a flatmate or sibling
a teacher you remember
yourself, ten years ago

dialogue.line: Someone’s at the door.
That’ll be Marco. He’ll have forgotten his keys again.
Again? Doesn’t he keep them on a hook?
He will insist on carrying them in his coat pocket, and then he changes coats.

rows: We used to swim every morning.
I used to believe in ghosts.
She used to have a scooter.
better after the frame is set

grammar.sound: Assumption ‘will’ is contracted and unstressed: “That’ll be Sam” /ðætl biː/. Irritation ‘will’ and ‘would’ are never contracted and carry heavy stress: “He WILL keep doing that” /hiː ˈwɪl/.

speaking.text: Speak for two minutes: ‘How far can we trust our own memories?’ Prompt ideas: eyewitness testimony, family stories, photographs and social media. Use a range of modals to show degrees of certainty.

Look at five scenarios in which people made poor decisions (buying an expensive car on impulse, hiring a confident but unqualified candidate, ignoring a doctor’s advice, investing in a ‘sure thing’, trusting a first impression). Discuss which bias might have influenced each person, what they should have done, and agree on which mistake was the most understandable.

Is intuition a reliable guide to decision-making? Discuss situations in which a gut feeling may well be wiser than analysis — and situations in which it can’t have been. Refer to experiences of your own.

In groups, the teacher gives you an unexplained situation (‘A man walks into a bar and asks for water; the barman points a gun at him; the man says thank you and leaves’). Speculate using must / might / can’t have, ask yes/no questions and reach a conclusion.

tips: Place every claim on the certainty scale: ‘must have’ (I’m sure), ‘may well have’ (probably), ‘might have’ (possibly), ‘can’t have’ (I’m sure not).
Never write ‘must of’ or ‘could of’: the /əv/ you hear in speech is always ‘have’.
‘I needn’t have worried’ = I did worry, but it was unnecessary; ‘I didn’t need to worry’ = there was no need, and usually I didn’t.
In a CPE review, balance description and evaluation, and finish with a clear recommendation that says who the experience is (and isn’t) for.

quiz.q: I ___ so much — in the end the presentation was cancelled.

test.q: She ___ the email — she replied to it within minutes.
test.explain: Her quick reply is evidence she saw it, so missing it is impossible: ‘can’t have + p.p.’.

test.q: The lights are off and the car’s gone. They ___ out for the evening.
test.explain: Logical deduction from evidence about the past: ‘must have + p.p.’.

test.q: Don’t phone him now; he ___ his afternoon nap.
test.explain: ‘Will + be + -ing’ expresses an assumption about an activity in progress now.

test.q: When we were children, my grandmother ___ us stories about her village every night.
test.explain: ‘Would + base verb’ describes a repeated past action.

test.q: Which sentence is INCORRECT?
options: I used to live in Seville.
I would visit my aunt every summer.
I used to visit my aunt every summer.
I would live in Seville as a child.
test.explain: ‘Would’ cannot describe past states such as ‘live’; use ‘used to’.

test.q: ‘You ___ me you were bringing guests!’ — she was clearly annoyed.
test.explain: Stressed ‘might / could have + p.p.’ expresses reproach.

test.q: Despite the noise, the pilot ___ land the plane safely.
test.explain: For a single past achievement, use ‘was able to / managed to’, not ‘could’.

test.q: The new evidence ___ well change the court’s view of the case.
test.explain: ‘May well’ = it is quite probable.

test.q: Researchers looking only for evidence that supports their hypothesis are falling prey to ___.
test.explain: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour information that confirms existing beliefs.

test.q: Sorry, the phone rang and I’ve completely lost my ___ of thought.
test.explain: The fixed phrase is ‘to lose your train of thought’.

test.q: It took months before the scientists could ___ any pattern in the data.
test.explain: ‘Discern’ = notice or recognise something that is not obvious, often abstract.

test.q: Don’t let your anger ___ your judgement; sleep on it before replying.
test.explain: ‘To cloud someone’s judgement’ = make them less able to think clearly.

dynamics.name: The unreliable witness
dynamics.how: The teacher shows a busy photo for ten seconds, then hides it. Groups write five statements about what was in it, each with a different modal of certainty (‘There must have been a dog’, ‘The woman might have been holding a map’). The photo is revealed and groups score points for accuracy and appropriate certainty.
dynamics.payoff: Demonstrates memory distortion while making students calibrate certainty grammatically.

dynamics.name: Regret auction
dynamics.how: Pairs write three short ‘decision stories’ on cards. Cards are redistributed; each pair must respond to a story with one ‘needn’t have’, one ‘should(n’t) have’ and one ‘could have’ sentence. The class votes for the wisest piece of hindsight.
dynamics.payoff: Contextualised practice of all the past modal perfects in one task.

dynamics.name: Typical!
dynamics.how: Each student describes a fictional ‘nightmare flatmate’ using stressed WILL for annoying habits and ‘will’ assumptions for what the flatmate will be doing right now. The others must guess which habits are true of real people they know.
dynamics.payoff: Practises the intonation of irritation, which carries meaning in this structure.

writing.title: Seeing Is Deceiving
writing.brief: A cultural website has invited readers to review an exhibition, museum or event that changed the way they think. Write a review of an exhibition about perception and the mind, describing what visitors can experience, evaluating how successfully it achieves its aims, and saying who would most benefit from a visit.
writing.briefEs: Escribe una reseña para una web cultural de una exposición sobre la percepción y la mente: describe, evalúa y recomienda.
criteria: A clear balance of description and evaluation, with a recommendation that identifies the ideal (and less suitable) visitor.
Precise speculation and deduction (must have, may well, can’t have) and at least one ‘should have’ or ‘could have’ to evaluate the exhibition’s shortcomings.
One use of ‘will’ or ‘would’ for typical behaviour or assumption (e.g. visitors will find themselves…; as regular readers will know…).
Rich, accurate vocabulary of perception and cognition (discern, glimpse, perceive, confirmation bias, blind spot) in an engaging, sophisticated register.
writing.model:
Seeing Is Deceiving: a review

The first room of this exhibition contains nothing but a chessboard painted on the wall, and yet visitors will stand in front of it for minutes, refusing to believe that two of its squares are exactly the same shade of grey. That stubborn disbelief is the point. ‘Seeing Is Deceiving’ sets out to show that perception is less a window on the world than a story the brain tells itself, and for the most part it succeeds brilliantly.

The curators must have spent years selecting the illusions on display, because each one isolates a different shortcut the mind takes. In one corridor, faces seem to follow you as you walk; in another, a recorded voice appears to say a different word depending on the subtitle beneath it. The most unsettling installation invites you to count passes in a short basketball video. Most visitors, myself included, fail to discern the person in a bear costume strolling through the middle of the game — a humbling glimpse of our own blind spots.

What lifts the exhibition above a mere funfair of tricks is its final section, which applies these lessons to real life. Short case studies show how confirmation bias may well have influenced court verdicts and medical diagnoses, and how eyewitnesses can’t have seen what they later swore to. Here, though, the organisers could have gone further. The texts are rather dense, and the section should have included some interactive element to match the playfulness of the earlier rooms; many visitors were clearly drifting towards the café by this point.

Nevertheless, this is a thought-provoking and genuinely entertaining experience. Families with older children will love the illusions, while anyone who prides themselves on being a rational decision-maker would benefit most from the final room. Allow at least two hours — and be prepared to leave trusting your own eyes a little less.

homework.title: The case of the vanishing memory
homework.task: Write a 200-word short narrative about a person who remembers an event differently from everyone else. Use at least six modal forms of speculation (present, past and continuous), one ‘needn’t have’, one ‘should have’ and two uses of ‘would’ for past habits. Underline each modal form. Then record yourself reading the story aloud, paying attention to weak forms (/ˈmʌstəv/, /ˈkɑːntəv/).

board: Left: a vertical certainty thermometer — MUST / WILL (top), MAY WELL / SHOULD, MAY / MIGHT / COULD, MIGHT NOT, CAN’T / COULDN’T (bottom).
Beside it, the time switch: modal + VERB (now) · modal + BE + -ING (in progress) · modal + HAVE + P.P. (past) · modal + HAVE BEEN + -ING (past activity).
Centre: two speech bubbles — “I needn’t have rushed” (✓ I did) and “I didn’t need to rush” (usually ✗ I didn’t).
Right: SHOULD HAVE (regret) · COULD HAVE (missed chance) · MIGHT HAVE! (reproach) with a small arrow showing the fall-rise intonation.
Bottom: “That’ll be Sam” (assumption) · “She’ll read for hours” (habit) · “He WILL do that!” (irritation) · would vs used to with a red cross over “I would live in Porto”.

units.title: AMBITION AND ACHIEVEMENT

overview.intro: This unit is about how we define success — at work, in education and in life — and what we do with failure. Do we live in a meritocracy, or is ambition rewarded unequally? To discuss these questions at C2 you need the dense, precise style of professional and academic English: packing ideas into complex noun phrases, compressing clauses with participles, and choosing the exact verb pattern that changes ‘I stopped to think’ into ‘I stopped thinking’.
goals: Turn verb- and adjective-based clauses into nominalised, complex noun phrases for formal reports and essays.
Use participle clauses and reduced relative clauses (-ing, -ed, to-infinitive) accurately, avoiding dangling participles.
Choose between gerund and infinitive after verbs whose meaning changes (mean, propose, go on, regret, need, try).
overview.outcome: By the end you can discuss whether talent or circumstance explains success, rewrite a conversational text in a concise professional style, and write a CPE report evaluating a workplace scheme with recommendations.

vocab.term: to get a foot in the door
vocab.def: to get a first, often small, opportunity to enter an organisation or profession.
vocab.use: Implies that the first position is a starting point for something better. Often with ‘just’ or ‘at least’.
examples: The unpaid internship was exploitative, but it got her a foot in the door at the agency.
Freelance translation is a good way to get a foot in the door of publishing.
vocab.colloc: get / have a foot in the door · help someone get a foot in the door

vocab.def: to make progress, especially when it is difficult.
vocab.use: Often in the negative or with ‘little / some / considerable’. More formal and vivid than ‘make progress’; the noun is uncountable — never ‘a headway’.
examples: Negotiators made little headway on the question of pay.
We’re finally making some headway with the new software.
vocab.colloc: make headway with / on / in · make little / considerable headway

vocab.def: to decide to do something risky or important after thinking about it for a long time.
vocab.use: Common for career changes, starting a business, marriage. Often with ‘finally’ or ‘decide to’.
examples: After ten years in banking, he finally took the plunge and opened a bakery.
If you never take the plunge, you’ll always wonder what might have been.
vocab.colloc: take the plunge · finally take the plunge · decide to take the plunge

vocab.def: to deserve praise or show someone’s good qualities.
vocab.use: Formal and slightly old-fashioned. Pattern: ‘something does someone credit’ or ‘it does you credit that…’. Also ‘to someone’s credit’.
examples: Your honesty about the mistake does you credit.
To her credit, she accepted full responsibility for the failure.
vocab.colloc: do someone credit · it does you credit · to his credit · take credit for

vocab.term: to have a lot riding on (something)
vocab.def: to depend heavily on the result of something.
vocab.use: The ‘riding’ image comes from betting. Usually ‘have a lot / everything / too much riding on’.
examples: The start-up has everything riding on this funding round.
There’s a lot riding on her presentation tomorrow.
vocab.colloc: a lot / everything riding on · too much riding on · there’s a lot riding on

vocab.def: (of a moment or decision) that will result in either complete success or complete failure.
vocab.use: Used before a noun: a make-or-break year, deal, moment. Hyphenated when it modifies a noun.
examples: The next quarter will be make-or-break for the company.
For many young athletes, the national trials are a make-or-break moment.
vocab.colloc: a make-or-break moment / year / deal · it’s make or break

vocab.def: an invisible barrier that prevents certain groups, especially women and minorities, from reaching senior positions.
vocab.use: You break, shatter or crack the glass ceiling. Related: ‘sticky floor’ (being kept in low-paid jobs) and ‘glass cliff’ (being promoted into a crisis).
examples: She was the first woman to shatter the glass ceiling at the bank.
Despite equality policies, a glass ceiling persists in many professions.
vocab.colloc: break / shatter the glass ceiling · hit the glass ceiling · a glass cliff

vocab.def: to fail to continue or to be abandoned before completion.
vocab.use: For people (who give up or drop out) and for plans or projects. Neutral to formal.
examples: Of the forty applicants who started the programme, half fell by the wayside.
Many of the reforms fell by the wayside when funding dried up.
vocab.colloc: fall by the wayside · many / several fell by the wayside

vocab.def: to be so satisfied with past success that you stop making an effort.
vocab.use: Mostly negative: ‘We can’t afford to rest on our laurels.’ Laurels were a symbol of victory in ancient Greece.
examples: Having won the award, the team was determined not to rest on its laurels.
Companies that rest on their laurels are soon overtaken.
vocab.colloc: rest on your laurels · can’t afford to rest on its laurels

vocab.def: very fast success or progress, especially in a career.
vocab.use: Ironically, meteors fall rather than rise, but the phrase is fixed. Often contrasted with a sudden fall: ‘a meteoric rise and an equally spectacular fall’.
examples: Her meteoric rise from intern to chief executive took just eight years.
The band’s meteoric rise was followed by a long silence.
vocab.colloc: a meteoric rise to fame / power · a meteoric career

vocab.def: to stop doing something that is failing in order to avoid losing more.
vocab.use: From business and gambling; also used about relationships and projects. Opposite pattern: ‘to throw good money after bad’.
examples: After two years without profit, the investors decided to cut their losses.
Sometimes the bravest decision is to cut your losses and start again.
vocab.colloc: cut your losses · decide to cut your losses · throw good money after bad

vocab.def: a system in which people are chosen and rewarded according to their ability and achievement rather than wealth or social class.
vocab.use: Key term in debates about education and work. Adjective: meritocratic. The word was originally coined as satire, warning against a society that sorts people by measured ‘merit’.
examples: Critics argue that our so-called meritocracy rewards the children of the already privileged.
Firms like to describe themselves as meritocratic, but promotion data tell a different story.
vocab.colloc: a true meritocracy · a meritocratic system · the myth of meritocracy

grammar.name: Nominalisation and complex noun phrases
grammar.short: Turn actions and qualities into nouns — ‘the company expanded rapidly’ → ‘the rapid expansion of the company’.
grammar.rule: Nominalisation means expressing as a noun an idea that could be expressed as a verb or adjective: decide → decision, fail → failure, reliable → reliability. The resulting noun can carry pre-modifiers (adjectives, nouns) and post-modifiers (prepositional phrases, relative and infinitive clauses), creating complex noun phrases that pack a great deal of information into the subject or object of a sentence. This is the backbone of formal reports, academic writing and journalism.
form: Verb → noun: the + adjective + noun + of + noun → The company expanded rapidly → the rapid expansion of the company.
Adjective → noun: the + noun + of + noun → Staff were reluctant → the reluctance of staff.
Noun + preposition pattern: increase in · demand for · reliance on · impact on → a sharp increase in staff turnover.
Noun + to-infinitive: failure / decision / refusal + to + verb → the board’s refusal to reconsider.
Heavy subject: complex noun phrase + verb → The failure to retain experienced staff has damaged productivity.
Extent phrase: the extent to which + clause → the extent to which success depends on luck.
notes: Why use it: nominalisation lets you make an action the topic of the next sentence — “Profits fell. This decline was attributed to…” — which builds cohesion.
Agent: nominalisation hides who did what, which is useful for objectivity but can be evasive — “mistakes were made” style. Add ‘by’ or a possessive when the agent matters: “the CEO’s decision”.
Prepositions: learn the noun with its preposition — an increase IN, a demand FOR, an emphasis ON, a solution TO, an obstacle TO, a reason FOR.
Don’t stack too many nouns: “staff performance review process improvement plan” is hard to read; unpack with ‘of’ and ‘for’.
Balance: a good formal text mixes nominal and verbal styles; overuse of nouns makes writing heavy and vague.
examples: The introduction of flexible working led to a marked improvement in staff retention.
Her refusal to compromise on quality was central to the brand’s success.
There is growing recognition of the extent to which early opportunities shape later careers.
grammar.watch: Use the right preposition after the noun: write “an increase in applications”, not “an increase of applications” when you mean a change in number.
grammar.deep: Spoken English tends to tell stories with verbs: someone does something to someone else. Written professional English tends to discuss things, and nominalisation is how it converts processes into things that can be described, evaluated and linked. ‘Employees left the company because they were dissatisfied with how they were managed’ becomes ‘Employee dissatisfaction with management practices led to high turnover’ — half the length, with the cause and effect expressed as a relation between two noun phrases. This has three advantages that examiners reward at C2: density (more information per sentence), cohesion (a noun phrase can summarise the previous sentence and become the theme of the next) and an impersonal, objective tone. It also has dangers. Nominal style can obscure responsibility, hide the agent, and produce strings of abstract nouns that feel bureaucratic. The skill is to control it: nominalise when you want to discuss an idea as a concept, but return to clear verbs when describing who did what. Complex noun phrases also require precision in the small words — the preposition after the head noun, and the choice between possessive (‘the board’s decision’) and ‘of’-phrase (‘the decision of the board’), which tends to be preferred for longer and inanimate modifiers.

drill.name: Report-speak
drill.prompt: Rewrite each informal sentence as a single formal sentence built around a nominalised subject. Then underline the head noun and its preposition.
items: Lots of people left because the managers didn’t listen to them.
We trained the staff and they made fewer mistakes.
The company grew really fast and that caused problems.

dialogue.line: So why did so many graduates leave last year?
Basically, nobody told them how to get promoted.
Right. For the board, we’ll need something like ‘a lack of clarity regarding progression routes’.
And ‘the absence of structured mentoring’?
Exactly — leading to ‘a significant rise in early resignations’.

grammar.sound: Long noun phrases are spoken with one main stress near the end and a slight pause before the verb: “The failure to retain experienced STAFF | has damaged productivity.” That pause tells the listener where the subject ends.

grammar.name: Participle and reduced relative clauses
grammar.short: Compress clauses with -ing, -ed and to-infinitive forms: ‘candidates applying…’, ‘the report published…’, ‘the first to…’.
grammar.rule: A relative clause can often be reduced to a participle phrase: ‘the employees who work remotely’ → ‘the employees working remotely’; ‘the report which was published in May’ → ‘the report published in May’. After ordinals, superlatives and ‘the only / the last’, a to-infinitive can replace the relative clause. Adverbial participle clauses (‘Having secured funding, the team…’) express time, cause, condition or result. All these forms make writing more concise, but the implied subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause.
form: Active reduced relative: noun + -ing → Employees working remotely report higher satisfaction.
Passive reduced relative: noun + past participle → The figures published last week are misleading.
Infinitive relative: the first / last / only / superlative + to + verb → She was the first woman to chair the board.
Time / reason: -ing clause + main clause → Realising the risk, the investors withdrew.
Perfect participle: having + past participle, main clause → Having failed twice, he succeeded on the third attempt.
Passive perfect: having been + past participle, main clause → Having been passed over for promotion, she resigned.
notes: -ing for ongoing or general actions only: “the candidate winning the award” suggests an ongoing event; for a single completed action use a full clause — “the candidate who won the award”.
Dangling participles: the participle’s subject must match the main subject — “Walking into the office, I saw the notice”, not “Walking into the office, the notice caught my eye”.
Fixed participle expressions are exceptions: ‘Given…’, ‘Considering…’, ‘Generally speaking…’, ‘Judging by…’, ‘Assuming…’ can begin any sentence.
Negatives: put ‘not’ before the participle — “Not having a degree, he was rejected.”
Conjunction + participle adds precision: ‘while working’, ‘after graduating’, ‘when asked’, ‘once completed’, ‘unless instructed’.
examples: Applicants holding a professional qualification will be given priority.
The strategy adopted by the new director has transformed the company’s fortunes.
Having spent a decade in finance, she brought rare commercial insight to the charity.
grammar.watch: Avoid dangling participles: write “Having reviewed your application, we would like to invite you”, not “Having reviewed your application, you are invited”.
grammar.deep: Participle constructions are a hallmark of mature written style because they let a writer subordinate information without the weight of ‘who’, ‘which’, ‘because’ and ‘after’. A reduced relative clause tells the reader that the modifying information is background description; an adverbial participle clause tells the reader that the action is background to the main event, leaving the precise relation — time, cause, condition — to be inferred. That inference is both the power and the risk of the structure. ‘Seeing the figures, the board panicked’ suggests both time and cause, which is efficient. But because the participle has no subject of its own, the reader assumes it is the subject of the main clause; when it is not, the result is a dangling participle, often unintentionally comic (‘Having been promoted, my office is now on the top floor’). The tense relation is carried by the form: the simple -ing participle suggests simultaneity or immediate sequence; ‘having + past participle’ makes the earlier action explicit; ‘having been + past participle’ adds the passive. At C2, writers also exploit infinitive relatives after superlatives and ordinals (‘the youngest person ever to receive the prize’) and fixed participle expressions (‘Given the circumstances…’) to compress and connect ideas.

Try a participle clause: ‘Having spent three years in retail, I…’

Careful — that says your interest spent three years in retail!
Ah. ‘Having spent three years in retail, I developed a keen interest in marketing.’

grammar.name: Advanced verb patterns: gerund vs infinitive with change of meaning
grammar.short: mean, propose, go on, regret, need, try, remember, stop — the pattern changes the message.
grammar.rule: A group of verbs can be followed by either a gerund or a to-infinitive with a clear change in meaning. Typically, the infinitive looks forward (purpose, intention, future, a new stage), while the gerund refers to an action already happening, already done or considered as a whole. Beyond the familiar ‘remember / forget / stop / try’, C2 users master ‘mean’, ‘propose’, ‘go on’, ‘regret’, ‘need’ and adjectives such as ‘afraid’, ‘sorry’ and ‘interested’.
form: mean + to-infinitive = intend → I meant to call you, but I forgot.
mean + -ing = involve → Accepting the promotion would mean moving to Dubai.
propose + to-infinitive = intend → The board proposes to restructure the department.
propose + -ing = suggest → She proposed holding the meeting online.
go on + to-infinitive = do something new next → After the internship, he went on to found three companies.
go on + -ing = continue → She went on working long after she could have retired.
regret + to-infinitive = formal bad news → We regret to inform you that your application has been unsuccessful.
need + -ing = passive meaning → The appraisal system needs reviewing.
notes: regret + -ing looks back: “I regret not taking the job in Singapore.” Regret + to-infinitive is used with verbs of saying — inform, announce, tell, say.
need + -ing (= needs to be done) is more common in British English: “The office needs painting” = “The office needs to be painted.”
be afraid to do (too scared to try) vs be afraid of doing (worried something might happen): “I was afraid to ask for a raise” / “I was afraid of losing my job.”
be sorry to do (sad about now) vs be sorry for doing (apologising for the past): “I’m sorry to hear about the redundancies.” / “I’m sorry for missing the deadline.”
try to do (attempt something difficult) vs try doing (experiment to see if it works): “Try to stay calm.” / “Try restarting the server.”
stop to do (pause in order to) vs stop doing (cease): “She stopped to take the call.” / “She stopped taking calls after six.”
examples: Starting your own business often means sacrificing a regular income for years.
After a modest start in a regional office, she went on to become chief executive.
I deeply regret not having asked for feedback after the interview.
grammar.watch: Don’t confuse the two meanings of ‘mean’: write “Taking the job would mean relocating”, not “Taking the job would mean to relocate”.
grammar.deep: The contrast between the to-infinitive and the gerund follows a broadly consistent logic. The infinitive is prospective: it points towards an action that is potential, intended or subsequent to the main verb. That is why ‘mean to’ and ‘propose to’ express intention, why ‘go on to’ introduces the next stage in a career, and why ‘remember to’ and ‘stop to’ refer to something that follows the remembering or stopping. The gerund names the action as a fact or activity in itself, already under way or already accomplished, or as something considered as a whole: ‘mean doing’ describes what an action involves, ‘propose doing’ puts an activity forward for consideration, ‘go on doing’ continues an activity in progress, and ‘regret doing’ looks back at something done. The pattern ‘need + -ing’ is a special case with passive meaning, like ‘want + -ing’ in informal British English (‘The car wants washing’). Adjectives follow similar logic: ‘afraid to do’ concerns a deliberate action you are too scared to take, while ‘afraid of doing’ concerns something that might happen to you. C2 candidates are tested on these contrasts in key-word transformations and multiple-choice cloze, where a single pattern changes the meaning of the whole sentence.

dialogue.line: Did you accept the post in Singapore?
I meant to, but it would have meant leaving my father on his own.
Do you regret turning it down?
Sometimes. But the colleague who took it went on to burn out within a year.
So maybe your gut feeling was right.
Maybe. I propose not thinking about it until I’ve had a coffee.
