I’d be interested to hear your view.

grammar.sound: ‘Meant to’ is usually pronounced /ˈmentə/, with the /t/ sounds merging; ‘regret to inform’ links smoothly as /rɪˈɡret tʊ ɪnˈfɔːm/. In ‘go on to’, ‘on’ is stressed less than the following verb: “went on to WIN”.

speaking.text: Speak for two minutes: ‘Is success mainly the result of talent and hard work, or of luck and circumstance?’ Prompt ideas: family background, education, timing. Include a nominalised point such as ‘the role of chance’ or ‘the absence of opportunity’.

A company wants to reward its staff more fairly. Discuss five possible criteria for promotion (results, length of service, peer feedback, qualifications, leadership potential). Decide which two should carry the most weight, and agree on what each would mean in practice.

Is failure necessary for success? Discuss famous people who failed before succeeding, the ‘fail fast’ culture of start-ups, and whether schools should teach students how to fail. Use ‘go on to do’ and ‘regret doing’ naturally.

A job interview with a twist: the candidate (Student A) has a gap of three years in their CV; the interviewer (Student B) probes politely. A must present the gap positively, using participle clauses (‘Having decided to…’, ‘Faced with…’).

tips: In reports and essays, nominalise to build cohesion: end one sentence with an action and begin the next with its noun — ‘…profits fell. This decline…’.
Every participle clause needs a matching subject: check that the person doing the -ing is the subject of the main clause.
Learn meaning-changing verbs as pairs of contrasting sentences, not as lists: ‘It means moving’ vs ‘I meant to move’.
A CPE report needs a clear purpose statement, headings, an impersonal tone and specific, justified recommendations; avoid opinions with no basis in the findings.

quiz.q: Taking the job in Dubai would ___ leaving my family for at least two years.
quiz.explain: ‘Mean + -ing’ = involve or have as a consequence.

test.q: The ___ of the new appraisal system has been delayed until spring.
test.explain: A noun is needed as the head of the noun phrase: ‘the implementation of’.

test.q: There has been a sharp rise ___ the number of graduates starting businesses.
test.explain: ‘Rise / increase / fall’ take ‘in’ to describe what changes.

test.q: Staff ___ in the Madrid office will receive the new contract next week.
test.explain: Active reduced relative clause: ‘staff (who are) working…’.

test.q: She was the first woman ___ the national rowing team.
test.explain: After ‘the first’, use the to-infinitive as a reduced relative.

test.q: Which sentence contains a dangling participle?
options: Having missed the bus, I took a taxi.
Feeling tired, she went home early.
Having missed the bus, a taxi was the only option.
Given the cost, we cancelled the trip.
test.explain: ‘A taxi’ did not miss the bus; the implied subject doesn’t match the main subject.

test.q: We regret ___ you that the post has now been filled.
test.explain: ‘Regret + to-infinitive’ with verbs of saying announces bad news.

test.q: After a difficult start, the young chef went on ___ two Michelin stars.
test.explain: ‘Go on + to-infinitive’ describes the next stage or a subsequent achievement.

test.q: The whole recruitment process badly needs ___.
test.explain: ‘Need + -ing’ has a passive meaning: it needs to be modernised.

test.q: After years of losses, the investors decided to cut their ___.
test.explain: ‘To cut your losses’ = stop something failing to avoid losing more.

test.q: Having won the league, the team must not rest on its ___.
test.explain: ‘To rest on your laurels’ = stop trying because of past success.

test.q: Negotiators made little ___ on the question of pensions.
test.explain: ‘Make headway’ is uncountable: ‘make little / some headway’.

test.q: Your honesty about the error does you ___.
test.explain: ‘Something does someone credit’ = it shows their good qualities.

dynamics.name: Boardroom translation
dynamics.how: Student A reads a chatty voice-note transcript about problems at work (‘Loads of people quit because no one ever got promoted’). Student B ‘translates’ each sentence into board-report English using nominalisation and participle clauses. Then they swap with a second transcript and compare word counts.
dynamics.payoff: Shows how nominal style compresses and depersonalises information.

dynamics.name: Dangling detectives
dynamics.how: Groups receive ten sentences with participle clauses, half of them dangling (‘Driving to work, a deer ran across the road’). They sketch the absurd literal meaning, then correct each sentence two ways.
dynamics.payoff: Humour makes the error memorable and the correction rule clear.

dynamics.name: Career timeline
dynamics.how: Each student receives a card with a fictional career path. They mingle and tell their story using ‘go on to / go on doing’, ‘mean to / mean doing’, ‘regret doing’ and ‘stop to / stop doing’. Listeners note any pattern used incorrectly and report back.
dynamics.payoff: Contextualised oral practice of the meaning-changing pairs.

writing.title: The graduate mentoring scheme
writing.brief: Your organisation introduced a mentoring scheme for newly recruited graduates two years ago. The director has asked you to write a report evaluating how successful the scheme has been, identifying any problems that have emerged, and making recommendations for its future.
writing.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la dirección evaluando un programa de mentoría para recién graduados, sus problemas y tus recomendaciones.
criteria: Clear report format: title, purpose statement, headed sections and recommendations linked to findings.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases used to present findings concisely and impersonally (e.g. a marked improvement in retention).
At least three participle or reduced relative clauses (graduates participating…, having reviewed…, the first cohort to…) with no dangling participles.
One or more meaning-changing verb patterns (mean doing, go on to do, need doing) and precise vocabulary of success and failure.
writing.model:
Evaluation of the Graduate Mentoring Scheme

Purpose
The aim of this report is to assess the effectiveness of the mentoring scheme introduced two years ago, to identify the main difficulties encountered and to recommend improvements. Having reviewed retention figures and interviewed twenty participants, I present the following findings.

Achievements
The scheme has led to a marked improvement in graduate retention. Of the cohort recruited in the first year, 84% remain with the organisation, compared with 61% before mentoring was introduced. Graduates interviewed consistently mentioned the value of having an experienced colleague to consult, particularly during their first six months. Several have gone on to take on project leadership roles earlier than is usual, which suggests that the scheme is accelerating professional development.

Problems identified
However, the quality of mentoring varies considerably. Mentors selected on the basis of seniority rather than willingness have, in some cases, cancelled meetings repeatedly, and a minority of graduates described the relationship as a formality. A further concern is the absence of any training for mentors, many of whom admitted being unsure what was expected of them. Finally, the reliance on informal arrangements means that progress is rarely recorded, making the scheme difficult to evaluate.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, the following measures are recommended:
• Mentors should be recruited on a voluntary basis and offered a short training course before taking on a mentee.
• A simple framework, setting out the frequency of meetings and agreed goals, needs introducing so that expectations are clear.
• Graduates should be able to request a change of mentor without this being regarded as a failure.

Conclusion
Overall, the scheme has proved a worthwhile investment. Provided that the inconsistencies noted above are addressed, there is every reason to believe it will make an even greater contribution to retaining and developing talent.

homework.title: Success story, two styles
homework.task: Choose a person whose career you admire. Write their story twice in about 150 words each: first as a friendly blog post using mostly verbs and personal language, then as a formal profile for an awards ceremony using nominalisation, reduced relative clauses and participle clauses. Include ‘go on to do’ and one other meaning-changing pattern. Highlight the main differences between the two versions.

board: Top: VERB → NOUN arrow with examples — expand → expansion, fail → failure, rely on → reliance on, reluctant → reluctance.
Under it, a noun-phrase ‘sandwich’: [the] + [rapid] + EXPANSION + [of the company] + [into Asia].
Left: reduced relatives — WHO ARE WORKING → working · WHICH WAS PUBLISHED → published · WHO LED → the first to lead.
Right: a red warning box with the dangling participle “Having finished the report, the computer crashed” and a cartoon computer typing.
Bottom: two-column table TO (forward, intention, next stage) vs -ING (activity, involvement, the past) with mean / propose / go on / regret / need.

units.title: SCIENCE, TECHNOLOGY AND ETHICS
units.theme: AI, bioethics, privacy and the price of progress

overview.intro: This unit is about the moral questions raised by scientific and technological progress — artificial intelligence, gene editing, surveillance and the use of personal data. Writing and speaking about science at C2 means sounding authoritative without overclaiming. You will learn the impersonal grammar of scientific reporting (‘The drug is thought to have been tested…’), the causative structures we use for services, misfortunes and instructions, and the hedging that lets you make careful, defensible claims.
goals: Use reporting passives and passive infinitives (is said to have been, it is believed that, appears to have been altered) across all time references.
Use causative structures with precise meaning: have / get something done, have someone do, get someone to do, and causatives for misfortune.
Hedge and depersonalise claims appropriately with modal, lexical and impersonal devices, avoiding both overclaiming and overhedging.
overview.outcome: By the end you can report scientific claims with appropriate distance, discuss an ethical dilemma in technology with balanced, hedged arguments, and write a CPE Part 1 essay summarising and evaluating two texts on artificial intelligence.

vocab.def: used to say that something can be supported by good reasons, even if not everyone agrees.
vocab.use: A hedge that also signals the writer’s view: ‘arguably the most important invention of the century’. It softens a strong claim without abandoning it. Usually placed before the claim it qualifies.
examples: The printing press was arguably more disruptive than the internet.
Privacy is arguably the defining ethical issue of the digital age.
vocab.colloc: arguably the most / best · it is arguable that · an arguable point

vocab.def: according to what is claimed, although this may not be true.
vocab.use: Signals scepticism more strongly than ‘reportedly’. Related: ‘purported’ (adj) — the purported benefits — and ‘to purport to be’ (to claim to be).
examples: The app purportedly detects early signs of depression from typing patterns.
The document purports to be an internal memo, but its origins are unclear.
vocab.colloc: purportedly shows · the purported benefits · purport to be

vocab.def: a cautious way of saying that something seems to be true from the available evidence.
vocab.use: ‘Would’ adds extra tentativeness to ‘it appears’. Also: ‘it would seem’, ‘there would appear to be’. Ideal for academic writing and diplomatic speech.
examples: It would appear that the data were collected without explicit consent.
There would appear to be a correlation, although causation has not been established.
vocab.colloc: it would appear that · it would seem that · there would appear to be

vocab.def: a situation or subject full of hidden moral dangers and difficult decisions.
vocab.use: A metaphor common in journalism and debate. Also: ‘a legal / political minefield’. You ‘navigate’ or ‘tread carefully through’ a minefield.
examples: Using patients’ genetic data for commercial research is an ethical minefield.
The committee had to navigate an ethical minefield when approving the trial.
vocab.colloc: an ethical / legal minefield · navigate a minefield · a moral maze

vocab.def: a course of action that seems likely to lead to something much worse.
vocab.use: Often used to argue against a first step: ‘a slippery slope towards…’. In logic, the ‘slippery slope argument’ can be a fallacy if the chain of consequences is not justified.
examples: Critics warn that facial recognition in schools is a slippery slope towards mass surveillance.
Not every regulation is the start of a slippery slope.
vocab.colloc: a slippery slope towards / to · start down a slippery slope · the slippery slope argument

vocab.def: to make decisions that affect the life or nature of living things, as if you had divine power.
vocab.use: Critical; typical of debates on genetic engineering, cloning and end-of-life medicine. Usually followed by ‘with’: playing God with nature.
examples: Opponents accuse the scientists of playing God with the human genome.
Doctors are sometimes forced to play God when resources are scarce.
vocab.colloc: play God with · accuse someone of playing God

vocab.def: permission given by someone who fully understands the risks and consequences of what they are agreeing to.
vocab.use: A key principle in medical research and data ethics. You give, obtain or seek informed consent.
examples: No participant was enrolled without giving informed consent.
Clicking ‘accept’ on a 40-page agreement hardly amounts to informed consent.
vocab.colloc: obtain / seek / give informed consent · without informed consent

vocab.def: to produce a result, answer or piece of information.
vocab.use: Formal collocation in scientific writing: experiments yield results, data yield insights. Also ‘to yield to pressure’ (to give way).
examples: The trial yielded promising results in patients over sixty.
Analysing millions of search queries may yield valuable insights into public health.
vocab.colloc: yield results / insights / data · yield promising / mixed results

vocab.def: results of an action that were not planned or foreseen, often negative.
vocab.use: A favourite phrase in essays on technology and policy. ‘The law of unintended consequences’ refers to the idea that interventions always have unforeseen effects.
examples: Recommendation algorithms have had unintended consequences for political debate.
Regulators must anticipate the unintended consequences of banning encryption.
vocab.colloc: have unintended consequences · the law of unintended consequences · unforeseen consequences

vocab.def: to remain convincing or valid when examined carefully.
vocab.use: Often in the negative: ‘The claims do not stand up to scrutiny.’ Synonyms: hold water, withstand examination.
examples: The company’s claims about energy savings did not stand up to scrutiny.
Only findings that stand up to independent scrutiny should shape policy.
vocab.colloc: stand up to / withstand scrutiny · close / public scrutiny · come under scrutiny

vocab.def: people have not yet reached a decision or agreement about something.
vocab.use: A neat hedge for unresolved scientific or public debates. Followed by ‘on’ or a wh-clause.
examples: The jury is still out on whether screen time harms adolescent mental health.
Ten years on, the jury is still out on the long-term effects of the treatment.
vocab.colloc: the jury is (still) out on · the jury is out as to whether

vocab.def: at a very early stage of development.
vocab.use: Common with technologies, fields of research and industries. Opposite: ‘a mature technology / field’.
examples: Quantum computing is still in its infancy.
When the research began, the science of gene editing was in its infancy.
vocab.colloc: still in its infancy · a technology in its infancy · relatively in its infancy

grammar.name: Advanced passives: reporting passives and passive infinitives
grammar.short: It is believed that… / The drug is thought to have been tested… — reporting claims with distance.
grammar.rule: Reporting passives let us present information as other people’s claims, opinions or knowledge without naming them, which is essential in academic, scientific and journalistic writing. There are two patterns: ‘It + passive reporting verb + that-clause’ and ‘Subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive’. In the second pattern, the form of the infinitive shows the time relation: simple (same time), continuous (in progress), perfect (earlier) and passive (the subject is affected).
form: It-pattern: It + is / was + said / believed / thought + that-clause → It is widely believed that AI will transform medicine.
Same time: subject + is said + to + verb → The algorithm is said to outperform doctors.
In progress: subject + is thought + to be + -ing → The company is thought to be developing a rival model.
Earlier: subject + is believed + to have + past participle → The hackers are believed to have accessed millions of records.
Passive infinitive: subject + is reported + to have been + past participle → The data are reported to have been sold to advertisers.
There-pattern: There + is said / thought + to be + noun → There are thought to be over a thousand such devices in use.
notes: Reporting verbs: say, believe, think, consider, expect, know, report, allege, claim, estimate, understand, rumour, presume, suppose. ‘Rumour’ is almost only used in the passive: “She is rumoured to be resigning.”
Tense of the reporting verb: “He was thought to have left” = people thought (then) that he had left (earlier).
Passive infinitives also follow verbs and adjectives: expect / hope / deserve / need to be done; likely / due / certain to be done — “The bill is likely to be amended.”
Perfect passive infinitive for earlier passive events: “The results appear to have been manipulated.”
Passive gerunds: “Nobody likes being monitored.” / “She denied having been paid by the company.”
Consider + object + (to be) + complement: “The trial is considered (to be) a success.”
examples: The new vaccine is expected to be approved by the end of the year.
The first genetically edited babies are reported to have been born in 2018.
It has been estimated that a third of the data collected is never used.
grammar.watch: Use the perfect infinitive for earlier events: write “The files are believed to have been deleted last year”, not “The files are believed to be deleted last year”.
grammar.deep: Reporting passives are the grammar of attributed knowledge. They allow a writer to say that a claim exists without committing to it personally and without needing to identify precisely who holds it, which is exactly what scientific and journalistic writing often needs: ‘the treatment is thought to reduce inflammation’ signals a current consensus, while ‘the company is alleged to have concealed the risks’ protects the writer legally. The it-pattern foregrounds the claim as a whole and is common at the start of a paragraph; the personal pattern (subject + passive + infinitive) makes the thing being discussed the topic of the sentence, which usually improves cohesion. The real C2 challenge lies in the infinitive. Because the reporting verb carries one time reference and the infinitive another, writers must coordinate the two: ‘is said to have been working’ combines a present report with a past, ongoing activity. Passive infinitives add a further layer when the subject is affected by the action: ‘the patients are understood to have been given a placebo’. Choosing the reporting verb is equally important. ‘Know’ asserts fact, ‘believe’ and ‘think’ suggest opinion, ‘claim’ and ‘allege’ signal doubt, and ‘estimate’ marks a calculation — so the verb itself is a form of hedging.

chart.title: Personal reporting passives: time and voice
rows: The chip is said to cost under a dollar.
Regulators are thought to be investigating.
The firm is alleged to have ignored warnings.
They are believed to have been collecting data for years.
The system is expected to be launched in May.
The images are reported to have been altered.

more: The leaked model is rumoured to have been trained on copyrighted material.
It is now generally accepted that the earlier study was flawed.
The device was known to be overheating long before the recall.
There is said to be no reliable way of detecting AI-generated essays.
The participants were understood to have been given a placebo.
The project deserves to be funded, given its potential impact.

fix.wrong: It is said the CEO to have resigned.
fix.right: The CEO is said to have resigned. / It is said that the CEO has resigned.
fix.why: Don’t mix the patterns: use either ‘It is said that…’ or ‘Subject + is said to…’.

fix.wrong: People are rumouring that the company will close.
fix.right: The company is rumoured to be closing.
fix.why: ‘Rumour’ is used almost exclusively in the passive.

fix.wrong: The results seem to be manipulated before publication.
fix.right: The results seem to have been manipulated before publication.
fix.why: An earlier passive action needs the perfect passive infinitive ‘to have been + p.p.’.

drill.name: Newsroom rewrite
drill.prompt: Rewrite each active report twice: once with ‘It is… that’ and once with ‘Subject + passive + infinitive’. Choose the infinitive that matches the time relation.
items: People say the robot can recognise emotions.
Experts believe the virus originated in bats.
Sources report that the company is testing the drug on volunteers.
Investigators think someone altered the data last year.
Scientists expect that regulators will approve the trial soon.

dialogue.line: Have you seen the headline? ‘AI system discovers new antibiotic.’
Read the article, though. The compound is only thought to have antibacterial properties.
It says it’s been tested.
It’s said to have been tested on mice. Human trials aren’t expected to begin for years.
So the headline’s a bit premature.
It would appear so.

contrast.title: Choosing the reporting verb
rows: Smoking is known to cause cancer.
The species is thought to be extinct.
The market is estimated to be worth $2bn.
The app is claimed to cure insomnia.
The firm is rumoured to be for sale.

grammar.sound: In ‘is said to have been’, everything except the lexical verbs is weak: /ɪz ˈsed tə həv bɪn/. Stress ‘said’ and the final participle, and keep ‘to have been’ light and fast.

grammar.name: Causatives: have/get something done; have someone do
grammar.short: Arranging services, suffering misfortunes and getting others to act: have it checked, get him to sign, have my data stolen.
grammar.rule: Causative structures show that the subject causes something to be done rather than doing it personally. ‘Have / get + object + past participle’ focuses on the action and the result (‘We had the software updated’). ‘Have + person + base verb’ and ‘get + person + to-infinitive’ focus on the person who does the action. The same ‘have / get + object + past participle’ pattern also describes unpleasant experiences that happen to the subject (‘She had her account hacked’).
form: Service: have + object + past participle → We had the servers moved to a secure site.
Service (informal / effort): get + object + past participle → I finally got my laptop repaired.
Instruction: have + person + base verb → The lab had an independent team verify the results.
Persuasion: get + person + to-infinitive → We couldn’t get the company to release the code.
Misfortune: have + object + past participle → Thousands of users had their passwords stolen.
Result / tolerance: have + object + -ing → The new interface had everyone complaining within a day.
notes: Get vs have: ‘get’ is more informal and often implies effort or persuasion — “I eventually got the bank to refund me.”
Get + object + past participle can also mean finishing a task yourself: “I need to get this report written by Friday.”
Make + person + base verb = force; in the passive ‘to’ appears — “They made us sign a non-disclosure agreement” / “We were made to sign…”.
Won’t have + object + -ing = refuse to tolerate: “I won’t have my students using AI to write their essays.”
Need / want + object + past participle: “I want this data deleted by tomorrow.”
examples: Patients can now have their entire genome sequenced for a few hundred dollars.
The editor had two independent experts review the paper before publication.
Several celebrities have had their voices cloned without permission.
grammar.watch: Keep the object before the participle: write “I had my phone repaired”, not “I had repaired my phone” (which means you repaired it yourself).
grammar.deep: Causatives encode a division of labour: the grammatical subject is the instigator, while the real doer either stays offstage or appears as the object. This is why the structures are so frequent when we talk about services (‘get your eyes tested’), institutions (‘The university had the claims investigated’) and technology (‘We had the system audited’). The ‘have + object + past participle’ pattern is grammatically identical whether the subject wanted the action or not, so context alone tells us whether ‘She had her car towed’ was a service or a misfortune; in discussions of privacy and cybercrime, the misfortune reading is especially common (‘millions had their data exposed’). The person-focused patterns differ in nuance. ‘Have someone do’ suggests the authority to give instructions — a manager, a client, a professional relationship — while ‘get someone to do’ suggests persuasion or overcoming reluctance. ‘Make someone do’ adds compulsion. A further, less familiar use, ‘have + object + -ing’, describes a result the subject brings about (‘The demo had investors queuing up’) or, with ‘won’t’, something the subject refuses to tolerate. Mastering these distinctions allows a speaker to describe who is responsible for an action — a central question in any ethical debate.

chart.title: Causative patterns compared
rows: I got the bug fixed at last.
I’ll have IT reset your password.
We got the CEO to apologise.

more: The hospital had all its records digitised in a single year.
Campaigners finally got the government to publish the algorithm’s criteria.
Users were made to agree to new terms before they could log in.
I won’t have my children carrying a phone that tracks their location.
You should get that contract checked by a lawyer before signing.
The researchers had volunteers wear sensors for a month.

fix.wrong: I had the technician to install the update.
fix.right: I had the technician install the update.
fix.why: ‘Have + person’ is followed by the base verb, without ‘to’.

fix.wrong: We got the manager approve the budget.
fix.right: We got the manager to approve the budget.
fix.why: ‘Get + person’ takes the to-infinitive.

fix.wrong: She had stolen her bank details online.
fix.right: She had her bank details stolen online.
fix.why: For a misfortune, the object comes before the past participle; otherwise she is the thief.

drill.name: Who did it?
drill.prompt: For each situation, make one sentence focusing on the action (have / get something done) and one focusing on the person (have someone do / get someone to do). Then say whether it was a service, an instruction, persuasion or a misfortune.
items: A hacker accessed my email account.
An engineer checked the code for security flaws.
We persuaded the hospital to share anonymised data.
The manager told the intern to rewrite the summary.
A lab analysed my DNA to trace my ancestry.

dialogue.line: I had my DNA analysed last month — one of those ancestry kits.
Did you have them delete the data afterwards?
I tried. I couldn’t get anyone to give me a straight answer.
That’s worrying. A friend of mine had her health records leaked after a similar company was hacked.
Right — I’m going to get a lawyer to look at their privacy policy.

contrast.title: Who did the action?
rows: I had the shop repair it.
I got the shop to repair it for free.
I need to get this repaired by Monday.

grammar.sound: Stress the object and the participle, not ‘have’: “I had my PHONE rePAIRED.” If you stress ‘had’, listeners may hear the past perfect — “I HAD repaired…”.

grammar.name: Hedging and impersonal structures in academic English
grammar.short: may suggest, it would appear, tends to, arguably, there is some evidence that — claims that are careful, not weak.
grammar.rule: Hedging is the use of language to qualify a claim so that it reflects exactly how strong the evidence is. Academic and professional writers hedge to show caution, to anticipate objections and to stay accurate. Impersonal structures (it-clauses, there-clauses, passives, abstract subjects) remove the writer from the text and make claims sound objective. Together they create the measured voice expected in a CPE essay.
form: Modal hedge: may / might / could + verb → These findings may indicate a link between screen use and sleep.
Lexical verb: appear / seem / tend + to-infinitive → Users tend to overestimate the security of their data.
Impersonal it: It + would + seem / appear + that-clause → It would seem that the benefits outweigh the risks.
Impersonal passive: It + could be + argued / suggested + that-clause → It could be argued that regulation stifles innovation.
There-structure: There + is + some / growing + evidence + that-clause → There is growing evidence that the treatment is effective.
Adverb / adjective: arguably / seemingly / likely / to some extent + claim → This is arguably the most significant risk.
notes: Degrees of commitment: ‘proves’ → ‘demonstrates’ → ‘shows’ → ‘indicates’ → ‘suggests’ → ‘may suggest’. Choose the verb that matches the evidence.
Approximators soften numbers and scope: approximately, roughly, in the region of, to some extent, in most cases, broadly speaking.
Boosters are the opposite of hedges (clearly, undoubtedly, it is evident that); use them only when the evidence is overwhelming.
Distancing the source: ‘According to…’, ‘Proponents claim…’, ‘The data purportedly show…’ attribute a claim without endorsing it.
Overhedging weakens writing: “It might possibly perhaps suggest” is not careful but evasive. One or two hedges per claim are usually enough.
Impersonal does not mean passive everywhere: abstract subjects (“This analysis shows…”, “The evidence points to…”) are equally impersonal and more dynamic.
examples: The results would appear to suggest that the algorithm is less accurate for darker skin tones.
It could be argued that the right to privacy is incompatible with the business model of social media.
Gene therapy is likely to become more affordable, although the jury is still out on its long-term safety.
grammar.watch: Don’t stack hedges: write “The data suggest a possible link”, not “The data might possibly seem to suggest a possible link”.
grammar.deep: Hedging is often misunderstood by learners as a sign of weakness or uncertainty, but in academic and professional culture it is a sign of credibility. A writer who claims that a single study ‘proves’ that smartphones cause depression invites immediate rejection; one who writes that the study ‘provides some evidence of an association’ is far harder to dismiss. Hedges operate at several levels. Modal verbs adjust probability; lexical verbs such as ‘suggest’, ‘indicate’ and ‘appear’ adjust the strength of the link between evidence and claim; adverbs and adjectives such as ‘arguably’, ‘likely’ and ‘apparently’ adjust the writer’s commitment; approximators adjust the precision of numbers and scope. Impersonal structures work alongside them by shifting attention from the writer to the evidence: ‘It is widely acknowledged that…’, ‘There is little doubt that…’, ‘This would suggest…’. The aim is calibration, not vagueness. A C2 writer uses boosters when the evidence warrants them and hedges when it does not, and avoids accumulating hedges until the claim disappears. In a CPE Part 1 essay, careful hedging is also how you evaluate the input texts: pointing out that a writer ‘seems to assume’ something or ‘arguably overstates’ a risk is evaluation expressed with academic tact.

chart.title: The hedging toolkit
rows: This is arguably the key issue.
likely, possible, a tendency, a possibility
There is a strong likelihood of delays.
approximately, to some extent, in most cases
It would seem that… / There is evidence that… / It could be argued that…
It would seem that consent was not obtained.

more: To some extent, the concerns about job losses appear to have been exaggerated.
There is little evidence to suggest that the technology is safe for children.
It is widely acknowledged that informed consent is difficult to obtain online.
The purported benefits of the app do not appear to stand up to scrutiny.
In most cases, users seem unaware of how much data they share.
This would suggest that further research is needed before the policy is adopted.

fix.wrong: This study proves that social media causes depression.
fix.right: This study suggests that social media use may be associated with depression.
fix.why: A single correlational study cannot ‘prove’ causation; hedge the verb and the relationship.

fix.wrong: It is seemed that the data were incomplete.
fix.right: It seems / It would seem that the data were incomplete.
fix.why: ‘Seem’ and ‘appear’ are not used in the passive.

fix.wrong: I think that maybe perhaps the risks are possibly overstated.
fix.right: The risks may be overstated.
fix.why: Overhedging makes the writer sound evasive; one well-chosen hedge is enough.

drill.name: Calibrate the claim
drill.prompt: Rewrite each overconfident claim with appropriate hedging for an academic essay. Then rewrite one of them with too many hedges and ask your partner to fix it.
items: AI will replace all doctors within twenty years.
Facial recognition is completely accurate.
Video games make children violent.
Gene editing will eliminate hereditary diseases.
Nobody reads privacy policies.

dialogue.line: Your conclusion says the app ‘definitely improves’ mental health.
Well, the users said they felt better.
Self-reported, sixty people, no control group. I’d write ‘would appear to be associated with’.
Doesn’t that sound weak?
It sounds honest. And it could be argued that honesty is what reviewers look for.

contrast.title: Booster, neutral or hedge?
rows: clearly demonstrates, it is evident that
The data clearly demonstrate a fall in errors.
The trial shows the drug is effective.
The findings suggest a possible link.
may suggest, it would appear that
It would appear that some data are missing.
The device is claimed to halve energy use.

grammar.sound: Hedges are spoken with a slight fall-rise and often a short pause: “It would ap↘pear↗ … that consent was not obtained.” Stressing the hedge itself (‘it may’) signals deliberate caution.

speaking.text: Speak for two minutes: ‘Should there be limits on what scientists are allowed to research?’ Prompt ideas: gene editing, artificial intelligence, animal testing. Use reporting passives to refer to what experts think and hedge your own conclusions.

A city council is considering five technologies: facial recognition cameras, AI-assisted triage in hospitals, smart meters that share energy data, predictive policing software and digital identity cards. Discuss the benefits and ethical risks of each, then agree on which one the council should introduce first and which it should reject.

‘If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.’ Discuss this argument about surveillance and privacy. Refer to experiences of having data collected, accounts hacked or decisions made by algorithms, using causatives naturally (‘I had my account suspended’, ‘We got the company to delete it’).

In groups of four, you are an ethics committee. Your teacher presents a case (an AI that predicts which patients will miss appointments; a company that wants to sell anonymised location data). Each member takes a perspective — scientist, patient, lawyer, investor — and the group must reach a hedged, reasoned decision.

tips: Match the reporting verb to the evidence: ‘is known to’ for facts, ‘is thought to’ for consensus, ‘is claimed to’ or ‘purportedly’ when you doubt the source.
With personal reporting passives, check the infinitive: ‘is said to work’ (now), ‘is said to have worked’ (before), ‘is said to have been tested’ (before, passive).
Word order is meaning in causatives: ‘I had my bag stolen’ (victim) vs ‘I had stolen a bag’ (thief!).
In CPE essays, evaluate the input texts with tactful hedges — ‘the writer arguably overstates…’, ‘this seems to assume…’ — rather than blunt judgements.

quiz.q: The leaked files are believed ___ by a former employee last spring.
quiz.explain: An earlier action with a passive meaning requires the perfect passive infinitive: ‘to have been + past participle’.

test.q: It ___ that the first human clinical trials will begin next year.
test.explain: Impersonal reporting passive: ‘It is expected that…’.

test.q: The company is thought ___ a rival chatbot at the moment.
test.explain: ‘To be + -ing’ shows an activity in progress at the time of reporting.

test.q: Millions of users are reported ___ their personal data exposed in the breach.
test.explain: Perfect infinitive + causative of misfortune: ‘to have had + object + p.p.’.

test.q: The pop star is ___ to be planning a comeback tour.
test.explain: ‘Rumour’ is used almost exclusively in the passive: ‘is rumoured to’.

test.q: We finally got the hospital ___ the anonymised data.
test.explain: ‘Get + person + to-infinitive’ = persuade someone to do something.

test.q: The professor had her research assistants ___ the interviews.
test.explain: ‘Have + person + base verb’ = instruct someone to do something.

test.q: Which sentence describes a misfortune?
options: She had her laptop stolen at the airport.
She had the technician fix it.
test.explain: ‘Have + object + p.p.’ describes something bad that happened to the subject when the action is unwanted.

test.q: Which claim is most appropriately hedged for a single small study?
options: The study proves the app reduces anxiety.
The study clearly shows the app reduces anxiety.
The study might possibly perhaps suggest some effect.
The study suggests the app may help reduce anxiety.
test.explain: ‘Suggests … may help’ matches limited evidence without overhedging.

test.q: It ___ that the participants were not fully informed of the risks.
test.explain: ‘It would appear that…’ is an impersonal hedge; ‘seem / appear’ are not passive.

test.q: Clicking ‘I agree’ on a forty-page document hardly amounts to ___ consent.
test.explain: The fixed collocation is ‘informed consent’.

test.q: Critics warn that allowing police drones is a ___ slope towards constant surveillance.
test.explain: ‘A slippery slope’ = a first step that leads to something worse.

test.q: The manufacturer’s claims about battery life did not stand up to ___.
test.explain: ‘To stand up to scrutiny’ = remain valid after careful examination.

dynamics.name: Headline vs abstract
dynamics.how: Pairs receive four sensational science headlines (‘Coffee cures cancer!’) and the short invented study summaries behind them. They rewrite each headline as a responsible first sentence for a science article, using reporting passives and hedging. The class votes on the version that is most accurate yet still engaging.
dynamics.payoff: Shows why hedging and reporting passives exist and practises calibrating claims.

dynamics.name: Service or disaster?
dynamics.how: Each group gets a pile of picture or word cards (hair, passport, car, data, roof, phone). Students take turns making causative sentences that are either a service or a misfortune; the others must guess which and justify it from context or intonation.
dynamics.payoff: Highlights the ambiguity of ‘have something done’ and the role of context.

dynamics.name: Ethics committee
dynamics.how: Each group role-plays a committee deciding on a controversial project (an AI therapist for teenagers, editing crops to resist drought). Each member must use at least two hedging devices and one reporting passive. A secretary records the final decision in three hedged sentences to read to the class.
dynamics.payoff: Integrates all three grammar points in an authentic professional discussion.

writing.title: Should algorithms make decisions about people?
writing.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Consistency over intuition: Human decision-makers are far less consistent than we like to believe. Studies of judges, doctors and recruiters show that the same case can receive very different outcomes depending on the time of day, the decision-maker’s mood or the previous case they handled. A well-designed algorithm, by contrast, applies the same criteria every time. Used carefully, automated systems could make decisions about loans, diagnoses and job applications not only faster but fairer than the people they replace.

Text 2 — The trouble with black boxes: An algorithm is only as fair as the data it learns from, and historical data often reflect decades of discrimination. Worse, many systems are so complex that even their designers cannot explain why a particular decision was made. When a person is refused a mortgage or a medical treatment, they deserve to know why, and to appeal to someone who can be held responsible. No efficiency gain justifies decisions that cannot be explained or challenged.
writing.briefEs: Lee los dos textos y escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe sus ideas sobre el uso de algoritmos para tomar decisiones sobre personas, con tu propia opinión.
criteria: Both key points of each text are summarised accurately in your own words: the inconsistency of human judgement and the fairness of fixed criteria; biased data and the lack of explanation and accountability.
Each argument is evaluated with tactful, hedged judgements, and your own position is clearly argued.
At least two reporting passives or passive infinitives and a range of hedging devices (would appear, arguably, tends to, it could be argued).
A formal, impersonal academic register with precise vocabulary (informed consent, unintended consequences, stand up to scrutiny).
writing.model:
The two texts consider whether automated systems should be trusted to make important decisions about people’s lives, reaching markedly different conclusions.

The first writer argues that human judgement is surprisingly unreliable. Decisions made by professionals such as judges and doctors are said to vary according to factors as trivial as fatigue or the order in which cases are heard. Algorithms, the author contends, would avoid such inconsistency by applying identical criteria to every case, potentially producing outcomes that are both quicker and more equitable. This argument is persuasive as far as consistency is concerned. However, it arguably assumes that consistency and fairness are the same thing, which is not necessarily the case: a system can apply biased criteria with perfect consistency.

It is precisely this weakness that the second text addresses. Its author points out that algorithms are trained on historical data which may well encode past prejudice, and that the internal workings of many systems are too opaque to be explained. Consequently, people affected by automated decisions are denied both an explanation and someone to hold accountable. This would appear to be the more fundamental objection, since a decision that cannot be questioned is difficult to reconcile with basic principles of justice.

In my view, the solution lies between the two positions. Algorithms could usefully be employed to flag inconsistencies in human decisions, but final judgements about loans, treatment or employment should remain with people who can be required to justify them. Until automated systems can be shown to be both transparent and free from inherited bias, they should assist human decision-makers rather than replace them.

homework.task: Find a recent news article (in English or Spanish) about a scientific or technological breakthrough. Write a 200-word summary in English for an academic audience, using at least three reporting passives with different infinitive forms, two causative structures and five hedging devices. Then add two sentences evaluating whether the original article overstated the findings, using tactful hedged language.

units.title: THE NATURAL WORLD

overview.intro: Environmental debate is full of counterfactuals: what would the landscape look like now if we had acted then, and what will happen should we fail to act today? At C2 the challenge is to handle these hypotheses with precision and in the right register — mixing time frames, inverting for formality and choosing the exact connector of condition rather than defaulting to “if”.
goals: Discuss climate, conservation and rewilding with precise collocations, compound adjectives and nature idioms.
Combine past and present time frames in mixed and implied conditionals.
Express conditions formally with inversion and with alternatives such as but for, provided and were it not for.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write a formal letter objecting to an environmental decision, arguing from past consequences to present risks with at least two inverted conditionals and three alternatives to if.

vocab.def: to return land to a natural state, often by reintroducing species that once lived there.
vocab.use: Usually transitive: “rewild a valley / an estate”. The noun “rewilding” is uncountable and names the whole movement.
examples: The estate was rewilded after decades of intensive grazing.
Rewilding is not about abandoning land but about letting natural processes lead.
vocab.colloc: rewild an estate · a rewilding project · large-scale rewilding

vocab.def: a species on which a whole ecosystem depends, so that its loss changes everything else.
vocab.use: Countable, but the plural is also “species”. Beavers, wolves and sea otters are classic examples in conservation writing.
examples: Beavers are a keystone species: their dams create entire wetlands.
Remove a keystone species and the food web begins to unravel.
vocab.colloc: a keystone species · reintroduce a keystone species · the role of a keystone predator

vocab.def: a forest, ocean, soil or bog that absorbs more carbon dioxide than it releases.
vocab.use: Its opposite is a “carbon source”. Scientists warn that some sinks may turn into sources as temperatures rise.
examples: Peat bogs are among the most efficient carbon sinks on the planet.
Degraded forests can stop acting as carbon sinks altogether.
vocab.colloc: a natural carbon sink · act as a carbon sink · turn from a sink into a source

vocab.def: the moment at which a gradual change becomes sudden, self-reinforcing and hard to reverse.
vocab.use: Common with “reach”, “pass”, “cross” and “approach”. In climate science it refers to thresholds such as ice-sheet collapse.
examples: The reef may already have passed a tipping point.
Scientists fear the rainforest is approaching a tipping point beyond which it turns to savannah.
vocab.colloc: reach / cross a tipping point · a climate tipping point · beyond the tipping point

vocab.def: to reduce the amount of a resource until little or none is left.
vocab.use: Formal; very often passive or as the adjective “depleted”. The noun is “depletion”.
examples: Overfishing has severely depleted cod stocks in the North Atlantic.
The aquifer is being depleted faster than it can recharge.
vocab.colloc: deplete stocks / reserves · severely depleted · ozone depletion

vocab.def: to prevent something bad from happening, or to delay it, for a while.
vocab.use: Separable but usually kept together with a long object: “stave off collapse / extinction / a crisis”. It implies the threat has not gone away.
examples: Emergency feeding staved off starvation among the young seals.
Short-term measures may stave off disaster, but they do not solve it.
vocab.colloc: stave off extinction · stave off collapse · stave off the worst effects

vocab.def: having a wide influence and many effects, often for a long time.
vocab.use: Mostly before a noun: “far-reaching consequences / reforms”. Hyphenated in that position; it is not normally graded with “very” — use “wide-ranging” or “profound” for variety.
examples: The ban on single-use plastics had far-reaching consequences for the packaging industry.
The report recommends far-reaching changes to land use.
vocab.colloc: far-reaching consequences · far-reaching reforms · far-reaching implications

vocab.def: made or caused by people rather than by nature.
vocab.use: Neutral and very common: “man-made climate change”. In inclusive or scientific style, “human-made”, “anthropogenic” or “artificial” are increasingly preferred.
examples: Most of the lakes in the region are man-made reservoirs.
The scale of man-made warming is no longer seriously disputed.
vocab.colloc: man-made fibres · man-made disaster · man-made / anthropogenic emissions

vocab.def: completely untouched, clean and in its original condition.
vocab.use: Collocates with wilderness, beaches, forest and condition. It is close to ungradable, so “absolutely pristine” is fine but “very pristine” sounds odd.
examples: Few truly pristine habitats remain anywhere in Europe.
The coastline, once pristine, is now lined with hotels.
vocab.colloc: pristine wilderness · pristine condition · a pristine coastline

vocab.def: to fill something up again or restore it to its former level.
vocab.use: Formal; used for stocks, supplies, water tables and soil. Often paired with “deplete” in contrast.
examples: Heavy winter rain replenished the reservoirs for the first time in years.
Fish stocks need decades to replenish once they collapse.
vocab.colloc: replenish stocks · replenish groundwater · naturally replenished

vocab.def: an amount so small compared with what is needed that it makes almost no difference.
vocab.use: Often used critically about funding or individual action. American English also has “a drop in the bucket”.
examples: Planting a thousand trees is a drop in the ocean compared with what was felled.
Critics dismissed the pledge as a drop in the ocean.
vocab.colloc: only / merely a drop in the ocean · dismiss something as a drop in the ocean

vocab.term: to nip something in the bud
vocab.def: to stop a problem at an early stage, before it can develop.
vocab.use: The image comes from gardening: pinching off a bud stops the flower. Usually used about problems, never about good things.
examples: Had the invasive weed been nipped in the bud, the river banks would not be choked with it now.
Rangers try to nip poaching in the bud by working with local communities.
vocab.colloc: nip a problem in the bud · nip it in the bud early on

grammar.name: Mixed and implied conditionals
grammar.short: Past cause with a present result — or the reverse — and conditions left unspoken.
grammar.rule: Mixed conditionals combine two different time frames. An unreal past condition can have a present result (If + past perfect, would + base verb), and an unreal present or permanent condition can have a past result (If + past simple, would have + past participle). Implied conditionals keep the result clause but carry the condition in a phrase — with, without, otherwise, in that case — or leave it to the context.
form: If + past perfect, would + base verb: If we had protected the wetlands, the town wouldn’t flood every winter.
If + past simple, would have + past participle: If the river weren’t so polluted, the otters would have returned years ago.
without / with + noun, would + base verb / would have + past participle: Without the seed bank, these varieties would have vanished.
would / could / might + base verb (condition implied): A ban on peat compost would make a real difference.
notes: Time words decide the type: ‘now’, ‘today’ and ‘still’ point to a present result; ‘then’, ‘last year’ and ‘in 1990’ point to a past one.
Present traits use the past simple in the if-clause: “If I weren’t so cautious, I would have joined the protest camp” — the caution is permanent, the missed protest is past.
Implied conditions hide in phrases: “Without the reserve, the lynx would have died out” means if there had not been a reserve.
‘Would’ alone can carry a condition the listener supplies: “I wouldn’t drink that water” (if I were you).
examples: If we had acted on the warnings in the 1990s, we wouldn’t be facing such severe droughts now.
If I weren’t so cautious by nature, I would have joined the protest camp.
Without the seed bank, these varieties would have vanished entirely.
grammar.watch: “If we would have acted sooner” is wrong — say “If we had acted sooner”: would belongs in the result clause, never in the if-clause of an unreal past.
grammar.deep: Textbook conditionals keep both clauses in one time frame, but real argument rarely does. Environmental reasoning in particular runs from past decisions to present consequences — “If the marsh hadn’t been drained, we would still have cranes here” — and from permanent present facts to past outcomes — “If the island weren’t so remote, it would have been developed long ago”. The trick is to treat each clause independently: choose the form of the if-clause for its own time (past perfect for an unreal past, past simple for an unreal present) and the form of the result for its own time (would + base for now, would have + participle for then). Implied conditionals go one step further and delete the if-clause altogether. The condition survives in a prepositional phrase (without, but for, in that case), in an adverb (otherwise), in an infinitive (“To hear him talk, you’d think he owned the forest”) or purely in context. At C2 these are the forms that make writing sound fluent rather than mechanical, because a reader never needs the full if-clause spelled out when the logic is already on the page.

chart.title: Mixed and implied conditionals
rows: If they hadn’t drained the marsh, we’d have cranes here today.
If + past simple → would have + p.p.
If she weren’t so stubborn, she’d have accepted the deal.
If + past perfect → would have + p.p.
If it had rained, the fire would have died down.
Without the levee, the village would have flooded.
We cut emissions; otherwise the reef would be gone.

more: If the council had listened to the ecologists, the river would still be full of salmon.
If beavers weren’t protected here, the farmers would have removed the dams last spring.
Had the forest not burned, the valley would look completely different today.
With a little more funding, the project could have doubled its reach.
Given the choice, most residents would keep the green belt exactly as it is.
If I were more of a scientist, I would have understood the data at first glance.

fix.wrong: If the dam wasn’t built in 1960, the valley would still be farmland.
fix.right: If the dam hadn’t been built in 1960, the valley would still be farmland.
fix.why: The condition is a dated past event, so it needs the past perfect even though the result is present.

fix.wrong: If she would be braver, she would have spoken at the hearing.
fix.right: If she were braver, she would have spoken at the hearing.
fix.why: A permanent present trait takes the past simple (were) in the if-clause, never would.

fix.wrong: If we hadn’t planted those hedges, there wouldn’t have been any birds here now.
fix.right: If we hadn’t planted those hedges, there wouldn’t be any birds here now.
fix.why: ‘Now’ signals a present result, so the main clause takes would + base verb.

drill.name: Then and now
drill.prompt: Turn each pair of facts into one mixed conditional, linking a past cause to a present result or a present trait to a past result.
items: They drained the wetland in 1975. / There are no cranes now.
She is a marine biologist. / She noticed the bleaching first.
The city banned cars from the centre. / The air is cleaner today.
I am not a patient person. / I gave up on the allotment.
Nobody replanted the slope after the fire. / The hillside is eroding.

dialogue.line: Look at this photo from 1980 — the whole bay was covered in seagrass.
If they hadn’t dredged it for the marina, it would still be like that now.
And if the town weren’t so dependent on tourism, nobody would have approved the marina in the first place.
True. Without that money, though, half the shops would be closed.

contrast.title: Which time does each clause refer to?
rows: If I had studied ecology, I would be a ranger now.
If I were a ranger, I would have seen the lynx.
If I had seen it, I would have photographed it.
If I were a ranger, I would patrol at night.
Without the rain, the crops would have failed.
Otherwise we would be in serious trouble.

grammar.sound: In fast speech “would have” shrinks to /ˈwʊdəv/ or even /ˈwʊdə/, and “had” to /əd/: “If we’d known, we’d’ve left.” In mixed conditionals the same ’d appears in both clauses with different meanings, so listen to what follows it: a participle after had, a base verb after would.

grammar.name: Inverted conditionals (Should…, Were…, Had…)
grammar.short: Formal conditions without if: the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.
grammar.rule: In formal English the word ‘if’ can be dropped and the auxiliary placed before the subject. ‘Should’ introduces a possible but unlikely or tentative future condition, ‘Were’ an unreal present or future one (often Were + subject + to-infinitive), and ‘Had’ an unreal past one. Only these three auxiliaries invert in this way, and the result clause stays exactly as it would be with if.
form: Should + subject + base verb: Should you require further information, please contact the reserve office.
Were + subject + to-infinitive: Were the ice sheet to collapse, sea levels would rise by several metres.
Were + subject + complement: Were I in your position, I would oppose the scheme.
Had + subject + (not) + past participle: Had the warnings been heeded, the fishery would not have collapsed.
notes: Negatives are never contracted in inversion: “Had it not been for the volunteers” — never ‘Hadn’t it been’.
Inverted ‘should’ is the standard polite formula in formal letters: Should you wish to object, please write before 30 June.
Only ‘were’ inverts for unreal present conditions; ‘Was I to…’ is not a conditional in standard English.
Mixed time frames still work: “Had we listened then, we would not be in this position now.”
examples: Should the drought continue, the authorities will impose water restrictions.
Were the government to scrap the subsidy, thousands of hectares would be ploughed up.
Had the beavers not been reintroduced, the village would have flooded again.
grammar.watch: “Hadn’t we ignored the data, …” is wrong — say “Had we not ignored the data, …”: in conditional inversion the negative follows the subject and is never contracted.
grammar.deep: Inversion is the formal face of the conditional. It belongs to official letters, reports, legal notices, academic prose and speeches, and it signals a register shift as clearly as vocabulary does. Each auxiliary keeps the meaning of its if-equivalent. “Should you need assistance” is the inverted form of “If you should need assistance”, a first conditional made more tentative; it is why the result clause can be an imperative or use will. “Were the river to burst its banks” corresponds to “If the river were to burst its banks” — a hypothetical future presented as remote; “Were I you” corresponds to “If I were you”. “Had we known” corresponds to “If we had known”, the unreal past. Two mechanical rules catch most errors. First, nothing else inverts: you cannot write ‘Did we act’ or ‘Could we act’ as a condition. Second, negatives stay uncontracted and follow the subject: “Were it not for”, “Should it not prove possible”, “Had they not intervened”. Used once or twice in a formal text, inversion sounds authoritative; used in every paragraph, it sounds like a parody of legal English.

chart.title: Three inverted conditionals
rows: Should the river rise, residents will be evacuated.
Were the dam to fail, the town would be submerged.
Were it my decision, I would halt the felling.
Had we acted sooner, the species would have survived.
Had it not been for the storm, the nests would be intact.
Had the forest been protected, it would still store carbon.

more: Should any member of the public find an injured bird, they are asked to call the sanctuary.
Were the moorland to be planted with conifers, the wading birds would disappear.
Had the oil company invested in safety, the spill would never have occurred.
Were it not for the wardens, the dunes would have been destroyed by quad bikes.
Should the consultation reveal strong opposition, the plan will be withdrawn.
Had I known how fragile the reef was, I would never have touched it.

fix.wrong: Hadn’t the council intervened, the meadow would have been built on.
fix.right: Had the council not intervened, the meadow would have been built on.
fix.why: Conditional inversion uses an uncontracted negative after the subject.

fix.wrong: Was the river to flood, the bridge would be closed.
fix.right: Were the river to flood, the bridge would be closed.
fix.why: Only ‘were’ is used in this inversion, whatever the subject.

fix.wrong: Did we protect the bog, it would absorb more carbon.
fix.right: Were we to protect the bog, it would absorb more carbon.
fix.why: Only should, were and had can replace if by inversion.

drill.name: Drop the if
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence in formal style by removing ‘if’ and inverting. Then say which time each condition refers to.
items: If you have any questions about the survey, please contact us.
If the glacier were to retreat further, the valley would lose its water supply.
If the company had carried out an impact study, the protest would not have happened.
If it weren’t for the funding from the trust, the reserve would close.
If the wolves hadn’t returned, the deer would still be overgrazing the riverbanks.

dialogue.line: We are confident the new road will have minimal impact on the woodland.
Had your consultants surveyed it in spring, they would have found three protected species.
Should that prove to be the case, we would of course revise the route.
Were you to revise it now, you would save everyone a very public dispute.

contrast.title: If or inversion?
rows: If you see a heron, send me a photo.
Should you see a heron, please record it.
If they were to close the park, there’d be uproar.
Were the park to close, there would be uproar.
If I’d known, I’d have come.
Had I known, I would have come.

grammar.sound: Inverted conditionals open with a fully stressed, unreduced auxiliary — SHOULD you, WERE it, HAD we — unlike the weak /həd/ in an ordinary clause. The condition ends with a slight rise and a pause before the result, which is how listeners recognise a condition rather than a question.

grammar.name: Alternatives to if: but for, otherwise, provided, supposing, were it not for
grammar.short: Connectors of condition that say more precisely what kind of condition you mean.
grammar.rule: English has a family of conditional connectors more precise than ‘if’. ‘Provided (that)’, ‘providing’, ‘as long as’ and ‘on condition that’ set a strict requirement. ‘Supposing’ and ‘suppose’ invite the listener to imagine a situation. ‘Otherwise’ means ‘if not’ and refers back to the previous clause. ‘But for’ + noun, ‘were it not for’ + noun and ‘had it not been for’ + noun name the single factor that prevents or prevented a different outcome. ‘Unless’ means ‘except if’, while ‘in case’ expresses precaution, not condition.
form: provided (that) / as long as + present tense: The wolves will be released provided that farmers are compensated.
Supposing / Suppose + past simple, would + base verb: Supposing the lynx strayed onto farmland, who would pay?
but for / were it not for + noun, would + base verb: But for the volunteers, the beach would be buried in plastic.
had it not been for + noun, would have + past participle: Had it not been for the storm, the nests would have survived.
clause; otherwise + clause: We must restore the bogs; otherwise, they will keep releasing carbon.
notes: Like if, these connectors take a present tense for future meaning: Provided it rains, not ‘Provided it will rain’.
‘But for’ is followed by a noun phrase, not a clause: “But for your help”, never “But for you helped”.
‘Otherwise’ is an adverb, not a conjunction: in formal writing put a full stop or semicolon before it.
Compare: ‘in case’ is precaution — “Take a map in case the path is closed” means take it anyway; ‘if’ would mean only when it is closed.
‘Supposing’ with the present is a real possibility; with the past it is more hypothetical: Supposing it rains / Supposing it rained.
examples: The trees will recover provided that the soil is left undisturbed.
But for the reintroduction of beavers, the stream would have dried up completely.
Supposing the ice melted entirely, how many cities would be under water?
grammar.watch: “Provided the funding will arrive, the work will start” is wrong — say “Provided the funding arrives, the work will start”: like if, these connectors take a present tense for future meaning.
grammar.deep: Choosing a connector of condition is choosing a stance. ‘Provided that’ and ‘on condition that’ are contractual: they make the result depend on a requirement and are typical of negotiation (“We will support the scheme provided that the hedgerows are kept”). ‘As long as’ does the same in a less formal register. ‘Supposing’ and ‘suppose’ open a thought experiment and are often used to challenge an opponent: “Suppose the reintroduction fails — what then?” ‘Otherwise’ is a compressed negative condition: “Act now; otherwise it will be too late” means “if we do not act now”. ‘But for’, ‘were it not for’ and ‘had it not been for’ are the most powerful in argument, because they isolate one cause and credit or blame it for an entire outcome: “Were it not for the Gulf Stream, Britain would have the climate of Labrador.” Note that ‘but for’ fits any time frame, and that ‘unless’ cannot replace ‘if … not’ when the result is unreal and the condition is the only thing that matters: “I’d be surprised if it didn’t rain”, not “unless it rained”.

chart.title: Connectors of condition
rows: Provided the soil stays wet, the moss will spread.
as long as / on condition that
You can camp here as long as you leave no trace.
Suppose the bees disappeared — what would we eat?
Replant now; otherwise the slope will erode.
but for / were it not for + noun
this one thing prevents a different result
Were it not for the dykes, the fields would flood.
had it not been for + noun
this one thing prevented a past result
Had it not been for the rangers, the rhinos would have been killed.

more: As long as the river stays clean, the otters will stay.
The land can be leased on condition that no pesticides are used.
Supposing we doubled the size of the reserve, would the birds actually return?
Water the saplings daily; otherwise they won’t survive the summer.
But for a single photograph, nobody would have believed the species still existed.
Were it not for the sea breeze, the town would be unbearable in August.

fix.wrong: But for the dam was built, the canyon would be intact.
fix.right: But for the dam, the canyon would be intact.
fix.why: ‘But for’ takes a noun phrase, not a clause.

fix.wrong: Provided the council will approve it, work starts in May.
fix.right: Provided the council approves it, work starts in May.
fix.why: Conditional connectors take a present tense for future meaning.

fix.wrong: Take a torch, in case it will get dark.
fix.right: Take a torch in case it gets dark.
fix.why: ‘In case’ also takes a present tense, and it expresses precaution, not a condition.

drill.name: Choose your connector
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the connector given, keeping the meaning. Then say what shade of meaning the connector adds.
items: If it hadn’t been for the fog, we would have seen the eagles. (had it not been for)
If we don’t reduce grazing, the heather will disappear. (otherwise)
The scheme will go ahead only if the landowners agree. (provided that)
Imagine the rainforest disappeared completely. What would happen to rainfall? (supposing)
If there weren’t a buffer zone, the wetland would be polluted. (but for)

dialogue.line: Supposing the farmers refuse to sell, what happens to the rewilding plan?
It still goes ahead, provided we can lease the upland fields.
And the funding? Were it not for the lottery grant, we’d have nothing.
Exactly. We have to apply by Friday; otherwise the grant goes to another region.

contrast.title: Unless, in case, provided
rows: We’ll cancel the walk if it rains.
We’ll go provided the path is open.
Take a coat in case it rains.
Leave early; otherwise you’ll miss the tide.
But for the rain, it was a perfect day.

grammar.sound: “Provided that” and “supposing” carry a strong stress on their second syllable: pro-VI-ded, sup-PO-sing. “Otherwise” is stressed on the first syllable and followed by a pause in speech, mirroring the comma or semicolon in writing: “Hurry — OTHerwise | we’ll miss it.”

speaking.text: Talk for two minutes on this question: “Can rewilding succeed in densely populated countries?” Refer to at least one real place, and include one mixed conditional about what would be different today had decisions been taken earlier.

With a partner, you are advising a city council with a limited budget. Choose two of these projects and justify your choice: reintroducing beavers upstream, planting an urban forest, banning cars from the centre, restoring a drained wetland. Use provided, otherwise and supposing to set conditions.
“Individual action is a drop in the ocean; only governments can stave off a climate crisis.” To what extent do you agree? Give reasons and examples, and respond to your partner’s points.
This house believes that conservation should prioritise keystone species over charismatic ones. Prepare an opening statement using two inverted conditionals (Should…, Were…, Had…).

tips: Treat each clause of a mixed conditional separately: choose its tense for its own time — past perfect for an unreal past, past simple for an unreal present.
Only should, were and had invert in conditionals, and their negatives never contract: “Had it not been for…”, never “Hadn’t it been for…”.
‘But for’ and ‘were it not for’ take a noun phrase; ‘provided’, ‘supposing’ and ‘as long as’ take a clause with a present tense for future meaning.
Common slip: ‘man-made’ and ‘far-reaching’ are hyphenated before a noun, and ‘pristine’ is close to ungradable — say ‘absolutely pristine’, not ‘very pristine’.

quiz.q: ___ the warnings been heeded, the fishery would still be thriving today.
quiz.explain: Inverted ‘Had’ replaces ‘If … had’: an unreal past condition with a present result, so this is also a mixed conditional.

test.q: If the marsh hadn’t been drained in the seventies, cranes ___ there now.
test.explain: Unreal past cause, present result (‘now’): would + base verb.

test.q: If she ___ so impatient, she would have waited for the eagles to return.
test.explain: Impatience is a permanent present trait, so the if-clause takes the past simple ‘weren’t’; the result is past.

test.q: ___ you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact the trust.
test.explain: Inverted ‘should’ is the standard polite formula for a possible future condition in formal letters.

test.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Hadn’t the rangers intervened, the rhinos would have died.
Had the rangers not intervened, the rhinos would have died.
Had not the rangers intervened, the rhinos would have died.
If had the rangers not intervened, the rhinos would have died.
test.explain: In conditional inversion the negative is uncontracted and follows the subject: Had + subject + not + participle.

test.q: ___ the ice sheet to collapse, sea levels would rise dramatically.
test.explain: Were + subject + to-infinitive is the inverted form of ‘If the ice sheet were to collapse’. ‘Was’ never inverts in this way.

test.q: ___ the Gulf Stream, northern Europe would be far colder.
test.explain: ‘Were it not for’ + noun names the one factor that prevents a different present result.

test.q: The wolves will be released ___ farmers receive compensation for any losses.
test.explain: ‘Provided that’ sets a strict requirement for the result to happen.

test.q: We need to replant the slope this autumn; ___, it will erode in the winter rains.
test.explain: ‘Otherwise’ means ‘if we don’t’ and refers back to the previous clause.

test.q: Which word completes both sentences? ‘Overfishing has severely ___ cod stocks.’ / ‘The aquifer is being ___ faster than it can recharge.’
test.explain: To deplete = to reduce a resource until little is left; ‘replenish’ is its opposite.

test.q: Scientists fear the rainforest may soon reach a ___, after which it will turn into savannah.
test.explain: A tipping point is the threshold beyond which change becomes sudden and self-reinforcing.

test.q: Emergency measures may ___ collapse for a few years, but they will not solve the problem.
test.explain: To stave off = to prevent or delay something bad temporarily; the threat remains.

test.q: Critics dismissed the pledge to plant 500 trees as ___ given the scale of deforestation.
test.explain: ‘A drop in the ocean’ is an amount too small to make a real difference.

dynamics.name: The butterfly chain
dynamics.how: Each group receives one historical environmental decision (draining a lake, introducing rabbits to Australia, building a dam). Student 1 says a mixed conditional about today; student 2 must build on the result with an implied conditional (without, otherwise); student 3 inverts it formally; student 4 rewrites it with but for or were it not for. The chain continues until a group repeats a structure.
dynamics.payoff: Forces students to move between the four ways of expressing one counterfactual.

dynamics.name: Formal or friendly
dynamics.how: Student A reads an informal conditional (If you see a heron, text me). Student B must instantly produce the version for an official notice (Should you see a heron, please record it). Roles swap after five sentences; pairs score a point for every correct, uncontracted negative inversion.
dynamics.payoff: Builds the register reflex that CPE writing tasks reward.

dynamics.name: Planning committee
dynamics.how: The class becomes a planning committee deciding whether to rewild a reservoir. Roles: farmers, ecologists, a water company, residents. Each speaker must set at least one condition with provided, supposing or on condition that before the final vote.
dynamics.payoff: Real negotiation makes the choice of connector meaningful, not decorative.

writing.title: Objection to the drainage of Holloway Marsh
writing.brief: Your local council plans to drain part of a wetland nature reserve to build 300 homes. Write a formal letter to the head of planning objecting to the scheme. Explain what the marsh has already done for the area, set out the risks of the plan and propose an alternative, stating under what conditions you would support development.
writing.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal al responsable de urbanismo oponiéndote a desecar un humedal; explica sus beneficios, los riesgos del proyecto y propone una alternativa con condiciones.
criteria: Formal letter conventions: appropriate opening and closing, a clear statement of purpose and a courteous but firm tone throughout.
At least two inverted conditionals (Should…, Were…, Had…) and one mixed conditional linking past decisions to present consequences.
Three alternatives to if (provided that, otherwise, but for, were it not for, supposing) used with precise meaning.
Four items of unit vocabulary, including one compound adjective and one nature idiom, used naturally.
writing.model:
Dear Ms Okafor,

I am writing on behalf of the Holloway Residents’ Association to object to the proposal to drain the eastern section of Holloway Marsh for housing.

The marsh is far more than an attractive green space. It acts as a natural sponge: had it not absorbed the floodwater in February 2020, more than eighty homes on Mill Lane would have been inundated. It is also a significant carbon sink, and it supports the only breeding colony of bitterns in the county. Its reed beds also filter run-off from the surrounding farmland, which is why the river below Holloway Bridge now meets bathing-water standards for the first time in decades. Were it not for the marsh, the town would be both more vulnerable and considerably poorer in wildlife.

The consequences of drainage would be far-reaching. If the council had consulted hydrologists before drafting the plan, it would now be aware that the remaining wetland could not cope with the run-off from 300 new roofs. Should the scheme proceed, the risk of flooding downstream will increase, and the new residents themselves may find their properties uninsurable.

We do not oppose new housing in principle. We would support development on the disused depot site on Station Road, provided that the council commits to protecting the marsh in its local plan. Supposing the depot site proved insufficient, a smaller scheme on the existing car park could make up the shortfall. Every alternative should be examined; otherwise, the council risks repeating mistakes that neighbouring towns are now spending millions to reverse.

I would therefore urge you to reject the current proposal and nip this costly mistake in the bud. Should you wish to discuss our findings, I would be glad to meet you at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,

Daniel Restrepo
Chair, Holloway Residents’ Association

homework.title: One landscape, four counterfactuals
homework.task: Choose a real landscape you know that has changed (a river, a coast, a forest, a city park). Write eight sentences about it: two mixed conditionals (past cause → present result and present trait → past result), two inverted conditionals, and four sentences using but for, otherwise, provided that and supposing. Underline the verb forms in both clauses and label each clause with its time (past / present / future).

board: Top left: a two-column timeline — IF-CLAUSE TIME | RESULT TIME — with arrows: past → present (If + had done, would do) and present → past (If + did, would have done).
Top right: three formal doors — SHOULD you… / WERE it to… / HAD we…, each with its if-equivalent written underneath.
A red box: “Hadn’t it been for…” crossed out → “Had it not been for…” (no contraction, not after the subject).
Bottom left: the connector ladder — provided / as long as (requirement) · supposing (imagine) · otherwise (if not) · but for + NOUN (this one thing).
Bottom right: vocabulary web around CARBON SINK: deplete ↔ replenish · stave off · tipping point · far-reaching · a drop in the ocean.

units.title: ARTS, CULTURE AND CRITICISM
units.theme: Art, cinema, literature, taste and cultural value

overview.intro: Good criticism is precise: it says exactly how good, how original and how moving a work is, without repeating itself. This unit gives you the tools critics rely on — ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition, a finely graded scale of intensifiers and downtoners, and dense noun phrases built with stacked adjectives and compound modifiers.
