goals: Evaluate films, books, exhibitions and performances with critical vocabulary and idioms of praise and criticism.
Avoid repetition with ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, one).
Grade your judgements precisely with intensifiers, downtoners and well-ordered, compound modifiers.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write a balanced, publishable review of a cultural event, calibrating praise and criticism with precise modifiers and without a single unnecessary repetition.

vocab.def: copying the ideas or style of other works, and lacking originality.
vocab.use: Always critical in reviews: “a derivative thriller”. As a noun it means something developed from something else (a derivative of a drug or a financial product).
examples: The plot is so derivative that you can predict every twist.
Her early paintings were derivative of Matisse, but she soon found her own voice.
vocab.colloc: derivative of someone · hopelessly derivative · a derivative plot

vocab.def: used so often that it has lost its effect and become boring.
vocab.use: For phrases, plots, images and themes. Near-synonyms: clichéd, trite, stale.
examples: The dialogue is full of hackneyed lines about following your dreams.
The ‘chosen one’ narrative feels hackneyed by now.
vocab.colloc: a hackneyed phrase · hackneyed imagery · a hackneyed plot device

vocab.def: a performance or achievement of outstanding skill.
vocab.use: Borrowed from French and used in the singular: “Her performance is a tour de force.” Plural: tours de force.
examples: The final ten-minute tracking shot is a technical tour de force.
Critics hailed the novel as a tour de force of comic writing.
vocab.colloc: a technical tour de force · an acting tour de force · hailed as a tour de force

vocab.def: the complete body of work of a writer, artist or composer.
vocab.use: Formal, usually singular: “his entire oeuvre”, “a minor work in her oeuvre”. Pronounced /ˈɜːvrə/.
examples: This film is an anomaly in an otherwise sombre oeuvre.
The retrospective covers her entire oeuvre, from sketches to murals.
vocab.colloc: an artist’s entire oeuvre · a key work in his oeuvre · the late oeuvre

vocab.def: a work that imitates the style of another artist or period, either as homage or without originality.
vocab.use: Can be neutral (a playful homage) or critical (an empty imitation); context and modifiers decide. Unlike parody, pastiche does not necessarily mock.
examples: The film is an affectionate pastiche of 1950s melodrama.
At its worst, the building is a lifeless pastiche of classical architecture.
vocab.colloc: an affectionate pastiche · a pastiche of something · mere pastiche

vocab.def: new and experimental, especially in art; or the artists who create such work.
vocab.use: Adjective: “an avant-garde composer”. Noun with ‘the’: “the Parisian avant-garde”. Hyphenated in both uses.
examples: The festival champions avant-garde theatre that rarely reaches mainstream stages.
In the 1920s she was at the heart of the European avant-garde.
vocab.colloc: avant-garde art / music · the avant-garde · resolutely avant-garde

vocab.def: intellectual and serious, often in a way that seems inaccessible to most people.
vocab.use: Can be slightly mocking. Opposites: lowbrow (unsophisticated) and middlebrow (accessible but conventional).
examples: The station’s highbrow reputation scares off younger listeners.
She moves effortlessly between highbrow fiction and pulp detective novels.
vocab.colloc: highbrow culture · highbrow tastes · highbrow and lowbrow

vocab.def: to criticise a film, play or book very severely.
vocab.use: Informal but standard in journalism; very often passive: “The film was panned by critics.” Opposite: to rave about.
examples: The sequel was universally panned on its release.
Critics panned the production, yet audiences queued round the block.
vocab.colloc: be panned by critics · universally / roundly panned

vocab.def: to have a special meaning or emotional effect for someone because it relates to their experience.
vocab.use: Intransitive: “The novel resonates with young readers.” The adjective resonant and noun resonance are common in criticism.
examples: The film’s portrait of migration resonates with audiences far beyond Colombia.
Her lyrics still resonate with anyone who has lost a parent.
vocab.colloc: resonate deeply with · resonate with audiences · emotional resonance

vocab.def: deliberately restrained or subtle, in an effective and attractive way.
vocab.use: Positive in criticism (unlike ‘bland’): “an understated performance”. The verb is to understate.
examples: His understated performance makes the final scene all the more devastating.
The gallery’s understated design lets the paintings speak for themselves.
vocab.colloc: an understated performance · understated elegance · quietly understated

vocab.def: to praise something so weakly that you are actually showing you think it is poor.
vocab.use: Usually describes another person’s review: “The critic damned it with faint praise, calling it ‘perfectly competent’.”
examples: Calling the novel ‘pleasantly readable’ was a classic case of damning with faint praise.
The review damned the director with faint praise, noting that the costumes were lovely.
vocab.colloc: damn something with faint praise · a case of faint praise

vocab.def: to attract the most attention and praise, often unexpectedly, in a performance or event.
vocab.use: Typically about a supporting actor, a minor element or an unexpected participant.
examples: The leads are fine, but the eight-year-old twins steal the show.
The costumes almost steal the show from the singers.
vocab.colloc: steal the show from someone · effortlessly steal the show

grammar.name: Ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, one)
grammar.short: Leave out or replace what the reader already knows.
grammar.rule: Ellipsis omits words that the context makes recoverable; substitution replaces them with a short pro-form. ‘So’ replaces a positive that-clause after verbs of thinking and hoping, and ‘not’ replaces a negative one. ‘Do so’ replaces a verb phrase in formal style. ‘One / ones’ replaces a countable noun. An auxiliary or ‘to’ alone can stand for a whole verb phrase.
form: think / hope / expect / suppose + so: Is the sequel worth seeing? — I don’t think so.
hope / be afraid / suppose + not: Will the show be cancelled? — I hope not.
do so / did so: The critic urged readers to see the play, and many did so.
adjective + one / ones: I preferred her early novels to the recent ones.
auxiliary / to (ellipsis): She promised to review it, and she has. / I didn’t want to go, but I had to.
notes: With think, believe, expect and suppose, the negative normally moves to the main verb: “I don’t think so”; “I think not” is formal or emphatic.
With hope and be afraid the negative cannot move: “I hope not”, never “I don’t hope so”.
‘Do so’ is formal and refers to deliberate actions; it does not replace states: not ‘She loves jazz and I do so too’.
‘One’ replaces countable nouns only: say “I prefer Italian cinema to French cinema”, not ‘to French one’.
After modals and ‘to’, keep the auxiliary or the ‘to’: “I’d love to”, not ‘I’d love’.
examples: Will the exhibition travel to Bogotá? — I very much hope so.
The jury was asked to reconsider its verdict, but declined to do so.
Of all his films, the black-and-white ones have aged best.
grammar.watch: “I don’t hope so” is wrong — say “I hope not”: unlike think, hope never moves the negative to the main verb.
grammar.deep: Repetition is the most visible marker of a writer who is not yet in control of English, and ellipsis and substitution are how native writers avoid it. They work on different units. ‘So’ and ‘not’ substitute for whole clauses after verbs of opinion (think, believe, expect, suppose, hope, be afraid, appear, seem): “Is it his best film? — It would appear so.” ‘Do so’ substitutes for a verb phrase, is markedly formal and implies agency, which is why it suits reports and reviews but not states (“She owns several Picassos, as does her brother” — not ‘does so’). ‘One’ and ‘ones’ substitute for count nouns and usually need a modifier (“the red one”, “a better one”); with uncountables we simply repeat or omit the noun. Ellipsis goes further and leaves a gap: “She can paint and he can too”; “The first act was gripping; the second, less so”; “Some critics loved it; others didn’t.” At C2 the challenge is not knowing these forms but deploying them without ambiguity: the reader must always be able to reconstruct exactly what has been left out, so the antecedent should be close and unambiguous.

chart.title: Pro-forms and what they replace
rows: Is it worth seeing? — I believe so.
Will they cut the scene? — I hope not.
She was asked to resign and did so.
His early films are better than his recent ones.
a verb phrase after the auxiliary
I haven’t read it, but my sister has.
The first act is tense; the second, less so.

more: Is it the director’s best film? — I’d say so, yes.
Will the gallery reopen next year? — I’m afraid not.
Visitors were invited to touch the sculptures, and most did so with obvious delight.
Her new film is far darker than her last one.
Some critics adored the ending; others didn’t.
The original novel is subtle; the adaptation, considerably less so.

fix.wrong: Will the band reunite? — I don’t hope so.
fix.right: Will the band reunite? — I hope not.
fix.why: With hope, the negative stays with the substitute: hope not.

fix.wrong: I prefer classical music to the modern one.
fix.right: I prefer classical music to modern music.
fix.why: ‘One’ cannot replace an uncountable noun such as music.

fix.wrong: He knows the script by heart, and his co-star does so too.
fix.right: He knows the script by heart, and so does his co-star.
fix.why: ‘Do so’ replaces deliberate actions, not states such as know; use ‘so does’.

drill.name: Say it once
drill.prompt: Answer or rewrite each item without repeating any words, using so, not, do so, one(s) or an auxiliary.
items: Is the new production better than the last production? (yes, I think…)
Will they release the director’s cut? (negative, hope)
The audience were asked to switch off their phones, and most of the audience switched off their phones.
I haven’t seen the exhibition yet, but my parents have seen the exhibition.
The first season was brilliant; the second season was not as brilliant.

dialogue.line: Did you manage to get tickets for the opening night?
I tried to, but they’d sold out. Are there any left for Saturday?
I don’t think so — only the restricted-view ones.
Never mind. The critics say the matinée cast is just as good, if not more so.

contrast.title: So or not: which verbs allow what?
rows: I don’t think so. (formal: I think not.)
I don’t expect so. / I suppose not.
I hope not. (never: I don’t hope so)
It appears not. / It doesn’t seem so.
I don’t know. / I’m not sure.

grammar.sound: In ellipsis the stranded auxiliary is always stressed and never contracted: “She HAS”, “I DID”, “they WILL”. In substitution the pro-forms are unstressed — “I THINK so”, “I HOPE not” — unless you contrast them: “I hope SO” (rather than not).

grammar.name: Intensifiers, downtoners and gradable vs ungradable adjectives
grammar.short: Match the modifier to the adjective: very good, absolutely superb.
grammar.rule: Gradable adjectives (good, original, moving) express qualities that can exist in degrees and take ‘very, extremely, rather, fairly, slightly, a little’. Ungradable adjectives are either extreme (superb, dreadful, breathtaking) or absolute/classifying (unique, impossible, perfect, black-and-white) and take ‘absolutely, utterly, totally, completely, entirely’. ‘Really’ and ‘pretty’ work with both; ‘quite’ means ‘fairly’ with gradable adjectives and ‘completely’ with ungradable ones. Downtoners (slightly, somewhat, mildly, a touch) soften a judgement.
form: very / extremely / fairly / slightly + gradable adjective: The second act is slightly uneven.
absolutely / utterly / totally / completely + ungradable adjective: The final scene is absolutely devastating.
really / pretty / quite + either type: The soundtrack is quite remarkable.
collocational intensifier + adjective: deeply moving · highly acclaimed · painfully slow · wildly overrated
notes: Extreme adjectives already contain ‘very’: “absolutely superb”, never “very superb”.
Compare ‘quite’: with a gradable adjective it softens (quite good = fairly good); with an ungradable one it intensifies (quite brilliant = completely brilliant).
C2 writers prefer collocational intensifiers to ‘very’: deeply moving, highly original, bitterly disappointing, strikingly beautiful, painfully slow.
Downtoners create critical nuance: somewhat laboured, mildly amusing, a touch sentimental, not entirely convincing.
Litotes — understatement with a negative — is a classic critical tool: not without its charms, far from perfect, no mean feat.
examples: Her performance is utterly mesmerising.
The plot is somewhat predictable, but the dialogue is highly original.
The exhibition is not without its flaws, though the final room is quite breathtaking.
grammar.watch: “The ending is very terrifying” is wrong — say “The ending is absolutely terrifying”: extreme adjectives take non-grading adverbs such as absolutely or utterly.
grammar.deep: The grammar of degree divides adjectives into two classes. Gradable adjectives sit on a scale, so they accept comparison and grading adverbs: rather slow, extremely slow, slower. Ungradable adjectives sit at the end of a scale (extreme: superb, appalling, hilarious) or outside it (absolute or classifying: unique, impossible, wooden, digital), so grading makes no sense and only non-grading ‘totality’ adverbs fit: utterly appalling, entirely digital. Several words belong to both classes depending on meaning — ‘unique’ is ungradable in careful usage, though ‘very unique’ is common informally; ‘dead’ is absolute, but ‘dead tired’ uses it as an intensifier. Beyond this grid, C2 precision comes from collocation. English has strong preferred pairings — deeply moving, highly acclaimed, bitterly disappointed, painfully self-aware, wildly uneven — and choosing them instead of ‘very’ is one of the clearest signs of proficiency. Equally important are downtoners and understatement, because criticism rarely deals in absolutes: ‘somewhat overlong’, ‘not entirely successful’, ‘a touch too neat’ allow a reviewer to criticise while remaining fair.

chart.title: Which adverb with which adjective?
rows: The set is almost entirely digital.
a deeply moving, highly original debut
somewhat, mildly, a touch, not entirely
The ending is a touch sentimental.

more: The cinematography is absolutely stunning, even if the script is fairly conventional.
I found the second half mildly irritating and the first half utterly gripping.
It is a highly accomplished debut, if a little overlong.
The performances are uniformly excellent.
The ending is quite perfect; the middle section is quite slow.
Her first novel was wildly overrated; her second is quietly brilliant.

fix.wrong: The view from the gallery roof is very breathtaking.
fix.right: The view from the gallery roof is absolutely breathtaking.
fix.why: Breathtaking is an extreme adjective, so it takes a non-grading adverb.

fix.wrong: The plot was absolutely interesting.
fix.right: The plot was really / extremely interesting.
fix.why: Interesting is gradable, so it takes grading adverbs, not absolutely.

fix.wrong: It is a strongly moving film.
fix.right: It is a deeply moving film.
fix.why: The natural collocation is deeply moving; strongly does not combine with moving.

drill.name: Turn up, turn down
drill.prompt: For each adjective, give one stronger and one softer version with the right adverb, then use one of them in a critic’s sentence.
items: original
disappointing
hilarious
slow
convincing

dialogue.line: So, what did you make of the new adaptation?
The lead is absolutely superb, but the script is somewhat laboured.
Really? I found the dialogue quite brilliant.
Brilliant in places, perhaps — but not entirely convincing as a whole.

contrast.title: The two meanings of quite
rows: The film is quite good. (not great)

grammar.sound: Stress changes the force of the modifier. In British English, stressing ‘quite’ weakens the praise — “It was QUITE good” — while stressing the adjective strengthens it — “It was quite GOOD”. Extreme adjectives are often lengthened for effect: “absolutely sooo-perb”.

grammar.name: Adjective order and compound modifiers
grammar.short: Opinion before fact, and hyphens that hold modifiers together.
grammar.rule: When several adjectives precede a noun, opinion comes before fact, and factual adjectives follow a usual order: size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – purpose/type + noun. Compound modifiers (two or more words acting as one adjective) are hyphenated before the noun — a well-received film, a three-hour opera, a thought-provoking installation — but usually not after a linking verb. In a number + noun compound the noun stays singular.
form: opinion + size/age + colour + origin + material + noun: a striking small nineteenth-century Flemish oil painting
adverb-participle compound + noun: a well-crafted, long-awaited sequel
number-noun compound + noun: a three-hour opera · a five-star review · a ten-minute ovation
-ly adverb + participle (no hyphen): a highly acclaimed debut · a beautifully lit stage
notes: Coordinate adjectives of the same class take a comma or ‘and’: a tense, witty script; opinion adjectives from different classes do not: a beautiful old theatre.
Never hyphenate after an -ly adverb: a highly anticipated film, not a highly-anticipated film.
After the verb, the hyphen usually disappears: a well-known actor, but the actor is well known.
Numbers in compounds stay singular: a two-hour film, not a two-hours film.
Avoid stacking more than three adjectives; move the rest into a relative clause or a with-phrase.
examples: It is a beautiful little Art Deco cinema in the old town.
The festival opened with a thought-provoking, two-hour documentary.
This highly acclaimed debut is a long-awaited return to form for the studio.
grammar.watch: “a three-hours film” is wrong — say “a three-hour film”: the noun in a number compound stays singular, because the whole compound works like an adjective.
grammar.deep: English packs a great deal of information in front of the noun, and criticism exploits this more than any other genre: “a quietly devastating, beautifully shot Argentine family drama”. Two systems govern these noun phrases. The first is order. Evaluative adjectives (devastating, charming, dull) come first because they express the writer’s view; factual ones follow in a fairly stable sequence — size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, type — with the most noun-like, defining modifier closest to the noun (a ‘family drama’, a ‘horror film’). Native speakers rarely articulate this order but notice violations at once: ‘a Spanish beautiful old film’ sounds foreign. The second system is compounding. When two words jointly modify a noun, a hyphen shows they belong together and prevents misreading: ‘a little-known writer’ (not well known) versus ‘a little known writer’ (a small, famous writer?). Hyphens are used for adverb-participle (well-made), noun-participle (award-winning), adjective-noun (full-length) and number-noun (six-part) compounds before the noun, but never after an -ly adverb, whose ending already marks the relationship.

chart.title: Order of adjectives before a noun

more: She restored a magnificent eighteenth-century Spanish guitar.
It is a slow-burning, character-driven thriller.
The gallery bought a tiny square Japanese lacquer box.
Audiences gave the cast a fifteen-minute standing ovation.
The director is well known for her single-take, hand-held style.
His latest novel is a sprawling, multi-generational family saga.

fix.wrong: a French wonderful old film
fix.right: a wonderful old French film
fix.why: Opinion comes first, then age, then origin.

fix.wrong: a highly-anticipated sequel
fix.right: a highly anticipated sequel
fix.why: No hyphen after an -ly adverb.

fix.wrong: a six-parts series
fix.right: a six-part series
fix.why: The noun in a number compound stays singular.

drill.name: Build the noun phrase
drill.prompt: Put the modifiers in order before the noun and add hyphens where needed. Then write a sentence from a review using the phrase.
items: film / Iranian / black and white / haunting / short
sculpture / bronze / huge / modern / striking
opera / three hours / new / long awaited
novel / sprawling / Victorian / beautifully written
musical / award winning / Broadway / brash

dialogue.line: What’s the new exhibition like?
It’s built around one extraordinary sixteenth-century Venetian glass mirror.
Just one object? Isn’t that a bit thin for a ten-euro ticket?
Not at all — it’s a beautifully curated, thought-provoking show. Well worth it.

grammar.sound: Compound modifiers before a noun usually stress the first element — a WELL-made film, a THOUGHT-provoking show — while the main stress of the whole phrase falls on the noun: a well-made FILM. Pausing between the two halves of a compound breaks it and confuses the listener.

speaking.text: Talk for two minutes about a film, book or album that critics panned but you admire (or that critics loved and you found overrated). Explain why opinions differ, using at least three precise intensifiers or downtoners.

With a partner, you are selecting three works for a festival called “Overlooked Masterpieces”. Discuss five candidates (a silent film, a graphic novel, a video game, a folk album, a public mural) and agree on a final three, avoiding repetition with so, not and one(s).
Is there any objective way to judge artistic quality, or is all taste personal? Should public money support highbrow art that few people enjoy? Respond to your partner’s points and give examples.
Student A is a critic defending a harsh review; Student B is the artist. Each must use understatement (not entirely, not without its charms) and at least one idiom of praise or criticism.

tips: Avoid ‘very’ with extreme adjectives: absolutely superb, utterly dreadful, quite extraordinary — and prefer collocations such as deeply moving or highly original.
Use so and not to replace whole clauses after think, hope, expect and be afraid — but remember “I hope not”, never “I don’t hope so”.
Before a noun, put opinion first and hyphenate compound modifiers (a well-crafted, three-hour epic); never hyphenate after an -ly adverb.
Common slip: ‘one’ only replaces countable nouns — “I prefer jazz to classical music”, not “to the classical one”.

quiz.q: The ending is ___ heartbreaking; I left the cinema in tears.
quiz.explain: Heartbreaking is an extreme adjective, so it takes a non-grading adverb such as absolutely.

test.q: Will the gallery extend the exhibition? — I’m ___.
test.explain: ‘Be afraid’ keeps the negative in the substitute: I’m afraid not.

test.q: Members were invited to vote on the new artistic director, and most ___ online.
test.explain: ‘Do so’ replaces a deliberate action in formal style: most did so.

test.q: I loved her early albums but I’m less keen on the recent ___.
test.explain: ‘Ones’ replaces the plural countable noun ‘albums’.

test.q: The first season was gripping; the second, ___.
test.explain: ‘So’ substitutes for the adjective already mentioned: less so = less gripping.

test.q: Which sentence is correct?
test.explain: Spectacular is extreme, so grading adverbs such as very, fairly or slightly do not fit.

test.q: It is a ___ moving portrait of grief.
test.explain: The fixed collocation is deeply moving.

test.q: Choose the correct noun phrase.
test.explain: Order: opinion (charming) – age (old) – origin (Mexican) + noun.

test.q: Audiences gave the soprano a ___ ovation.
test.explain: In a number + noun compound before a noun, the noun is singular and hyphenated.

test.q: Which phrase is punctuated correctly?
test.explain: No hyphen after an -ly adverb, because the -ly ending already shows the link.

test.q: The thriller is entertaining but hopelessly ___: every twist is borrowed from older films.
test.explain: Derivative = copying the ideas of other works and lacking originality.

test.q: Describing a novel as ‘perfectly competent’ is a way of ___.
options: hailing it as a tour de force
test.explain: Weak praise that implies criticism is ‘damning with faint praise’.

test.q: The leads are solid, but a nine-year-old newcomer ___.
test.explain: To steal the show = to attract the most attention and praise, often unexpectedly.

dynamics.name: The critics’ dial
dynamics.how: Draw a dial from 0 (utterly dreadful) to 10 (absolutely superb) on the board. The teacher names a well-known film or song; students take turns placing it on the dial with a precise phrase (somewhat overrated, quietly brilliant, wildly uneven). Any phrase with a mismatched adverb (very superb) is challenged by the class.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the gradable / ungradable distinction audible and quick.

dynamics.name: Zero repetition
dynamics.how: Pairs hold a two-minute conversation about a recent cultural event. A third student listens and gives a point for every successful substitution or ellipsis (I think so, the other one, she has, less so) and deducts one for each repeated noun phrase.
dynamics.payoff: Turns ellipsis into a conscious strategy rather than an accident.

dynamics.name: Catalogue copywriters
dynamics.how: Each group receives images of three objects from a museum collection and writes a one-sentence catalogue label for each, using at least four ordered adjectives and one compound modifier. Labels are displayed; the class votes for the most precise and checks order and hyphenation.
dynamics.payoff: Practises dense, correctly ordered noun phrases in an authentic genre.

writing.title: A review for a cultural magazine
writing.brief: A cultural magazine has invited readers to review an exhibition, film or production that divided critics. Write a review describing the work, evaluating its strengths and weaknesses with precision, and saying who would — and would not — enjoy it.
writing.briefEs: Escribe una reseña para una revista cultural sobre una obra que dividió a la crítica, evaluando con precisión sus aciertos y fallos y a quién la recomiendas.
criteria: An engaging title and opening, a brief description, a balanced evaluation and a clear recommendation.
Precise grading: at least four intensifiers, downtoners or collocational intensifiers matched correctly to gradable and ungradable adjectives.
Two examples of ellipsis or substitution (so, not, do so, one, an auxiliary alone) and no unnecessary repetition.
Three dense noun phrases with correctly ordered adjectives and at least two hyphenated compound modifiers.
writing.model:
Beautiful Ruins: Light and Silence at the Botero Annex

Few exhibitions this year have divided critics quite so sharply as “Light and Silence”, a small but ambitious show of contemporary Andean photography. Some reviewers have called it a revelation; others have dismissed it as pretentious. Having visited twice, I find myself somewhere in between, though considerably closer to the former camp.

The show brings together forty large-format black-and-white prints by six photographers, most of them under thirty. The opening room is quite breathtaking: a series of long-exposure images of abandoned mountain chapels, in which candlelight and fog blur into something almost abstract. Here the curators’ understated approach works beautifully, with minimal captions and a single low bench inviting visitors to linger. The prints are hung low and generously spaced, so that each can be studied in near silence, an effect made all the more striking by the noise of the street outside.

The middle section is less successful. A sequence of glossy fashion-inspired portraits feels derivative of 1990s advertising, and the accompanying texts are somewhat laboured, full of hackneyed phrases about “memory” and “identity”. Did the curators need to include it? I suspect not; the show would be tighter, and more coherent, without it.

The final room, however, steals the show. A ten-minute video installation of a village festival, projected on three walls, is deeply moving without ever becoming sentimental, and it resonates long after you leave. It is the one moment at which the exhibition’s title truly makes sense.

This is not a flawless exhibition, but it is a thought-provoking and often beautiful one. Visitors who enjoy slow, contemplative art should go without hesitation; those expecting colour and spectacle should probably not. Either way, allow at least an hour — and visit on a weekday morning, when the rooms are at their most silent.

homework.title: A miniature review
homework.task: Write a 120-word review of a song, series episode or short film you watched this week. Include two intensifiers with extreme adjectives, two downtoners, one collocational intensifier, one example of so/not substitution and one compound modifier before a noun. Highlight each target structure and swap reviews with a classmate for a check next lesson.

board: Top: a horizontal scale — slightly · fairly · rather · very · extremely | absolutely · utterly — with GRADABLE (good, slow) under the left half and EXTREME (superb, dreadful) under the right.
A red box: “very superb” crossed out → “absolutely superb”; “I don’t hope so” crossed out → “I hope not”.
Left column: pro-forms — so / not (clause) · do so (action, formal) · one(s) (countable noun) · has / did / to (verb phrase).
Right column: the order train — OPINION → size → age → shape/colour → origin → material → type + NOUN.
Bottom strip: well-made film · a three-hour opera (no -s!) · a highly praised debut (no hyphen after -ly).

units.title: POWER, JUSTICE AND SOCIETY

overview.intro: The language of power is formal, ritualised and often deliberately evasive. To take part in debates about law, politics and protest at C2, you need the formal subjunctive of demands and recommendations, the unreal past of wishes and regrets, and concessive structures that let you acknowledge an opponent’s point before dismantling it.
goals: Discuss politics, justice and protest with precise legal and political vocabulary, and recognise euphemism and doublespeak.
Use the mandative subjunctive and formulaic expressions in formal proposals and demands.
Express wishes, regrets and preferences with the unreal past, and concede points elegantly with albeit, notwithstanding, much as and however + adjective.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write an opinion article about a social issue that concedes opposing arguments with sophistication and ends with formally worded demands.

vocab.def: to protect a right, principle or idea by including it in a law or constitution.
vocab.use: Very often passive: “be enshrined in law / in the constitution”. It suggests permanence and special status.
examples: The right to protest is enshrined in the constitution.
Campaigners want equal pay enshrined in law, not left to goodwill.
vocab.colloc: enshrined in law · enshrined in the constitution · enshrine a right / principle

vocab.def: the fair legal procedures that the state must follow before depriving anyone of their rights or freedom.
vocab.use: Uncountable, usually without an article: “without due process”, “a violation of due process”.
examples: The detainees were held for months without due process.
Even unpopular defendants are entitled to due process.
vocab.colloc: without due process · the right to due process · a breach of due process

vocab.def: a situation in which a court punishes someone who is innocent, or the legal system clearly fails.
vocab.use: Countable: “one of the worst miscarriages of justice in history”. Formal and journalistic.
examples: The conviction was later recognised as a miscarriage of justice.
Campaigners spent twenty years exposing the miscarriage of justice.
vocab.colloc: a grave miscarriage of justice · victims of a miscarriage of justice · expose a miscarriage of justice

vocab.def: to officially reject a legal decision, especially a conviction; also to stop something by force.
vocab.use: Legal sense: “quash a conviction / a verdict / a decision”. Political sense: “quash a rebellion / rumours / dissent”.
examples: The appeal court quashed both convictions.
The regime moved quickly to quash any sign of dissent.
vocab.colloc: quash a conviction · quash a verdict · quash dissent / rumours

vocab.def: deprived of the right to vote, or feeling excluded from power and influence.
vocab.use: Both literal (no vote) and figurative (powerless, ignored). The verb is disenfranchise; the noun disenfranchisement.
examples: Millions of prisoners remain disenfranchised in several countries.
Many young voters feel disenfranchised by a system that ignores them.
vocab.colloc: disenfranchised voters · feel disenfranchised · politically disenfranchised

vocab.def: to limit or reduce something, especially rights, powers or freedoms.
vocab.use: Formal and often critical: “curtail civil liberties / press freedom / spending”. Noun: curtailment.
examples: Emergency laws curtailed the right to assemble.
Critics fear the bill will curtail the independence of the judiciary.
vocab.colloc: curtail freedoms · severely curtailed · curtail the power of

vocab.def: to approve a decision automatically, without considering it properly.
vocab.use: Critical. Also a noun: “The parliament is a mere rubber stamp for the president.”
examples: The committee simply rubber-stamped the minister’s proposals.
Without real opposition, the assembly will rubber-stamp whatever it is given.
vocab.colloc: rubber-stamp a decision · a rubber-stamp parliament · merely rubber-stamp

vocab.def: involving ordinary people at a local level rather than leaders or official organisations.
vocab.use: As an adjective before a noun: “a grassroots campaign”. As a noun, with ‘the’: “support from the grassroots”.
examples: The movement began as a small grassroots campaign in one neighbourhood.
Party leaders have lost touch with the grassroots.
vocab.colloc: a grassroots movement · grassroots activism · support at grassroots level

vocab.def: to shock or excite people into taking action.
vocab.use: “Galvanise someone into action” or “galvanise support / opposition”. Spelled galvanize in American English.
examples: The footage of the arrest galvanised thousands into joining the march.
The ruling galvanised opposition across the political spectrum.
vocab.colloc: galvanise someone into action · galvanise support · galvanise public opinion

vocab.def: language that is deliberately ambiguous or euphemistic, used to hide the truth.
vocab.use: Uncountable and critical. Typical examples: ‘enhanced interrogation’ for torture, ‘rightsizing’ for job cuts, ‘revenue enhancement’ for tax rises.
examples: Calling the cuts ‘efficiency savings’ is pure doublespeak.
The report is a masterclass in bureaucratic doublespeak.
vocab.colloc: political doublespeak · bureaucratic doublespeak · see through the doublespeak

vocab.def: a military euphemism for civilian deaths and damage caused unintentionally during an attack; more widely, harm to people not directly targeted.
vocab.use: Uncountable. Often quoted critically to expose its euphemistic function.
examples: The deaths of civilians were described, chillingly, as collateral damage.
Small businesses became the collateral damage of the trade war.
vocab.colloc: dismiss something as collateral damage · minimise collateral damage

vocab.def: the existing state of affairs, especially in politics or society.
vocab.use: Always with ‘the’. Common verbs: maintain, preserve, challenge, upset, defend.
examples: Those who benefit from the status quo have little reason to change it.
The protests were a direct challenge to the status quo.
vocab.colloc: maintain / preserve the status quo · challenge the status quo · a return to the status quo

grammar.name: The subjunctive and formulaic expressions
grammar.short: The base form after demands and recommendations: “We insist that he resign.”
grammar.rule: The mandative subjunctive uses the base form of the verb, with no -s and no tense change, after verbs, adjectives and nouns of demand, recommendation, proposal and necessity (insist, demand, recommend, propose, suggest, request; essential, vital, imperative; the requirement that…). The negative is ‘not + base form’ and the passive ‘be + past participle’. British English often uses ‘should + base form’ instead. The subjunctive also survives in fixed formulaic expressions such as ‘be that as it may’, ‘come what may’ and ‘suffice it to say’.
form: demand / insist / recommend + that + subject + base verb: The committee recommends that the minister resign.
It is essential / vital / imperative + that + subject + (not) + base verb: It is vital that every citizen be informed of their rights.
that + subject + be + past participle: The protesters demanded that the law be repealed.
Formulaic: Be that as it may · Come what may · Suffice it to say · Far be it from me to · If need be · So be it
notes: The subjunctive does not change for person or tense: “They insisted that she be released” — not ‘was released’ or ‘is released’.
The negative comes before the base form without ‘do’: “We propose that the fee not be increased.”
British alternative: “The panel recommended that he should resign” — equally correct and less formal.
In informal British English an indicative is also heard (‘insisted that he resigns’), but formal writing and exams expect the subjunctive or should.
Formulaic expressions are frozen: “Suffice it to say, the vote was close” cannot become ‘Suffices it to say’.
examples: The union demanded that the dismissal be overturned.
It is imperative that the inquiry remain independent of the government.
Be that as it may, the court must still follow due process.
grammar.watch: “The panel insisted that he resigns” is wrong in formal English — say “The panel insisted that he resign”: the mandative subjunctive has no -s, even after he, she or it.
grammar.deep: English has almost lost its subjunctive mood, but two areas remain productive, and both are markers of formal register. The first is the mandative subjunctive, triggered by a meaning rather than a word: whenever a clause expresses what someone demands, proposes or considers necessary, the verb appears in its bare form — “The charter requires that every member state hold free elections”. Because the form is identical to the indicative in most persons, it is only visible in the third person singular (hold, not holds), with ‘be’ (be informed, not are informed), and in negatives without ‘do’ (that he not be named). American English uses it routinely; British English prefers ‘should’ in many contexts but still uses the subjunctive in legal and official prose. The second area is a set of fossilised formulae — long live the republic, God save the King, heaven forbid, be that as it may, come what may, so be it, suffice it to say, far be it from me to criticise, if need be, as it were — which are learned as chunks and cannot be altered grammatically. Used precisely, they give speech and writing a ceremonial, authoritative tone; overused, they sound archaic.

chart.title: Triggers of the mandative subjunctive
rows: verbs: demand, insist, propose, recommend, request, suggest
They insist that the vote be recounted.
adjectives: essential, vital, imperative, crucial, important
It is crucial that she attend the hearing.
the requirement that every voter show ID
We ask that the names not be published.
They recommended that he should step down.
Come what may, we will march on Friday.

more: The opposition has demanded that the minister appear before parliament.
It is essential that the judge be seen to be impartial.
The report recommends that the police not be given further powers.
Far be it from me to question the court, but the sentence seems excessive.
Suffice it to say that the reforms were not popular.
We will take the case to the supreme court, if need be.

fix.wrong: The judge ordered that the evidence is destroyed.
fix.right: The judge ordered that the evidence be destroyed.
fix.why: After a verb of command, the passive subjunctive is be + past participle.

fix.wrong: We propose that the fee doesn’t increase.
fix.right: We propose that the fee not increase.
fix.why: The subjunctive negative is not + base form, with no auxiliary do.

fix.wrong: Be it as it may, the law is the law.
fix.right: Be that as it may, the law is the law.
fix.why: Formulaic expressions are fixed; the phrase is ‘be that as it may’.

drill.name: Draft the resolution
drill.prompt: Turn each request into a formal resolution with the subjunctive. Then rewrite two of them with ‘should’.
items: The council must publish its accounts. (It is essential that…)
The police must not use tear gas. (The committee demands that…)
The minister has to resign. (The opposition insists that…)
Voters need to be told about the changes. (It is vital that…)
The company should compensate the victims. (The court recommends that…)

dialogue.line: The motion before us proposes that the council publish all lobbying meetings.
Far be it from me to oppose transparency, but it is essential that private citizens not be named.
Be that as it may, the public has a right to know who is influencing policy.
Then I suggest that the names be anonymised and the meetings disclosed. So be it.

contrast.title: Subjunctive, should or indicative?
rows: We insist that she be present.
We insist that she should be present.
We insist that she is present.
He insists that he was innocent.
It is vital that he not speak.
If need be, we will strike.

grammar.sound: Because the subjunctive form often looks like an error, speakers make it audible by stressing the bare verb slightly and not reducing ‘be’: “…that the law BE repealed”. In “Be that as it may” the stress falls on ‘be’ and ‘may’.

grammar.name: Unreal past: wish, if only, it's (high) time, would rather, as if
grammar.short: A past form for present unreality, a past perfect for past regret.
grammar.rule: After wish, if only, it’s (high / about) time, would rather and as if / as though, English uses a past tense to describe something that is not real or not happening. The past simple (or were) refers to the present or future; the past perfect refers to the past. ‘Wish / if only + would’ expresses irritation or a desire for someone else’s behaviour to change. ‘Would rather’ takes a base verb when the subject is the same and a past tense when it is different.
form: wish / if only + past simple: I wish the law were less complicated.
wish / if only + past perfect: If only the jury had heard that evidence.
wish + someone + would + base verb: I wish the government would listen to us.
It’s (high / about) time + subject + past simple: It’s high time the voting age was lowered.
would rather + subject + past simple: I’d rather you didn’t record the meeting.
as if / as though + past simple: He talks as if he owned the city.
notes: ‘Were’ is preferred for all persons in formal style: “If only I were in a position to help.”
‘Wish + would’ is for other people’s behaviour or events, not your own states: say “I wish I had more time”, not “I wish I would have more time”.
‘It’s time + to-infinitive’ is a neutral suggestion; ‘It’s high time + past simple’ is a criticism that something is overdue.
‘Would rather’ with the same subject takes a base verb: “I’d rather stay”; with a different subject a past tense: “I’d rather you stayed.”
With ‘as if’ a present tense means it may be true; a past tense means it is unreal: He looks as if he is tired / as if he were a king.
examples: I wish I had voted in the referendum.
It’s about time politicians started listening to young people.
Most residents would rather the council spent the money on housing.
grammar.watch: “I wish I would have voted” is wrong — say “I wish I had voted”: regret about the past takes the past perfect, never would have.
grammar.deep: These structures share a principle known as backshifting for unreality: moving a verb one step into the past signals distance from reality rather than past time. Thus ‘I wish I knew’ is about now, and ‘I wish I had known’ is about then. Each introducer adds its own pragmatic colour. ‘Wish’ is personal and ranges from longing to regret; ‘if only’ is more emotional and often stands alone as an exclamation. ‘Wish + would’ is different in kind: it expresses dissatisfaction with someone’s willingness to act (“I wish the minister would answer the question”), which is why it sounds odd with your own actions or with states. ‘It’s high time’ and ‘it’s about time’ carry criticism — the action should already have happened — and are frequent in political rhetoric. ‘Would rather’ and ‘would sooner’ express preference and, with a different subject, a polite request (“I’d rather you didn’t smoke here”). Finally, ‘as if’ and ‘as though’ allow the speaker to comment on how real an appearance is: a past form after them ironically marks the comparison as untrue (“He behaves as if the rules didn’t apply to him”).

chart.title: Unreal past at a glance
rows: I wish I lived in a fairer society.
I wish they would stop lying. (behaviour)
It’s high time the law changed.
I’d rather you hadn’t told them.
She acts as if she were in charge.
He looked as if he had seen a ghost.
Imagine we had lost the vote.

more: If only the courts were faster.
Many activists wish they had kept better records of the early protests.
I wish the senator would stop hiding behind doublespeak.
It’s high time we had an honest debate about inequality.
I’d rather the press didn’t publish the victims’ names.
The minister spoke as though nothing had happened.

fix.wrong: It’s high time the government listens to us.
fix.right: It’s high time the government listened to us.
fix.why: ‘It’s high time’ is followed by a past simple for present meaning.

fix.wrong: I’d rather you don’t mention my name.
fix.right: I’d rather you didn’t mention my name.
fix.why: With a different subject, ‘would rather’ takes a past tense.

fix.wrong: I wish I would be braver at the meeting yesterday.
fix.right: I wish I had been braver at the meeting yesterday.
fix.why: Regret about the past takes the past perfect.

drill.name: Regret, complaint or preference?
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the introducer given, choosing the correct unreal-past form.
items: I’m sorry I didn’t sign the petition. (I wish…)
The mayor keeps ignoring the residents. It annoys me. (I wish… would)
The voting system should have changed years ago. (It’s high time…)
Please don’t film the hearing. (I’d rather…)
He isn’t the owner, but he behaves like one. (as if…)

dialogue.line: I wish I had gone to the march on Saturday. It was enormous.
If only the media had covered it properly — they treated it as if it were a street party.
It’s high time someone held them to account.
Agreed, though I’d rather we organised our own coverage than waited for them.

contrast.title: wish + past, wish + past perfect, wish + would
rows: present situation you would like to be different
I wish I understood the law.
I wish I had read the contract.
annoyance; wanting someone to change behaviour
I hope the verdict is fair.
I wish to speak to the judge.

grammar.sound: In ‘I wish I’d known’ the ’d is almost inaudible; the clue to the past perfect is the participle ‘known’. ‘It’s HIGH time’ stresses ‘high’ to convey impatience, and ‘If ONLY…’ rises sharply on ‘only’ when used as an exclamation.

grammar.name: Concession and contrast: albeit, notwithstanding, much as, however + adjective
grammar.short: Admit a point gracefully before making your own.
grammar.rule: Formal English has concessive structures that are more compact and nuanced than although. ‘Albeit’ (= although it is / was) is followed by an adjective, adverb or phrase, never a full clause. ‘Notwithstanding’ (= despite) is followed by a noun phrase, and can also follow the noun. ‘Much as’ + clause (= although … very much) works with verbs of feeling such as like, admire, sympathise and regret. ‘However + adjective / adverb + clause’ means ‘no matter how’. The pattern ‘adjective + as / though + subject + verb’ is a fronted concessive.
form: albeit + adjective / adverb / phrase: The reform was a step forward, albeit a modest one.
notwithstanding + noun / noun + notwithstanding: Notwithstanding the court’s ruling, the protests continued.
much as + subject + verb, main clause: Much as I admire her courage, I cannot support her methods.
however + adjective + subject + verb, main clause: However peaceful the march is, it will be policed.
adjective + as / though + subject + verb, main clause: Controversial as the verdict was, it was legally sound.
notes: ‘Albeit’ cannot introduce a clause: write “albeit slowly” or “albeit with reservations”, not ‘albeit it was slow’.
‘Notwithstanding’ is formal and legal; it can follow a noun: “Objections notwithstanding, the bill passed.”
‘Much as’ needs a verb of feeling or attitude: like, love, admire, respect, sympathise, regret, want.
In ‘however + adjective’ the adjective comes immediately after however: “However hard they tried”, not ‘However they tried hard’.
Fronted concession uses as or though, not although: “Unpopular as it was” — never ‘Unpopular although it was’.
examples: The government accepted the recommendations, albeit reluctantly.
Much as I sympathise with the strikers, I cannot condone the violence.
However justified their anger may be, blocking ambulances is indefensible.
grammar.watch: “Albeit the reform was slow, it worked” is wrong — say “Although the reform was slow, it worked”: albeit is followed by a phrase, never a full clause.
grammar.deep: Concession is the backbone of persuasive writing. A writer who concedes intelligently appears fair-minded, and the concession sets up the counter-argument that follows. C2 English offers a range of concessive devices with distinct grammar and tone. ‘Albeit’ compresses a whole concessive clause into a phrase and attaches it to the end of a statement: “a victory, albeit a narrow one”. ‘Notwithstanding’ is the most formal, with a legal flavour; as a preposition it precedes or follows its noun (“notwithstanding these concerns” / “these concerns notwithstanding”), and it also survives as an adverb meaning ‘nevertheless’. ‘Much as’ concedes a feeling — usually a positive one — that the speaker will override: “Much as I respect the judge, I disagree with her.” ‘However + adjective’ and ‘no matter how’ concede any degree of something: “However strong the evidence, the jury may acquit.” And the fronted pattern ‘adjective / adverb + as / though + subject + verb’ is elegant in writing: “Small though the grant was, it transformed the project.” Combined with ‘for all + noun’, ‘granted’, ‘admittedly’ and ‘that said’, these give a writer a full toolkit for nuanced argument.

chart.title: Formal concessive structures
rows: an improvement, albeit a minor one
Much as I like him, he’s wrong.
However loudly they protest, nothing changes.
Rich as he is, he pays little tax.
For all its flaws, democracy endures.

more: The verdict was fair, albeit harsh.
The new law, notwithstanding its good intentions, will curtail free speech.
Much as we regret the disruption, the strike will go ahead.
However carefully the policy is worded, it will be challenged in court.
Brief though the protest was, it galvanised the whole region.
For all its talk of reform, the government has changed very little.

fix.wrong: Much as the minister is popular, she cannot win this vote.
fix.right: Popular as the minister is, she cannot win this vote.
fix.why: ‘Much as’ needs a verb of feeling; with an adjective use the fronted ‘adjective + as’ pattern.

fix.wrong: However the march was peaceful, the police intervened.
fix.right: However peaceful the march was, the police intervened.
fix.why: The adjective must follow ‘however’ directly in this concessive pattern.

fix.wrong: Notwithstanding that the opposition, the bill passed.
fix.right: Notwithstanding the opposition, the bill passed.
fix.why: ‘Notwithstanding’ as a preposition takes a noun phrase directly.

drill.name: Concede, then counter
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the structure in brackets, then add a counter-argument of your own.
items: Although the reform was limited, it was significant. (albeit)
Despite the court’s warning, the union went on strike. (notwithstanding)
I admire the activists a great deal, but I disagree with their tactics. (much as)
It doesn’t matter how peaceful the protest is; it will be filmed. (however + adjective)
The campaign was very small, but it changed the law. (adjective + though)

dialogue.line: Much as I support the cause, blocking the motorway seems counterproductive.
Disruptive as it was, it got the issue onto every front page.
True, albeit for all the wrong reasons.
However unpopular their methods, they’ve forced the government to respond. That has to count for something.

contrast.title: Although, despite, albeit, much as
rows: Although it was legal, it was unfair.
Despite being legal, it was unfair.
Notwithstanding its legality, it was unfair.
Much as I respect the law, this is unfair.
Legal as it was, it was unfair.

grammar.sound: ‘Albeit’ is pronounced /ɔːlˈbiːɪt/ — three syllables, stress on the second. In fronted concession the adjective is stressed and followed by a fall-rise: “CONtroversial as it WAS | …”, signalling that the main point is still to come.

speaking.text: Talk for two minutes on this question: “Is peaceful protest still effective in the age of social media?” Concede at least two points to the other side using much as, albeit or however + adjective.

With a partner, you are drafting three demands for a youth council to present to the mayor (on housing, transport and safety). Agree on the wording, using the subjunctive: “We demand that…”, “It is essential that…”.

Which matters more for a fair society: equal opportunities or equal outcomes? Should voting be compulsory? Should prisoners be disenfranchised? Respond to your partner and give examples from different countries.

A press conference after a controversial decision. Student A is a government spokesperson who uses euphemism and doublespeak; Student B is a journalist who exposes it and asks pointed questions with ‘I wish you would…’ and ‘It’s high time…’.

tips: After demand, insist, recommend and it is essential that, use the bare verb: “that he resign”, “that it be repealed”, “that they not be named”.
Backshift for unreality: wish / if only + past for now, + past perfect for then; it’s high time + past simple; would rather + past for someone else.
‘Albeit’ takes a phrase, ‘notwithstanding’ a noun, ‘much as’ a verb of feeling, and ‘however’ an adjective right after it.
Common slip: “I wish I would have known” is never correct — say “I wish I had known”.

quiz.q: The commission has recommended that the minister ___ immediately.
quiz.explain: After ‘recommend that’, formal English uses the mandative subjunctive: the base form, with no -s.

test.q: It is essential that every detainee ___ access to a lawyer.
test.explain: ‘It is essential that’ triggers the subjunctive; the passive form is be + past participle.

test.q: The residents asked that their names ___ published.
test.explain: The negative subjunctive is not + base form, with no auxiliary.

test.q: ___ that as it may, the court must reach a decision.
test.explain: ‘Be that as it may’ is a fixed formulaic subjunctive.

test.q: It’s high time the government ___ the housing crisis seriously.
test.explain: ‘It’s high time’ is followed by a past simple with present meaning.

test.q: I wish I ___ the petition before the deadline.
test.explain: Regret about the past takes the past perfect.

test.q: I’d rather you ___ my comments to the press.
test.explain: ‘Would rather’ with a different subject takes a past tense.

test.q: The bill was passed, ___ by a very narrow majority.
test.explain: ‘Albeit’ is followed by a phrase without a verb.

test.q: ___ I admire his integrity, I cannot vote for his party.
test.explain: ‘Much as’ + subject + verb of feeling concedes a point the speaker will override.

test.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: However the campaign was well organised, it failed.
However well organised the campaign was, it failed.
However was the campaign well organised, it failed.
However well the campaign organised was, it failed.
test.explain: ‘However’ is followed directly by the adjective or adverb, then subject + verb.

test.q: The appeal court ___ the conviction after new DNA evidence emerged.
test.explain: To quash a conviction = to officially reject it.

test.q: Critics say the parliament merely ___ whatever the president proposes.
test.explain: To rubber-stamp = to approve automatically without proper consideration.

test.q: Calling mass redundancies ‘workforce optimisation’ is a clear example of ___.
test.explain: Doublespeak is deliberately euphemistic language that hides the truth.

dynamics.name: The people’s assembly
dynamics.how: Each group is a citizens’ assembly on one issue (rent controls, compulsory voting, facial recognition cameras). Members propose motions orally using the subjunctive (I propose that…, It is imperative that…). Motions are voted on, and the secretary records the winning wording on the board, where the class checks every verb form.
dynamics.payoff: Gives the subjunctive its natural setting: formal proposals with real stakes.

dynamics.name: Doublespeak decoder
dynamics.how: Pairs receive cards with euphemisms from politics and business (negative growth, enhanced interrogation, collateral damage, rightsizing, revenue enhancement). They translate each into plain English, then write a sarcastic response using ‘I wish they would…’ or ‘They talk as if…’.
dynamics.payoff: Combines critical language awareness with the unreal past.

dynamics.name: Yes, but…
dynamics.how: Line A states an opinion on a social issue. The student opposite in line B must concede with a different structure each time (albeit, notwithstanding, much as, adjective + as, however + adjective) before countering. A repeated structure or a grammar slip passes the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Builds a repertoire of concessive openers under time pressure.

writing.title: Is it time to lower the voting age to 16?
writing.brief: A current-affairs magazine is publishing a series called “Whose democracy?”. Write an article arguing whether the voting age should be lowered to 16. Engage the reader, acknowledge the strongest arguments on the other side, and end with a clear call for change or caution.
writing.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista de actualidad sobre si se debería bajar la edad para votar a los 16 años, reconociendo los argumentos contrarios y terminando con un llamamiento claro.
criteria: An engaging title and opening, a personal but reasoned voice, and a memorable conclusion that addresses the reader directly.
At least two concessive structures from the unit (albeit, notwithstanding, much as, however + adjective, adjective + as).
One mandative subjunctive and two unreal-past structures (wish, it’s high time, would rather, as if).
Four items of political or legal vocabulary used precisely.
writing.model:
Old Enough to Pay Tax, Too Young to Vote?

At sixteen, Valentina works twenty hours a week in a bakery, pays income tax and volunteers at a food bank. Yet when her city voted on a new transport plan that would double her bus fare, she had no say whatsoever. It is hard to imagine a clearer case of a disenfranchised citizen.

The arguments against lowering the voting age are not trivial. Much as I respect those who make them, however, they rarely survive scrutiny. Sixteen-year-olds, we are told, are too easily influenced. Yet adults are hardly immune to slogans and online misinformation. Teenagers, critics add, lack life experience. True, albeit irrelevant: we do not test the life experience of any other voter. Nor are teenagers uniquely ill-informed: a sixteen-year-old who has just studied the constitution at school may well understand how parliament works better than many adults who have voted for decades.

Countries that have taken the step, such as Austria and Scotland, offer encouraging evidence. Turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds has been respectable, and, crucially, those who vote early tend to keep voting. Modest though these gains may seem, they suggest a lasting habit rather than a passing novelty.

The real obstacle is the status quo. Politicians often speak as if young people were a problem to be managed rather than citizens to be heard. Many older voters, I suspect, would rather the system stayed exactly as it is, because it serves them well.

It is high time we stopped treating democracy as a club with an age limit. I propose that the change be accompanied by serious citizenship education in schools, so that new voters arrive informed. Otherwise, in twenty years, we may wish we had trusted Valentina’s generation sooner.

homework.title: A letter of demands
homework.task: Choose a local issue (public transport, green spaces, safety, rents). Write a 150-word formal list of demands to the relevant authority: four demands with the mandative subjunctive (one negative, one passive), one formulaic expression, and two concessive sentences acknowledging the authority’s constraints. Highlight each target structure.

board: Top left: DEMAND / INSIST / RECOMMEND / IT IS ESSENTIAL + THAT + subject + BASE VERB, with examples: “that he resign” · “that it be repealed” · “that they not be named”.
Top right: formula cloud — Be that as it may · Come what may · Suffice it to say · Far be it from me · If need be.
Middle: a time arrow labelled UNREAL — wish / if only + PAST (now) | + PAST PERFECT (then); it’s high time + PAST; would rather + you + PAST; as if + PAST.
A red box: “I wish I would have voted” crossed out → “I wish I had voted”.
Bottom: the concession ladder — albeit + PHRASE · notwithstanding + NOUN · much as + I + FEEL · however + ADJ + clause · ADJ + as + clause.

units.title: BODY, RISK AND WELLBEING
units.theme: Health, risk-taking, sport and mental health

overview.intro: Stories about health and risk are often told with hindsight: the climber who was about to turn back, the athlete who would later win gold, the patient who was to make a full recovery. This unit combines that narrative grammar with the cohesive devices and precise verb choices that make reports and arguments about wellbeing read smoothly and authoritatively.
goals: Talk about health, risk and sport with precise collocations, medical idioms and sporting metaphors.
Narrate a future seen from the past with would, was to, was about to and was going to.
Connect ideas with C2 discourse markers and choose prepositional and phrasal verbs that suit formal writing.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write a cohesive formal report on a wellbeing initiative, recounting what was planned and what actually happened, and making clear recommendations.

vocab.def: a risk taken deliberately after carefully considering the chances of success and failure.
vocab.use: Positive or neutral: it implies judgement, not recklessness. Common with “take”.
examples: The surgeon took a calculated risk in operating so soon after the injury.
Investing in the new clinic was a calculated risk that paid off.
vocab.colloc: take a calculated risk · a calculated risk that paid off

vocab.def: to be in a situation where something bad may happen as a result of what you do.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “run the risk of injury / of losing everything”. Compare ‘put someone at risk’ and ‘at your own risk’.
examples: Athletes who train through pain run the risk of permanent damage.
If we cut the budget further, we run the risk of losing our best staff.
vocab.colloc: run the risk of + -ing · run a serious risk · at the risk of sounding rude

vocab.def: unwilling to take risks; preferring safe options.
vocab.use: Neutral to critical: “an overly risk-averse culture”. Opposite: risk-taking, a risk-taker.
examples: Schools have become so risk-averse that some have banned conkers.
Older investors tend to be more risk-averse.
vocab.colloc: highly / overly risk-averse · a risk-averse culture · risk-averse investors

vocab.def: making someone very weak or unable to function normally.
vocab.use: Collocates with illness, pain, condition, effect, anxiety. Stronger than ‘tiring’ or ‘unpleasant’.
examples: She lived with debilitating migraines for over a decade.
For some patients the side effects are more debilitating than the disease.
vocab.colloc: a debilitating illness · debilitating pain · debilitating anxiety

vocab.def: involving a lot of sitting and very little physical activity.
vocab.use: Typically “a sedentary lifestyle / job / population”. Formal; used in health reports.
examples: A sedentary lifestyle is linked to heart disease and depression.
Office workers in sedentary jobs are advised to stand every half hour.
vocab.colloc: a sedentary lifestyle · sedentary behaviour · a largely sedentary job

vocab.def: a state of physical and emotional exhaustion caused by long-term stress, usually at work.
vocab.use: Uncountable. The phrasal verb is “burn out”; the adjective “burnt out” / “burned out”.
examples: Burnout among junior doctors has reached alarming levels.
She took a sabbatical to recover from burnout.
vocab.colloc: suffer from burnout · prevent burnout · signs of burnout

vocab.def: to have a harmful effect, especially gradually and over a long period.
vocab.use: The subject is the cause: “Years of night shifts took their toll on his health.” Note the possessive matches the subject.
examples: The stress of caring for her father began to take its toll.
Constant travel has taken a heavy toll on the team’s performance.
vocab.colloc: take its / their toll on · take a heavy toll · take a physical / emotional toll

vocab.def: an official statement that someone is healthy, or that something is in good condition.
vocab.use: Usually with “give” or “get”. Also used for buildings, companies or systems after inspection.
examples: After a full check-up, the doctor gave her a clean bill of health.
The inspectors gave the hospital’s hygiene procedures a clean bill of health.
vocab.colloc: give / get / receive a clean bill of health

vocab.def: to be recovering after an illness or injury, or improving after a difficult period.
vocab.use: Informal to neutral. Also used of economies and relationships.
examples: He had a nasty bout of pneumonia, but he’s on the mend now.
After two difficult years, the club’s finances are finally on the mend.
vocab.colloc: be well on the mend · be on the mend after something

vocab.def: to give up, admitting that you cannot succeed.
vocab.use: From boxing: a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop a fight. Informal.
examples: Halfway through the marathon he was tempted to throw in the towel.
After three failed bids, the organisers finally threw in the towel.
vocab.colloc: be ready to throw in the towel · refuse to throw in the towel

vocab.def: to change the rules or targets of a situation unfairly, making success harder.
vocab.use: Critical; common in workplace and political contexts: “Every time we meet the target, management moves the goalposts.”
examples: Patients complain that the health service keeps moving the goalposts on waiting times.
Just as we reached the target, they moved the goalposts again.
vocab.colloc: keep moving the goalposts · accuse someone of moving the goalposts

vocab.def: a situation in which everyone has the same opportunities and no one has an unfair advantage.
vocab.use: Usually with “create”, “ensure” or “there is no”. Common in sport, business and policy.
examples: Strict anti-doping tests are meant to ensure a level playing field.
Without free school meals, there is no level playing field in education.
vocab.colloc: create / ensure a level playing field · compete on a level playing field

grammar.name: Future forms in the past (was to, was about to, would)
grammar.short: Looking forward from a point in the past.
grammar.rule: To describe something that was in the future at a past moment, English shifts the usual future forms into the past. ‘Would’ reports predictions and, in narratives, events that happened later (“She would later become…”). ‘Was / were going to’ describes past intentions, often unfulfilled. ‘Was / were to’ expresses arrangements or destiny seen in hindsight, and ‘was / were to have + past participle’ an arrangement that did not happen. ‘Was / were about to’ and ‘was / were on the point of + -ing’ describe something imminent.
form: would + base verb: She knew the recovery would take months.
was / were to + base verb: He was to win three Olympic medals before turning thirty.
was / were to have + past participle: The match was to have taken place in Lima, but it was cancelled.
was / were about to + base verb: I was about to give up when the pain suddenly eased.
was / were going to + base verb: We were going to run the marathon, but the heat made it impossible.
notes: ‘Was to’ in narratives signals destiny known to the narrator: “It was a decision she was to regret for the rest of her life.”
‘Was to have + past participle’ always means the plan failed: “The surgery was to have taken place on Monday.”
‘Was about to’ and ‘was on the point of’ are often followed by ‘when’ + an interrupting event.
‘Was due to’ and ‘was set to’ also look forward from the past in formal writing: “The clinic was due to open in May, but building work overran.”
Past continuous can also express past arrangements: “We were flying out the next day.”
examples: Nobody suspected that the injury would end his career.
It was a risk that she was to take many times in her life.
The team was about to abandon the climb when the weather cleared.
grammar.watch: “When I arrived, the surgeon would operate” is wrong — say “When I arrived, the surgeon was about to operate”: would does not describe an imminent event at a single past moment.
grammar.deep: A narrative often needs to look forward from inside the past, and English has a set of forms that do exactly this, each corresponding to a present future form. ‘Will’ becomes ‘would’ (“I knew I would be fine”), ‘be going to’ becomes ‘was going to’, ‘be about to’ becomes ‘was about to’, ‘be to’ becomes ‘was to’, and the present continuous for arrangements becomes the past continuous. Two forms deserve special attention at C2. The first is narrative ‘would’ and ‘was to’ used by a narrator who knows what happened next: “That afternoon he met the coach who would change his life”; “This was to be her last race.” This creates dramatic irony and is common in biographies, history and sports journalism. The second is the perfect infinitive after ‘was to’, ‘was going to’ and ‘was supposed to’, which emphasises that a plan was not carried out: “I was to have flown home on Friday, but I caught a fever.” Mastery of these forms lets you write about risk and decision-making with hindsight — what people intended, what they feared, and what really followed.

chart.title: The future seen from the past
rows: He would go on to coach the national team.
I was going to call, but I forgot.
She was to become the first woman to finish.
The race was to have started at dawn.
was about to / on the point of
He was on the point of quitting when…
We were leaving the following week.

more: Little did she know that the knee injury would turn out to be a blessing.
The expedition was to set off on 3 May, but storms delayed it for a week.
I was to have had the operation in June, but it was postponed twice.
We were just about to leave when the doctor called with the results.
He was on the point of throwing in the towel when his coach intervened.
That marathon was to be the last race of her career.

fix.wrong: The match was to have take place in Lima.
fix.right: The match was to have taken place in Lima.
fix.why: ‘Was to have’ is followed by a past participle.

fix.wrong: She was about to giving up when she reached the summit.
fix.right: She was about to give up when she reached the summit.
fix.why: ‘Be about to’ takes the base verb; ‘be on the point of’ takes -ing.

fix.wrong: I knew the treatment will be painful.
fix.right: I knew the treatment would be painful.
fix.why: Seen from a past moment, will shifts to would.

drill.name: With hindsight
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence from the point of view of a narrator who knows what happened next, using the form in brackets.
items: In 2010 she joined a running club. Later she became a national champion. (would / was to)
We planned to cycle across the Andes, but my knee gave out. (was going to)
The surgery was arranged for Friday. It didn’t happen. (was to have)
He was very close to quitting. Then his coach called. (was on the point of)
The climbers were ready to leave. The storm arrived. (was about to)

dialogue.line: I hear you were going to do the Ironman this year.
I was. I was to have flown to Lanzarote on the tenth, but I tore a ligament.
That’s awful. How did it happen?
On a training ride. I was about to turn home when a car pulled out. Little did I know it would keep me off the bike for six months.

contrast.title: Was going to, was to, was about to
rows: I was going to rest, but I trained anyway.
The final was to take place in Bogotá.
The final was to have taken place in Bogotá.
I was about to dive when the whistle blew.
Years later, she would win the title.
I was supposed to rest for a month.

grammar.sound: ‘Was to’ is pronounced /wəz tə/ in connected speech, so it can be mistaken for ‘was too’ or ‘wants to’. In ‘was to have taken’, ‘to have’ reduces to /təv/: “the race was /təv/ started at dawn”.

grammar.name: Discourse markers and cohesive devices at C2
grammar.short: The words that tie ideas together and tell the reader how to read them.
grammar.rule: Cohesion depends on reference (this, such, the former / the latter), substitution and ellipsis, lexical chains (synonyms and summary nouns) and discourse markers. At C2 the markers are chosen for fine distinctions: addition (moreover, furthermore, by the same token), contrast (by contrast, conversely, that said, even so), correction (on the contrary, if anything), concession (admittedly, granted, to be fair), consequence (thus, hence, consequently, accordingly) and reformulation (in other words, that is to say, or rather).
form: Sentence. + That said / Even so / Admittedly + clause: Running reduces stress. That said, overtraining can increase it.
hence + noun phrase: Recovery is slow; hence the need for patience.
This / Such + summary noun: Sleep loss impairs judgement. This impairment is rarely noticed by the sufferer.
the former … the latter: Both diet and sleep matter, but the latter is often ignored.
on the contrary (correction) / by contrast (comparison): It isn’t dangerous; on the contrary, it is very safe.
notes: ‘On the contrary’ rejects a statement just made; ‘by contrast’ and ‘in contrast’ compare two different things: never use them interchangeably.
‘Hence’ can be followed by a noun phrase without a verb: “hence the delay”; ‘thus’ usually needs a clause.
Summary nouns (this trend, such measures, these findings) are the most powerful C2 cohesive device: they refer back and push the argument forward.
‘By the same token’ means ‘for the same reason’; ‘conversely’ introduces the reverse relationship.
Avoid stacking markers: one per sentence is usually enough, and many sentences need none.
examples: Admittedly, extreme sports carry real dangers. Even so, participants are often more safety-conscious than the general public.
Exercise improves mood; conversely, inactivity is linked to depression.
Many patients stop the treatment early, hence the high relapse rate.
grammar.watch: “On the contrary, women recover faster” used for a comparison is wrong — say “By contrast, women recover faster”: on the contrary rejects a previous statement; it does not compare two groups.
grammar.deep: Cohesion is what turns a list of correct sentences into a text, and at C2 it operates on several levels at once. Grammatical cohesion uses reference words and substitution to link sentences without repetition: this, that, such, the former, the latter, one, do so. Lexical cohesion builds chains of related words — risk, hazard, danger, threat — and, crucially, summary nouns that encapsulate a previous idea: “Rates of anxiety among teenagers doubled in a decade. This rise has been linked to…”. Discourse markers make the logical relationship explicit and are where most errors at advanced levels occur, because near-synonyms differ in meaning and grammar. ‘On the contrary’ contradicts; ‘by contrast’ compares; ‘conversely’ reverses a relationship. ‘Admittedly’ and ‘granted’ concede; ‘that said’ and ‘even so’ return to the main argument after a concession. ‘Hence’ can take a noun phrase alone, while ‘therefore’ and ‘thus’ need a clause. ‘If anything’ corrects an expectation by suggesting the opposite is truer: “The new rules have not reduced injuries; if anything, they have increased them.” The most sophisticated writers use fewer markers, not more, letting summary nouns and paragraph structure carry much of the logic.

chart.title: C2 discourse markers by function
rows: moreover, furthermore, by the same token
By the same token, rest days should be planned.
Men under-report pain; women, by contrast, seek help sooner.
It isn’t harmful; if anything, it’s beneficial.
admittedly / granted … that said / even so
Granted, it’s risky. Even so, it’s worth it.
Funding was cut; hence the waiting lists.
in other words, that is to say, or rather
It was a setback, or rather a disaster.

more: The programme was popular with staff. Moreover, it cost less than expected.
Admittedly, the sample was small. That said, the results were striking.
Some injuries heal in weeks; others, conversely, become chronic.
Neither the coach nor the doctor was consulted, the latter being on holiday at the time.
Patients were not discouraged by the side effects; on the contrary, most asked to continue.
Screening detects the disease early, thus allowing less invasive treatment.

fix.wrong: Hence, it was a delay.
fix.right: Hence the delay.
fix.why: ‘Hence’ can introduce a noun phrase directly, without a verb or comma.

fix.wrong: Cycling is popular in the Netherlands. On the contrary, few people cycle in Texas.
fix.right: Cycling is popular in the Netherlands. By contrast, few people cycle in Texas.
fix.why: Comparing two places requires ‘by contrast’; ‘on the contrary’ contradicts a statement.

fix.wrong: Granted, the treatment works. Moreover, it is very expensive.
fix.right: Granted, the treatment works. Even so, it is very expensive.
fix.why: After a concession, return to the counter-argument with even so or that said, not an additive marker.

drill.name: Choose the link
drill.prompt: Join each pair of ideas with the most precise marker or cohesive device, and explain your choice.
items: Night shifts disrupt sleep. / Disrupted sleep weakens the immune system. (summary noun)
The new drug is not less effective. / It is more effective than the old one. (correction)
Running is risky for the knees. / Most runners never suffer a serious injury. (concession → return)
Budgets were cut. / The waiting lists grew. (hence + noun)
Children in cities exercise less. / Children in rural areas exercise more. (comparison)

dialogue.line: Surely free gym membership would make staff healthier?
Not necessarily. If anything, it mostly benefits people who already exercise.
Granted. That said, it might encourage a few newcomers.
