A few, perhaps — hence the case for something more inclusive, such as walking meetings.

contrast.title: Markers that are often confused
rows: rejects a claim / compares two things
Is it boring? On the contrary! / Rome is hot; Oslo, by contrast, is cool.
Hence the delay. / Therefore we waited.
opens a concession / returns to your point
Admittedly, it’s costly. That said, it works.
Stress raises cortisol; conversely, rest lowers it.
He quit — or rather, he was asked to leave.
Besides, it’s free. / Moreover, it is free.

grammar.sound: Sentence-initial markers are usually followed by a short pause and spoken on a separate tone unit: “That SAID | …”, “ADmittedly | …”. ‘Hence’ and ‘thus’ in mid-sentence are not followed by a pause: “hence the DElay”.

grammar.name: Prepositional and phrasal verb nuance in formal writing
grammar.short: Formal register prefers precise verbs — but not every phrasal verb is informal.
grammar.rule: In formal writing, many informal phrasal verbs are replaced by single verbs of Latin origin (put off → postpone, find out → establish, cut down on → reduce). However, a large set of phrasal and prepositional verbs is neutral and standard in academic and professional prose (carry out, set out, point out, bring about, account for, give rise to, draw on, rule out). Prepositional verbs also require exact dependent prepositions, some with differences in meaning (consist of / in, result in / from), and allow formal relative clauses with the preposition at the front (the risks to which patients are exposed).
form: verb + dependent preposition + noun: The improvement resulted from regular exercise.
preposition + which / whom (formal relative): the conditions under which athletes train
neutral phrasal verb + object: The study set out to rule out other causes.
Informal → formal: cut down on → reduce · put off → postpone · find out → establish · go up → increase
notes: Neutral phrasal verbs are perfectly acceptable in reports: carry out, set out, point out, account for, rule out, draw on, bring about.
Meaning changes with the preposition: result in = cause; result from = be caused by. Consist of = be made of; consist in = have as its essence.
Formal relatives move the preposition forward: “the treatment to which she responded” rather than “the treatment she responded to”.
Some formal verbs need no preposition at all: “discuss the issue”, not ‘discuss about’; “enter the room”, not ‘enter into’.
Do not over-formalise: ‘commence’ for ‘start’ or ‘endeavour’ for ‘try’ in every sentence sounds stilted.
examples: The researchers set out to establish whether the injury rate had increased.
Poor sleep accounts for a significant proportion of workplace accidents.
These are the risks to which participants were exposed.
grammar.watch: “The rise in injuries resulted in poor coaching” is wrong — say “The rise in injuries resulted from poor coaching”: result from introduces the cause; result in introduces the effect.
grammar.deep: Register is not simply a matter of avoiding phrasal verbs. It is true that informal multi-word verbs often have single-word equivalents that sound more objective in reports (look into → investigate, set up → establish, get over → recover from, deal with → address). But academic and professional English relies heavily on a core of neutral phrasal and prepositional verbs — carry out research, point out a flaw, rule out a cause, bring about change, draw on evidence, account for variation, give rise to complications — and replacing these with rarer Latinate verbs can make writing pompous. The C2 skill is to choose the most precise verb for the meaning and the reader. Prepositional verbs add a second layer: the preposition is fixed and sometimes meaningful (consist of / consist in, result in / result from, differ from / differ in, attribute something to, comply with, refrain from). Finally, formal style favours fronting the preposition in relative clauses and questions — “the extent to which”, “the conditions under which”, “With whom did you consult?” — though stranding remains correct and natural in less formal contexts.

The extent to which stress contributes to illness remains disputed.

fix.right: The programme consists of four workshops.

fix.right: Staff were asked to reduce overtime and the meeting was postponed.
fix.why: In a formal report, precise single verbs replace informal phrasal verbs.

drill.name: Register shift
drill.prompt: Rewrite each sentence for a formal report, replacing the informal verb or correcting the preposition. Keep neutral phrasal verbs where they are the best choice.

The manager put off the wellbeing survey until next year.
Most people got over the virus in a week.
The new rota has resulted from fewer accidents.
These are the people we worked with during the study.

It’s acceptable, but ‘we investigated the complaints’ is more precise.
And ‘carried out a survey’? Should I change that too?
No, that’s standard. Just check the prepositions: the factors to which the decline can be attributed, not ‘attributed for’.

be different in a particular aspect

grammar.sound: In phrasal verbs the particle is stressed — “carry OUT”, “rule OUT” — whereas in prepositional verbs the verb is stressed and the preposition is weak: “ACcount for”, “reSULT from” /frəm/. Stressing ‘from’ in ‘result from’ sounds contrastive.

speaking.text: Talk for two minutes about a time you or someone you know took a calculated risk with health, sport or work. Use at least three future-in-the-past forms (was going to, was about to, would later, was to have).

With a partner, you are designing a wellbeing programme for a sedentary office of 200 people with a small budget. Discuss these options — standing desks, mental-health days, a cycling scheme, free counselling, a sports league — and agree on two, linking your arguments with admittedly, that said, by contrast and hence.

Should people who take extreme risks (free solo climbing, base jumping) pay for their own rescue and medical care? Has modern society become too risk-averse, especially with children? Respond to your partner and give examples.

This house believes that professional sport does more harm than good to athletes’ bodies and minds. Use sporting metaphors (a level playing field, move the goalposts, throw in the towel) in your arguments.

tips: To look forward from the past, shift future forms back: will → would, is going to → was going to, is to → was to, is about to → was about to.
‘Was to have + past participle’ always signals a plan that did not happen: “The race was to have started at dawn.”
Use ‘on the contrary’ only to reject a statement; to compare two things, use ‘by contrast’ or ‘conversely’.
Common slip: ‘discuss about’ and ‘result in’ for a cause — write ‘discuss the risks’ and ‘the injury resulted from overtraining’.

quiz.q: The final ___ in Medellín, but it was moved to Cali at the last minute.
quiz.explain: ‘Was to have + past participle’ describes an arrangement that did not happen; the passive is needed because the final is held by someone.

test.q: That afternoon she met the coach who ___ change her life.
test.explain: Narrative ‘would’ describes a later event from the narrator’s point of view.

test.q: We were just ___ leave for the hospital when the contractions stopped.
test.explain: ‘Be about to + base verb’ describes something imminent at that past moment.

test.q: This injury ___ end her career, although no one knew it at the time.
test.explain: ‘Was to’ expresses destiny known to the narrator in hindsight.

test.q: Choose the sentence that means the operation did NOT take place.
options: The operation was to take place on Monday.
The operation would take place on Monday.
The operation was to have taken place on Monday.
The operation took place on Monday.
test.explain: ‘Was to have + past participle’ always signals an unfulfilled plan.

test.q: The drug isn’t harmful to the liver; ___, it may protect it.
test.explain: ‘On the contrary’ rejects the previous statement and asserts the opposite.

test.q: Funding for the clinic was cut by forty per cent; ___ the long waiting lists.
test.explain: ‘Hence’ can be followed by a noun phrase without a verb.

test.q: Granted, the programme is expensive. ___, it has halved sick leave.
test.explain: After a concession, ‘even so’ returns to the main argument.

test.q: The study ___ to determine whether walking meetings reduce stress.
test.explain: ‘Set out to’ = to begin with a specific aim; it is neutral and standard in reports.

test.q: The increase in knee injuries ___ the switch to artificial pitches.
test.explain: ‘Result from’ introduces the cause; ‘result in’ would introduce the effect.

test.q: Choose the most formal version.
options: These are the risks to which patients are exposed.
These are the risks patients are exposed to.
These are the risks which patients are exposed.
These are the risks to that patients are exposed.
test.explain: Formal relatives front the preposition before ‘which’ (never before ‘that’).

test.q: Years of night shifts had ___ on his health.
test.explain: To take its / their toll on = to have a gradual harmful effect.

test.q: Every time the nurses meet their targets, management ___.
options: gives a clean bill of health
test.explain: To move the goalposts = to change the rules or targets unfairly.

dynamics.name: Sliding doors
dynamics.how: Each student tells the story of a near miss (real or invented) in sport, travel or health. The partner retells it in the third person with hindsight, using was about to, was going to, was to have and narrative would, and the original teller corrects any facts.
dynamics.payoff: Moves future-in-the-past forms from recognition into fluent narration.

dynamics.name: Connector auction
dynamics.how: The teacher reads pairs of sentences on wellbeing. Teams bid points for the right to link them with the most precise marker (on the contrary, by contrast, hence, that said, if anything). A wrong function loses the points; a precise choice with a correct summary noun doubles them.
dynamics.payoff: Rewards precision in choosing between near-synonymous markers.

dynamics.name: Report editor
dynamics.how: Groups receive a deliberately informal paragraph from a wellbeing report full of phrasal verbs and stranded prepositions. They edit it for formal register, deciding which phrasal verbs to keep (carry out, point out) and which to replace. Groups compare versions and justify each change.
dynamics.payoff: Shows that formal register is about precision, not about eliminating every phrasal verb.

writing.title: Report on the Move More pilot programme
writing.brief: You coordinated a six-month pilot wellbeing programme at your workplace or college. Write a report for the management committee describing what was planned, what actually happened, the results and the problems encountered, and recommending whether the programme should be extended.
writing.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la dirección sobre un programa piloto de bienestar: qué se planificó, qué ocurrió, resultados, problemas y recomendaciones.
criteria: Report conventions: a title, clear headings, an impersonal and objective tone, and specific recommendations.
Three future-in-the-past forms (was to, was to have, was going to, would) to contrast plans with outcomes.
At least five precise discourse markers or summary nouns linking ideas across sentences and paragraphs.
Formal verb choice, including two neutral phrasal verbs (carry out, rule out, account for) and one fronted preposition in a relative clause.
writing.model:
Report on the Move More Pilot Programme

Introduction
The purpose of this report is to evaluate the six-month Move More programme, which was set up to reduce sedentary behaviour among administrative staff, and to recommend whether it should be extended.

Planned activities
The programme was to consist of three elements: standing desks, weekly walking meetings and a lunchtime exercise class. A cycle-to-work scheme was also to have been launched in March; however, it was postponed owing to delays with the supplier and did not take place.

Results
A survey carried out at the end of the pilot indicates that participation exceeded expectations. Seventy per cent of staff used the standing desks regularly, and reported back pain fell by almost a third. This improvement cannot be accounted for by seasonal factors alone, since a comparison group showed no similar change. Walking meetings, by contrast, proved less popular: many managers had intended to hold them weekly but found that heavy rain and tight schedules made this impractical.

Problems
The main difficulty was the exercise class, to which only a small group of already active employees were drawn. In other words, it largely failed to reach the people for whom the programme was designed. Admittedly, the class was held at an inconvenient time. Even so, it seems unlikely that a change of timetable alone would have transformed attendance. Feedback also suggests that several employees would have attended had they not been worried about appearing unproductive.

Recommendations
It is recommended that the programme be extended for a further year and that:
• the standing desks be made available to all departments;
• the exercise class be replaced by short, optional desk-based sessions;
• the cycle scheme be launched as originally planned.
These measures would build on the programme’s successes while addressing its weaknesses.

homework.title: Plans and outcomes
homework.task: Write a 150-word account of a plan you or your family made that did not work out as expected (a trip, a training goal, a health resolution). Use four future-in-the-past forms, including one ‘was to have + past participle’. Then rewrite the final paragraph in formal register as if for a report, adding three discourse markers and one summary noun.

board: Top: a timeline with a flag marked THEN (past viewpoint) and arrows pointing forward — would · was going to · was to · was about to · was to have + p.p. (✗ didn’t happen).
A red box: “on the contrary” for comparisons crossed out → “by contrast”; and “resulted in” for a cause crossed out → “resulted from”.
Middle: four marker families in columns — CONCEDE (admittedly, granted) → RETURN (that said, even so) · CORRECT (on the contrary, if anything) · CONSEQUENCE (hence + NOUN, thus + clause).
Bottom left: INFORMAL → FORMAL — cut down on → reduce · put off → postpone · find out → establish; KEEP: carry out, rule out, account for.
Bottom right: the formal relative — the conditions UNDER WHICH… · the people FOR WHOM…

units.title: TIME, CHANGE AND LEGACY
units.theme: The future, nostalgia, heritage and what we leave behind

overview.intro: The final unit looks both ways: back at what previous generations have left us, and forward at what we will leave behind. To talk about time at C2 you need future forms with fine shades of meaning, comparisons that measure change precisely, and the proverbs and fixed expressions through which every culture passes on its wisdom — together with a sense of when they suit the register and when they sound like cliché.
goals: Discuss heritage, nostalgia, change and legacy with precise vocabulary and time idioms.
Project into the future with the future perfect continuous, be to, be on the verge of and be due to.
Measure change with nuanced comparatives and use proverbs and fixed expressions in the right register.
overview.outcome: By the end you can write a CPE-style essay that summarises and evaluates two texts on heritage and progress, comparing their views precisely and reaching a reasoned conclusion of your own.

vocab.def: all the people who will live in the future.
vocab.use: Uncountable and formal, usually with “for”: “preserved for posterity”. It never takes an article.
examples: The letters have been digitised and preserved for posterity.
Posterity will judge whether we acted wisely.
vocab.colloc: for posterity · preserve / record for posterity · posterity will judge

vocab.def: an event or period that marks an important change in history or in someone’s life.
vocab.use: Countable; very often attributive: “a watershed moment / year / election”.
examples: The invention of the printing press was a watershed in European history.
For many families, the pandemic was a watershed moment.
vocab.colloc: a watershed moment · mark a watershed · a historical watershed

vocab.def: lasting for a very short time.
vocab.use: Formal; common in discussions of art, fashion and digital culture. Noun: ephemera (short-lived printed items such as tickets and posters).
examples: Social media fame is notoriously ephemeral.
The museum collects ephemera such as bus tickets and concert flyers.
vocab.colloc: ephemeral pleasures · the ephemeral nature of · an ephemeral trend

vocab.def: belonging to a time in the past that no longer exists.
vocab.use: Used before a noun and often nostalgic: “a bygone era / age”. The idiom “let bygones be bygones” means to forgive past disagreements.
examples: The hotel’s ballroom evokes a bygone era of elegance.
After years of feuding, the brothers decided to let bygones be bygones.
vocab.colloc: a bygone era / age · bygone days · let bygones be bygones

vocab.def: to be a sign that something important is about to happen.
vocab.use: Formal and journalistic: “herald a new era / the end of / the arrival of”. Also: “be heralded as” (= publicly praised as).
examples: The first smartphone heralded a new era in communication.
The treaty was heralded as a turning point for the region.
vocab.colloc: herald a new era · herald the end of · be heralded as

vocab.def: to make something, especially something bad, continue to exist.
vocab.use: Often critical: “perpetuate a myth / inequality / stereotypes / a cycle”. Noun: perpetuation.
examples: Old textbooks perpetuated a romanticised version of colonial history.
Without intervention, poverty perpetuates itself across generations.
vocab.colloc: perpetuate a myth · perpetuate inequality · perpetuate a cycle of

vocab.def: to remind people of something in the past, or to talk about the past, often longingly.
vocab.use: Not separable. Things can hark back (“The design harks back to the 1950s”) and so can people (“He’s always harking back to his schooldays”).
examples: The architecture harks back to the city’s colonial past.
Politicians who hark back to a golden age rarely say exactly when it was.
vocab.colloc: hark back to a golden age · hark back to the past · design that harks back to

vocab.def: to be full of a particular quality, especially history or tradition.
vocab.use: Usually passive: “steeped in history / tradition / mystery”. The image is of tea soaking in water.
examples: Cartagena is a city steeped in history.
The ceremony is steeped in centuries-old tradition.
vocab.colloc: steeped in history · steeped in tradition · steeped in folklore

vocab.term: to stand the test of time
vocab.def: to remain popular, useful or valid for a long time.
vocab.use: Used about ideas, buildings, works of art and relationships. Often in the present perfect: “has stood the test of time”.
examples: Few pop songs from that decade have stood the test of time.
Roman roads have stood the test of time remarkably well.
vocab.colloc: stand / withstand the test of time · has stood the test of time

vocab.def: in an unrealistically positive way, especially when remembering the past.
vocab.use: Also ‘rose-coloured spectacles / glasses’. Common with “see / view / look back on something through…”.
examples: We tend to view our childhood through rose-tinted glasses.
Nostalgic politicians look back at the 1950s through rose-tinted glasses.
vocab.colloc: look back / view the past through rose-tinted glasses

vocab.def: to have a lasting effect on someone or something.
vocab.use: The possessive changes with the subject: “She left her mark on the city.” A stronger version is “leave an indelible mark”.
examples: The architect left her mark on the skyline of three cities.
The war left an indelible mark on a whole generation.
vocab.colloc: leave your / its mark on · leave an indelible / lasting mark

vocab.def: eventually, when the right moment comes, often after a long wait.
vocab.use: Formal, slightly literary; can sound evasive when used by officials to avoid giving a date.
examples: In the fullness of time, historians will reassess her legacy.
The minister said details would be released in the fullness of time.
vocab.colloc: all will be revealed in the fullness of time

grammar.name: Advanced future forms: future perfect continuous, be to, be on the verge of, be due to
grammar.short: Durations up to a future point, official plans, imminent change and scheduled events.
grammar.rule: The future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) measures the duration of an activity up to a point in the future. ‘Be to + base verb’ expresses official arrangements and instructions, typical of news and formal notices. ‘Be on the verge / brink / point of + noun or -ing’ describes something very close to happening. ‘Be due to + base verb’ (or ‘be due’ + time) describes something scheduled. ‘Be set to’ and ‘be poised to’ are journalistic forms for likely or imminent events.
form: will have been + -ing (+ duration): By 2030, the museum will have been operating for a century.
be (not) to + base verb: The statue is to be moved to the city archive next spring.
be on the verge / brink / point of + noun / -ing: The language is on the verge of disappearing.
be due to + base verb / be due + time: The new heritage centre is due to open in May.
be set to / be poised to + base verb: The old quarter is set to become a World Heritage site.
notes: The future perfect continuous needs a duration and a future reference point: “By June she will have been restoring the fresco for five years.”
‘Be to’ is formal and impersonal; in headlines it often loses ‘be’: “PM TO VISIT FLOOD AREA”.
‘Be to’ can also express an order or prohibition: “You are not to touch the exhibits.”
‘On the brink of’ suggests danger or disaster; ‘on the verge of’ is neutral; ‘on the point of’ stresses immediacy.
‘Due’ is about timetables and schedules, not intentions: say “The train is due at six”, not ‘I am due to visit my aunt’ for a personal plan.
examples: By the time the cathedral is finished, they will have been building it for over a hundred years.
The archive is to be digitised over the next five years.
Several traditional crafts are on the brink of extinction.
grammar.watch: “By next year I will be working here for ten years” is wrong — say “By next year I will have been working here for ten years”: a duration up to a future point needs the future perfect continuous.
grammar.deep: English has no single future tense; it has a repertoire of forms, each foregrounding a different relationship between the present and what lies ahead. At C2 four of these are worth mastering. The future perfect continuous stands at a future point and looks back along a duration: it is the natural choice for anniversaries, milestones and complaints (“By Friday I’ll have been waiting for a month”). ‘Be to’ presents the future as an arrangement made by an authority, hence its frequency in news reports and official communication (“The site is to be closed to visitors”); it can also convey destiny or obligation. ‘Be on the verge / brink / point of’ places an event just ahead, with ‘brink’ adding a sense of peril. ‘Be due to’ ties the event to a schedule or expectation, and ‘be set to’ and ‘be poised to’ are the press’s preferred ways of saying something is likely and imminent. Because these forms carry register as well as time, choosing between ‘The museum will close’, ‘The museum is to close’, ‘The museum is due to close’ and ‘The museum is set to close’ is a decision about source, certainty and formality as much as about the future.

grammar.name: Comparative structures with nuance (the more…the more, nowhere near, every bit as)
grammar.short: Measure differences precisely: a little, a lot, not at all, or exactly as much.
grammar.rule: C2 comparison goes beyond ‘more than’ and ‘as … as’. The double comparative (the + comparative …, the + comparative …) shows two things changing together. Large differences are marked with far, much, considerably, a great deal, nowhere near as … as and not nearly as … as; small ones with slightly, marginally, a fraction, not quite as … as. Equality is emphasised with every bit as, just as and no less … than. ‘No + comparative + than’ means ‘just as (little)’, and ‘all the + comparative + for / because’ explains why something is even more so.
form: The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause: The older a building gets, the more it costs to maintain.
nowhere near / not nearly + as + adjective + as: Digital archives are nowhere near as durable as we assume.
every bit / just + as + adjective + as: The new library is every bit as impressive as the old one.
all the + comparative + for / because: The victory was all the sweeter for being so unexpected.
no + comparative + than: The replica is no less valuable to scholars than the original.
notes: In the double comparative, the comparative word moves to the front with its noun or adjective: “The more money we spend, the less we preserve” — not ‘The more we spend money’.
Short forms are common in speech: “The sooner, the better.” “The more, the merrier.”
‘Nowhere near’ is informal to neutral; ‘not nearly’ and ‘far less … than’ are more formal alternatives.
‘No better than’ is critical (= just as bad); ‘no less … than’ is emphatic (= equally): “She is no less a pioneer than her mother.”
Use ‘by far’ and ‘easily’ with superlatives: “by far the oldest building”, “easily the most visited site”.
examples: The longer we wait, the harder it will be to save the archive.
Today’s cities are nowhere near as dangerous as they were a century ago.
Oral traditions are every bit as important as written records.
grammar.watch: “The more it gets older, the more it is valuable” is wrong — say “The older it gets, the more valuable it is”: in the double comparative the comparative adjective moves to the front with the.
grammar.deep: Talking about change is talking about comparison, and C2 speakers are expected to quantify it with precision. The double comparative expresses proportional change — two variables rising or falling together — and has a strict word order: each half begins with ‘the’ followed immediately by the comparative element and whatever belongs with it (“The more tourists a town attracts, the less authentic it can feel”). The second clause is often reduced when the verb is obvious (“The bigger, the better”). Around ‘as … as’ and ‘-er than’, modifiers do the measuring: far, much, a great deal, considerably and significantly for large gaps; slightly, marginally, a little and a fraction for small ones; nowhere near and not nearly for a wide gap in the negative; every bit, just and quite for emphatic equality. Two constructions frequently confuse advanced learners. ‘No + comparative + than’ denies any difference and usually carries an evaluative edge (“The new policy is no better than the old one” = equally bad). ‘All the + comparative’ adds a reason that intensifies the comparison (“The achievement is all the more remarkable given her age”). Used well, these structures allow arguments about progress and decline to be both precise and persuasive.

dialogue.line: People say life was simpler in our grandparents’ day.
Simpler, maybe, but nowhere near as comfortable. The further back you go, the harder daily life was.
Still, their communities were every bit as rich as ours — richer, perhaps.
True. And their stories are all the more precious because so few were written down.

grammar.sound: In the double comparative both halves are stressed on the comparative and there is a rise at the end of the first half and a fall at the end of the second: “The MORE we learn ↗ | the LESS we know ↘”. In ‘every bit as’, ‘bit’ carries strong stress.

grammar.name: Proverbs, fixed expressions and register at C2
grammar.short: Frozen phrases carry culture — but they must suit the context.
grammar.rule: Proverbs (Rome wasn’t built in a day), binomials (sooner or later), idioms and other fixed expressions are frozen: their words and word order cannot normally be changed. Proverbs are often shortened when the listener can complete them (‘When in Rome…’) or playfully adapted. Register matters: many proverbs and informal idioms sound folksy or clichéd in formal essays, so C2 writers use them sparingly, signal them (‘as the saying goes’), or replace them with formal fixed expressions (to all intents and purposes, by the same token).
form: As the saying goes, + proverb: As the saying goes, Rome wasn’t built in a day.
Truncated proverb + …: Well, every cloud… — at least we found out early.
Binomial (fixed order): sooner or later · by and large · tried and tested · part and parcel
Formal register: to all intents and purposes · in the fullness of time · by the same token
Informal register: at the end of the day · when all’s said and done · the be-all and end-all
notes: Binomials have a fixed order that cannot be reversed: “sooner or later”, “odds and ends”, “law and order”, never ‘later or sooner’.
Proverbs are often truncated in speech: “Too many cooks…”, “Speak of the devil…”, “The early bird…”.
In formal essays, avoid stacking idioms; one well-placed fixed expression is more effective than several clichés.
Creative adaptation is a C2 skill, but only once the original is mastered: “Rome wasn’t digitised in a day.”
Know the meaning, not just the words: “The proof of the pudding is in the eating” means you judge something by testing it.
examples: As the saying goes, you can’t put an old head on young shoulders.
By and large, the restoration has been a success.
To all intents and purposes, the old town is now a museum.
grammar.watch: “later or sooner” is wrong — say “sooner or later”: binomials have a fixed order that cannot be reversed.
grammar.deep: Fixed expressions are one of the clearest markers of the C2 learner, because they cannot be generated by rules: they must be known. They range from fully frozen proverbs (“Don’t count your chickens before they hatch”) to semi-fixed frames (“the be-all and end-all of…”) and binomials whose order is conventional rather than logical (“black and white”, “bread and butter”, “sooner or later”). Their meanings are frequently non-literal, and their grammar is fossilised — “Far be it from me”, “Be that as it may”, “Come what may” preserve archaic subjunctives. Native speakers handle them flexibly: they truncate proverbs (“When in Rome…”), allude to them (“a classic case of too many cooks”) and twist them for effect (“Rome wasn’t digitised in a day”). The second skill is register. Proverbs and many idioms belong to conversation, journalism and informal argument; in an academic essay they can sound clichéd or patronising. Formal writing has its own set of fixed expressions — to all intents and purposes, by the same token, in the fullness of time, first and foremost, last but not least — that do similar work without the folksy tone. Choosing the right expression for the reader is precisely the ‘finer shades of meaning’ that the CEFR expects at C2.

speaking.text: Talk for two minutes on this question: “Should cities preserve their historic centres exactly as they are, or allow them to evolve?” Use at least two nuanced comparatives (nowhere near as, every bit as, the more … the more) and one future form from the unit.

With a partner, you are choosing five objects for a time capsule to be opened in 2126. Discuss what each would tell future generations about our time, using the future perfect continuous and be to (“By then, people will have been…”, “The capsule is to be opened…”), and agree on a final list.

Do we look back on the past through rose-tinted glasses? What legacy should your generation leave? Is digital culture too ephemeral to stand the test of time? Respond to your partner and give examples.
This house believes that proverbs are outdated and should no longer be taught. Defend or attack the motion, using at least three fixed expressions and commenting on their register.

tips: Use the future perfect continuous for a duration up to a future point: “By 2030 the museum will have been operating for a century.”
In the double comparative, put the comparative right after ‘the’: “The older it gets, the more valuable it is.”
Binomials and proverbs are frozen — sooner or later, tried and tested, Rome wasn’t built in a day — and most proverbs are too informal for an academic essay.
Common slip: ‘every bit as … as’ and ‘nowhere near as … as’ are completed by ‘as’, never by ‘than’.

dynamics.name: Time capsule press conference
dynamics.how: Each group announces the contents of a time capsule at a mock press conference. They must use be to (official plans), be due to (schedule), the future perfect continuous (durations by the opening date) and be set to. The audience asks follow-up questions and notes every advanced future form used.
dynamics.payoff: Puts four future forms with different registers into one coherent, realistic genre.

dynamics.name: Then and now auction
dynamics.how: Teams receive cards with pairs (letters / emails, village life / city life, vinyl / streaming). They compete to produce the most precise comparison, scoring extra points for nowhere near, every bit as, no less … than, all the more … for and correct double comparatives.
dynamics.payoff: Rewards precision in measuring difference, not just stating it.

dynamics.name: Proverb surgery
dynamics.how: Pairs receive ten proverbs cut in half and reassemble them, then decide for each whether it would suit a conversation, a newspaper column or an academic essay. Finally, they adapt one proverb creatively for a headline about heritage or technology.
dynamics.payoff: Develops both accuracy with frozen forms and sensitivity to register.

writing.title: Heritage and progress: summarising two views
writing.genre: Ensayo (resumen y evaluación de dos textos)
writing.brief: Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts, using your own words throughout as far as possible, and including your own ideas. Text 1 (“Keepers of Memory”) argues that historic buildings anchor a community’s identity and that once demolished they can never be replaced, although it admits that strict preservation can turn living cities into museums for tourists. Text 2 (“Cities Are Not Museums”) argues that every generation has the right to reshape its surroundings, that nostalgia distorts our view of the past, and that many celebrated buildings replaced older ones that were once equally loved.
writing.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe los puntos clave de dos textos sobre preservar el patrimonio o permitir el cambio urbano, con tus propias palabras y aportando tu opinión.
criteria: A concise, accurate summary of the key points of both texts in your own words, without copying phrases.
Evaluation of each argument, with your own ideas and a reasoned conclusion that weighs the two positions.
Nuanced comparison (nowhere near as, every bit as, the more … the more) and at least one advanced future form.
Formal academic register, with at most one carefully chosen fixed expression and cohesive linking between paragraphs.
writing.model:
Whether historic cities should be protected or allowed to evolve is a question that divides planners and residents alike. The two texts approach it from opposite directions, yet each contains a partial truth.

The first text maintains that old buildings are the physical memory of a community: they give people a sense of continuity, and once they are lost, nothing can bring them back. Its author nevertheless acknowledges a risk, namely that over-zealous preservation may leave historic centres frozen in time and given over almost entirely to tourism. The second text takes a more radical line. It contends that each generation is entitled to shape its own environment and that our attachment to the past is often sentimental rather than rational, pointing out that many of today’s cherished landmarks themselves replaced buildings that were once every bit as beloved.

In my view, the second writer is right to warn against nostalgia; we do tend to see the past through rose-tinted glasses. However, the argument is nowhere near as persuasive when applied to truly irreplaceable sites. A medieval cathedral and a 1970s car park are not equivalent, and treating all change as legitimate ignores the fact that demolition, unlike neglect, is irreversible.

The first text’s concern about ‘museum cities’ is, to my mind, the more useful insight. The more rigidly a centre is preserved, the less it serves the people who actually live there. The most promising approach, therefore, is adaptive reuse: keeping significant structures while allowing their functions to change. By the end of this century, many cities will have been experimenting with such compromises for decades, and posterity will judge which struck the right balance.

Then rewrite one paragraph in formal register, replacing any informal idioms.
